articles.title: What Russia Is Really Up To in Europe
articles.body:
What Russia Is Really Up To in Europe
Moscow doesn’t want a conventional war, but it is busy fighting a hybrid one.
On Russian state television, the Kremlin’s propagandists have for years threatened to bomb European capitals, even while the country’s diplomats insist that no such war is imminent. Lately, the denials have gotten hard to sustain, as European intelligence agencies have ascribed hundreds of clandestine sabotage operations—cyberattacks in Italy, arson in the United Kingdom, undersea-cable ruptures in the Baltic, severed pig heads left outside French mosques—to Russia.
U.S. intelligence assessments conclude that a conventional Russian attack on a NATO country is likely to happen sometime from this fall to 2029. But another possibility is that Moscow will remain content with sabotage and intimidation. This hybrid campaign is all the war Russia wants or needs—and stoking fear that Moscow just might directly strike Ukraine’s European allies is part of it.
If this is what Russian President Vladimir Putin is really up to in Europe, then he was telling the truth when he assured Trump this week that Russia has “no aggressive intentions against European statehood.” Moscow has not massed troops on any NATO member’s border. Rather, it has been sending a carefully calibrated message meant to persuade Europe to stop supporting Ukraine.
For Moscow, this has been a summer of setbacks in Ukraine. Russia stalled on the battlefield and sustained damage from thousands of Ukrainian long-range drones that plunged the country into fuel shortages. And so it escalated elsewhere in Europe: Fires broke out at ammunition plants in Italy, Bulgaria, and Estonia last month, and explosive-laden drones were discovered near a German power plant and at an airport in Leipzig, apparently intended to destroy Ukrainian cargo planes.
From the Kremlin’s point of view, Europe has been deepening its involvement in Ukraine. At the beginning of the full-scale war, Europe donated weapons to Ukraine from its own stocks. Within two years, European governments were paying Ukrainian factories to manufacture arms. Last year, Fire Point, a Ukrainian missile-and-drone manufacturer, announced that it would establish a solid-fuel production plant in Denmark, making it the first such arms company to expand production abroad. Today, Europe provides the bulk of financial assistance to Kyiv. It has also become Ukraine’s secure production base—Ukrainian weapons are manufactured in Germany, Britain, the Netherlands, Norway, Sweden, France, Romania, and Spain.
Because Kyiv is attacking Russia’s rear, it’s logical to worry that Moscow will attack Ukraine’s. Russian security services are almost certainly capable of carrying out a lethal attack on European soil. And Western war games have entertained many possibilities along those lines. Among them are a limited Russian incursion into a small Baltic town that has a Russian-speaking population; a full-scale invasion of the Baltic states, launched simultaneously from Belarus and Kaliningrad, Russia’s European exclave, to cut them off from the rest of Europe; the rapid creation of an impenetrable drone “kill zone” on European soil; and a strategic blockade of the Baltic Sea. Some of these scenarios are plausible; others would require hundreds of thousands of Russian troops to crisscross Europe.
Russia has not visibly prepared for any such scenario, however. Instead, it continues to wage its hybrid war—which European security services continue to thwart. Such are the headlines: Drones carrying explosives are discovered in Leipzig, improvised explosive devices are found near a German power plant, and flying objects are spotted near airports.
Moscow may not much care that these operations get foiled. In a way, the effect is similar to that of Russia’s harassment of journalists and embassy workers stationed in Moscow: Things in their apartment get rearranged, signs of eavesdropping are deliberately made obvious, or a window is left open in the middle of winter. Such interference conveys a sinister message: We’re watching you. We have access to you. You are not in control. But it’s still different from blowing up the apartment.
Putin has generally chosen to fully engage the Russian military only in conflicts that he feels (rightly or, in the case of Ukraine, wrongly) assured of winning. This does not describe any hypothetical attack on the Baltic states, which have heavily fortified borders, conduct regular military exercises, and spend 5 percent of their GDP on defense.
That’s not to mention the thousands of British, German, and Canadian troops stationed near the Baltics as part of NATO’s Enhanced Forward Presence. Moscow may be willing to wager that the United States won’t intervene should Russia attack Estonia. But Russia would then find itself at war with numerous European states armed with submarines, aircraft carriers, fifth-generation fighter jets, long-range cruise missiles, and even nuclear weapons—all while it was still fighting in Ukraine.
Russia’s hybrid war has not succeeded in its likely purpose: stopping weapons, money, and intelligence from flowing into Ukraine from Europe. Kyiv has more arms, funds, and—judging by its strikes on Russian soil—intelligence than ever before. Neither has the Russian campaign taken out a European satellite that supplies Ukraine with intelligence, say, or destroyed a shipment of Patriot missiles.
But Putin persists in this campaign for a reason. Through inexpensive means, expendable operatives, and a steady stream of chilling leaks, the Kremlin has millions of Westerners braced for it to wage a full-scale war against Europe. Regardless of whether that war is likely, Putin will be demanding concessions in exchange for bringing it to an end.

articles.title: Inside the IDF Military Intelligence's crusade to block Iran from getting nukes - exclusive
articles.body:
From the mid-1990s until August 2024, a running line of top Mossad and IDF officials made it their mission to block Iran from getting a nuclear weapon.
When Shlomi Binder was sworn in as the Military Intelligence chief in August 2024, he took up the baton and he and his team of top intelligence officials have pursued the crusade with tremendous tenacity.
Since August 2024, the IDF intelligence team under Binder, along with the Mossad, the air force, and others has managed the bombing of Natanz, Isfahan, and dozens of other sites, and provided the critical intelligence used by the US to bomb Fordow in June 2025.
This period also led to the direct assassination of Ayatollah Ali Khamenei and the dissection of Iran’s ballistic missile and wider military apparatus.
To be sure, the air force dropped the bombs, and the Mossad delivered on key special missions. But if Israel struck Iran around a staggering 4,000 times in June 2025 and around an unthinkable 18,000 times in 2026, the intelligence for well over 90% of those strikes came from Binder and his juggernaut IDF intelligence teams.
Where has IDF intelligence’s crusade left Iran’s nuclear weapons program, five months after the 2026 war and 15 months after the 2025 war?
The Jerusalem Post has learned that the positives are that Iran currently has no centrifuges enriching uranium, all or most of its more enriched uranium is not yet easily accessible, and that most of the regime’s nuclear facilities were destroyed or forced out of operation by the 2025-2026 strikes.
There has been no period of time in decades where enrichment was brought down to zero.
For decades, its facilities expanded and never really contracted, and while operations attributed to the Mossad managed to take one or more facilities offline for temporary periods, at no point was the whole active program broken or shuttered.
Even during “pause” periods from 2003 to 2007 and from 2015 to 2018, large aspects of Iran’s nuclear program were frozen, not broken, and new aspects were almost always being built, even if under the radar.
However, the Post has learned that despite these achievements, future concerns are greater than hoped for right after the 2025-2026 operations.
While the vast majority of Iran’s 20,000 centrifuge fleet was destroyed or rendered unusable, a not insignificant number of centrifuges survived deep underground.
Moreover, multiple sources have expressed concern to the Post that even if only a few hundred advanced IR-6 centrifuges (for enriching uranium) can be salvaged and hooked up again at some medium-term point, that could be enough, at some later undefined point, to secretly weaponize enough uranium for a bomb.
Also, multiple sources are worried that the Iranians could pull off some kind of clandestine digging mission to extract their more enriched uranium from under rubble and underground in a way that sidesteps US and other surveillance.
Regular satellite reports by the Institute for Science and International Security and others show that Iran has added structures on an ongoing basis to block certain areas from continuous satellite coverage.
These same open-source reports have noted the Iranians digging in a variety of areas, sometimes not all that close to the main parts of a nuclear facility that was struck.
Digging underground from a distance could take months or years to smuggle out the 60% enriched uranium, or in some areas 20% enriched uranium. But only maybe around one tenth would need to be clandestinely transferred to have a basis for a nuclear weapon.
Binder’s view is not that Iran is likely to outwit American and Israeli intelligence, but neither does he want to underestimate or discount Iranians’ often surprising and powerful resourcefulness.
That means that the key to the whole picture to some extent is again shifting from uranium enrichment to weapons group issues.
One of the highest priorities – but less reported aspects – of the Israeli attacks on Iran’s nuclear program sites was hitting not only the enrichment facilities, but also the facilities for converting enriched uranium into uranium metal and into hemispheres for use on a nuclear warhead.
Without these and other items, even large quantities of weaponized uranium will do Iran no good, because it will not be able to deliver the uranium 1,000 or more kilometers away in Israeli territory.
The Post understands that thwarting Tehran from rebuilding such weapons group facilities is one of Binder’s top focuses, and so far the regime has not made any serious progress on the issue.
All of this leaves a highly complex picture where the nuclear program is far more damaged than some critics have said, but where there are more gaps in that damage than top Israeli officials, political or defense, admitted right after each round of fighting.
Iran’s nuclear program was set back by some years, and its ability to reconstitute it was also set back. Yet in some ways, Iranian ingenuity has kept the threat alive and able to return, even if less broadly and with great difficulty.
Pickaxe Mountain
Major news was made in a July 13 interview on the Hugh Hewitt Show, when US President Donald Trump said, “We’re going to take out Pickaxe Mountain. Tell the Iranians to be ready,” while in another breath said, “We see no activity there.”
Pickaxe Mountain, once operational, will be the deepest underground nuclear facility the Iranians have ever built, significantly deeper than even the Fordow underground nuclear facility. It is hotly debated whether even the extremely unique and expensive 30,000-pound Massive Ordnance Penetrator mega bunker buster bomb could penetrate it.
The second part of Trump’s statement about Iran’s nuclear facility at Pickaxe Mountain – that there is no activity there; or as the hawkish Institute for Science and International Security has put it, that the facility is still not operational – is the major reason that neither the US president nor Israel has ordered a strike to date, despite his first statement promising to attack.
Across the board, top US and Israeli defense sources told the Post in classified briefings earlier in the summer that there was no current threat from the site, and that the best reason to target it would, at most, be to eliminate a potential future threat.
All of these views contradicted the stunning July 14 reports by The Wall Street Journal and CNN that Israeli intelligence had told the US that Iran had moved thousands of centrifuges and also enriched uranium to Pickaxe Mountain.
In an article on the issue on July 21, none of the several sources that had told the Post that there was no current threat at Pickaxe Mountain clarified the matter, despite several attempts by the Post to get to the bottom of the dispute.
Since then, the Post has more recently clarified the issue.
Both the Mossad and IDF intelligence view Pickaxe Mountain as a strategic threat that must be removed at some point, because it is so difficult to attack.
In addition, both agencies highly prefer to do so before it becomes operational and before the Iranians manage to move sufficient assets there to operate centrifuges and enrich uranium.
The Post understands that what occurred in July was that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu hoped to get Trump to strike Iran, with Pickaxe Mountain being one of the top-of-the-line potential targets.
Senior Israeli defense officials leaned into the issue also because they thought it might be a unique chance to finally rid themselves of the hovering potential threat.
It remains somewhat unclear whether Israeli political officials exaggerated how operational Pickaxe Mountain was, whether one or more Israeli defense officials assisted with this, or whether American officials afterward exaggerated what they had been told.
But as of early September, the Post understands that Pickaxe Mountain remains high on Binder’s list of concerns, but that the facility is still not operational.
One recent change is that some Israeli officials have voiced to the Post greater confidence than in the past about the ability of allied air forces to disable the facility, even if destroying it might not be possible.
All of this highlights that Binder’s view is that the Iranian threat has not passed, that any agreement that gives Tehran the right to enrich to 3.67%, like the 2015 deal, would keep the threat alive, and that Israel must be ready for the real possibility of needing to attack the Islamic Republic at some point in the not-so-distant future.
What about recent talk of Russia providing Iran with supersonic missiles which will be harder for Israel to shoot down?
No one is getting too detailed on this issue yet, and some of the challenges are just starting to evolve, but it does not yet seem to be at the top of the IDF’s list of concerns about Iran.
Regime change
While Netanyahu, Defense Minister Israel Katz, and Mossad Director Roman Gofman still mention regime change publicly and privately, that term has mostly disappeared from the IDF lexicon.
IDF officials are no less enthusiastic about the idea in theory. Regime change has the best chance of promising a long-term end to Iran threatening the Jewish state.
But IDF high command officials, including Binder, were highly skeptical that the regime would easily and quickly fall when they went to war with the Islamic Republic in early 2026, and they believe the chances of this occurring are even more dubious now.
Neither Binder nor other top IDF officials favored the plan to try to use the Kurds to foment an internal rebellion.
While Netanyahu and top officials in the Mossad believed that, along with other moves which Trump vetoed, supporting a Kurdish internal insurgency could potentially radically alter the playing field, Binder and others viewed this move as possibly propping up the regime.
The majority of Iran – regime supporters and opposition – is Shi’ite.
Just as the Kurds often see the Iranian Shi’ites as outsider oppressors, many of the Shi’ites, even those who hate the regime, hate or distrust the Iranian Kurds even more.
In other words, Binder and others in the IDF high command worried that bringing the Kurds in as an officially Israel-US sponsored kingmaker could lead to the largest group of opposition Shi’ites changing sides back into the hands of the regime.
They also noted other major issues, such as that dropping lots of bombs makes protesting harder.
While some said that careful coordination could lead to enabling protests to grow by only bombing regime oppression forces, this never really occurred in a significant way, and most protesters were just too scared and stayed home.
Of those who did not stay home, Binder and the IDF high command would note that many of the bravest protesters were killed during the largest fight between the protesters and the regime over January 8-9 or were killed or tortured after the main war ended on April 7.
None of this means that Binder and the IDF have given up on regime change.
But they believe that it will take longer than some in the Mossad believe, and compared to Netanyahu’s promises, and that in the immediate short term it may even be difficult to make progress, with progress waiting for the medium term when protesters regain their daring.
Despite these truths, Binder and the IDF high command were highly optimistic about the jump in pressure on Iran in late August-early September, with the pace of economic deterioration jumping significantly.
They hope this elevated economic pressure will give the US the upper hand in the standoff over the Strait of Hormuz and the nuclear issue.
All of the talk about the US has also crystallized a realization from Israeli intelligence: instead of leaving the Middle East, Trump has put the American military on the front lines of managing most of Israel’s conflicts with its neighbors.
With one brief 24-hour exception, Israel and Iran have not fought since April 7, whereas Washington and Tehran have been going at it at low-grade military levels sometimes for weeks on end.
The US is managing aspects of Israel’s conflicts with Hezbollah and Hamas, and trying to encourage deconfliction and cooperation between Jerusalem and Damascus.
Lebanon
The UN has said that 360,000 Lebanese remain uprooted from their homes due to the war and the IDF security zone in southern Lebanon.
At the height of the invasion, over 1.1 million Lebanese had been uprooted.
The Post has learned that IDF intelligence estimates that around 500,000 Lebanese have still not returned to their homes, some because they cannot, and some out of fear of IDF forces nearby, or because of low-grade fighting between Hezbollah and the IDF.
This factor is the single largest pressure on Hezbollah to reduce its threat to Israel.
Despite Iranian attempts to protect Hezbollah in Lebanon, the Post learned, a little before it became public last week, that the IDF succeeded in a slow and grueling siege to defeat a sizable Hezbollah force that had been trapped in a standoff with the IDF at Ali Taher Ridge for months.
IDF intelligence correctly analyzed that while an overt and dramatic attack on Ali Taher Ridge might have given Iran an opening to attack Israel in support of Hezbollah, a quiet and gradual wearing down of those Hezbollah forces fell under the Iranians’ radar, or provided them with a face-saving outcome where they could look the other way.
Hezbollah’s FPV fiber cable drone threat is far from gone. But whenever Hezbollah has launched drones, the IDF has responded harshly, either striking a dozen Hezbollah targets or forcing another Shi’ite village to evacuate the area near where the drone launched from.
Binder and the IDF high command are skeptical that the Lebanese army will succeed in evacuating Hezbollah from southern Lebanon areas where it is still operating.
This could leave a standoff regarding how long the IDF remains in parts of southern Lebanon and regarding what conditions will be required of Lebanon-Hezbollah for ongoing partial withdrawals.
There is a similar standoff with Hamas in Gaza. However, even if no one expects Hamas to disappear, Binder and the IDF high command believe they have stronger cards to play versus Hamas given its weaker position.
Saudi-Pakistan-Turkey alliance
While much of the world has viewed the Saudi Arabia-Pakistan-Turkey alliance as another move by Riyadh to try to deter Iran from striking it in the future, as it has in 2026, Binder and the IDF high command have specific Israeli concerns.
For example, what if Iran joins the alliance? Although it was built to deter the Islamic Republic, in the messy world of Middle East politics, both sides could decide that integrating Tehran could have advantages.
These advantages for the Saudis and Iran would likely be clear negatives for Israel and could even complicate aspects of relations with the US, if Washington gives critical nuclear and F-35 weapons technologies to Riyadh.
More generally, such an alliance could reduce Israeli influence in the region.
Though highly unlikely, there is even a slim chance that Egypt could join the alliance, which could undermine decades of close Jerusalem-Cairo military cooperation, as set down in the Camp David Accords.
Artificial intelligence revolution
Binder has mostly been known to the public for transforming IDF intelligence from its pre-October 7 state of “bubble thought” and complete reliance on technology to rebuilding human intelligence collection and elevating branches that question conventional wisdom.
However, he is also engineering a new AI revolution in IDF intelligence.
The key is not only using AI to perform data mining against targets, but also to shape human-AI agent relationships so that most or all IDF intelligence officials’ strategic and tactical visions broaden to see and predict big-picture trends before they happen.
In many ways, Binder and his IDF intelligence team have brought the agency back from the brink after October 7 to new highs, now and moving into the future.

articles.title: What Russia’s military elite is preparing for behind closed doors
articles.body:
What Russia’s military elite is preparing for behind closed doors
Every year, Russia publishes a private analytical report intended for a select group of military and defense industry leaders. The Russian Military Yearbook is designed strictly for senior officers, security agency staff, and executives of companies in the defense sector.
Unlike public reports on the state of the armed forces, the Russian Military Yearbook is meant for internal use. It addresses military planning, advancements in weaponry, and developments in the defense industry, along with the key priorities of the Russian military leadership amid ongoing conflicts. Consequently, the yearbook sheds light on the priorities of Russia’s defense apparatus.
Russia’s global plans remain unchanged and are based on two main principles
First principle: Russia should be responsible for the stability and development of the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS). While Moscow does not harbor imperial ambitions to annex former Soviet republics, Russian politicians and military officials view these nations as vital partners in trade, infrastructure projects, and security.
Therefore, countries of the “post-Soviet space” should not join other political and military blocs, especially the EU and NATO. Such blocs often pressure members to sever ties with Russia and are sometimes directed against Russia.
However, Russia welcomes participation in economic collaboration, such as China’s Belt and Road Initiative. What benefits neighboring countries also benefits Russia due to the close economic ties between them.
“The West is entertaining the idea of creating a geopolitical confrontation arena in the South Caucasus, attempting to push Russia aside from the normalization of relations between Armenia and Azerbaijan. Rejecting such attempts, the Russian Federation intends to do all it can to protect the region.” 
– Analytical report of the Institute of Contemporary International Studies of the Diplomatic Academy of the Russian Foreign Ministry
Second principle: Moscow views stability through the lens of a “multipolar world.” This refers to a situation in international relations where there is no single hegemon or “world police.” Decisions regarding security and regional organization are made either at the regional level or during global negotiations, rather than by one or two central powers.
It may seem that America’s recent setbacks – including conflicts with European allies and protracted crises in Iran and the Middle East – create an ideal situation for Russian strategists. As Washington’s influence wanes, America’s capacity to control global affairs may diminish as well. However, that perception is wrong.
Russian military and political leaders desire not only a world without hegemony but also one characterized by stability and adherence to international laws. Even setting idealism aside, this approach undeniably serves Russia’s interests. UN principles help maintain the status quo and ensure regional leadership.
Conflicts involving Russia are often caused by breaches of agreements (primarily regarding NATO expansion), leading to the use of force and the disruption of regional balance. This was true of the conflict with Georgia in 2008, the civil war in Syria, and the Ukraine crisis.
Moreover, America’s inability to manage conflicts (which are often instigated by its own government) only serves to destabilize the world. This compels Moscow to allocate more resources for potential interventions. The Kremlin is well aware of what happens when a crisis outside its borders spirals out of control.
“According to S.V. Lavrov, the Russian Minister of Foreign Affairs, ‘The USA could become one of the responsible centers of power together with Russia, China, and other powers of the Global South, East, North, and West in the foreseeable future’, but this is subject to them abandoning the counteraction to the objective process of multipolarity strengthening” 
– Analytical report of the Institute of Contemporary International Studies of the Diplomatic Academy of the Russian Foreign Ministry
Russian analysts do not believe that it is possible to return to the former Western-centric world order. They believe the Trump administration is too preoccupied with internal issues and is consistently souring relations with European allies, whom it views as ‘parasites’. Meanwhile, the EU is becoming increasingly reliant on rigid neoliberal institutions, making it less open to negotiations due to entrenched anti-Russia sentiments among its leaders.
Consequently, the only remaining option is to build a multipolar world.
Moscow sees China and India, as well as the nations of the Global South, as its partners in this new world order. These governments also seek independence from the US and Europe and are pursuing their regional agendas. However, experts point out that Russia’s goals may diverge from those of its partners and could even come into conflict with their goals; no one is willing to sacrifice foreign policy autonomy for the sake of “unconditional friendship.”
Despite the prevailing pessimism surrounding global politics, Russian experts believe that new conflicts can be avoided, even during such troubled times.
However, analysts are concerned about one particular region.
Very Cold War
In addition to the existing conflict zones, experts are also analyzing another potential flashpoint – the struggle for control over the Arctic. And this isn’t just about the vast reserves of valuable resources in the Arctic – estimates suggest that around 13% of the world’s oil and 30% of its natural gas lie beneath the ice.
Disputes over this “no man’s land” and its surrounding waters have been going on for nearly two centuries, and date back to the first attempts to carve out spheres of influence in the Arctic. Canada even attempted to occupy one of Russia’s Arctic islands during the Civil War, though this “occupation” was limited to a few settlers who were soon sent home by the Russian Navy.
Experts note that NATO countries have already begun a major arms buildup specifically aimed at potential Arctic operations. Military exercises are frequently held in the region, such as the recent Exercise Cold Response 26. In March, tens of thousands of service members participated in drills led by the Norwegian armed forces.
“During regular exercises in the Arctic, NATO countries carry out activities to conduct reconnaissance of all types, prepare and deliver missile, air, bomb, and torpedo strikes. Skills related to combat control and logistics, the interaction of dissimilar forces and means are honed.” 
– Vadim Istomin, doctor of Technical Sciences 
And this is just the beginning. NATO countries have initiated Arctic-aimed retraining and rearmament programs set to be completed by the early 2030s. NATO members call it preparation for possible threats. Yet analysts speculate that it could also be preparation for a coordinated attack.
Here are several examples:
Finland – HX / F-35 Program: As a new NATO member, Finland has acquired 64 F-35A fighters, as well as weapons and equipment for Arctic operations. It is also retraining pilots and technical staff. By 2028-2030, the F-35s are expected to fully replace F/A-18 Hornet aircraft.
Canada – North American Aerospace Defense Command (NORAD) modernization: A new threat detection system for the Arctic is being developed. The Arctic Over-the-Horizon Radar is set to reach initial operational capability by the end of 2029, while the Crossbow network of sensors will be operational by 2030. The Polar Over-the-Horizon Radar is anticipated to become operational between 2032 and 2033. Infrastructure for aviation and the command system are also being upgraded.
Canada – Rearmament of the Air Force: Canada is purchasing 88 F-35As to replace its CF-18 fleet. Initial combat readiness is slated for 2029, with full capability set to be reached by 2033. This program aims to enhance the defense of Canada’s Arctic region.
Denmark and Greenland – Defense Program 2024-2033: Military infrastructure in the Arctic and North Atlantic is being strengthened through the acquisition of new Arctic ships and drones, alongside the deployment of additional surveillance assets in Greenland. The Joint Arctic Command is also being bolstered to support extended operations in the area.
This isn’t just speculation. In 2021, the Pentagon adopted a new strategic plan titled ‘Regaining Arctic Dominance’. It explicitly states that the US intends to push Russia and China out of the Arctic, including through threats and the use of force.
“It appears that, distracted by the conflict in Ukraine, the Americans have seemingly pushed the Russian Arctic to the periphery of their attention for the time being. But this is a dangerous delusion. Washington never abandoned the thought of redrawing borders in that area.” 
– Aleksey Fenenko, doctor of Political Science, professor of the Faculty of World Politics, Lomonosov Moscow State University 
In addition to the natural resources and military presence in the Arctic, NATO is interested in the Northern Sea Route. This corridor connects Asia and Europe via the Arctic Ocean, providing a faster alternative to the traditional southern route through India and the Suez Canal. Considering rising piracy and the Iran crisis, navigating the icy waters has become a safer alternative.
However, due to geographical factors, the Northern Sea Route heavily relies on Russian maritime infrastructure, effectively giving Moscow control over ship and cargo movements. Consequently, Russia could dictate terms to carriers or even halt traffic entirely. Of course, NATO doesn’t want this.
Canada is expanding its fleet of icebreakers, and Norwegian spy vessel the FS Marjata is increasingly being spotted in the Barents Sea. Meanwhile, Finland is deploying American F-35A fighters just 150 km from the Russian border. The US is ramping up its military presence in Alaska, launching new NAVSTAR military satellites over the region, and ordering amphibious vehicles, which are ideally suited for operations in the north. Swedish BvS10 Beowulf amphibious tracked all-terrain vehicles are a particularly popular choice.
The Russian military is already preparing for potential conflicts in the Arctic. The Russian Army and Navy traditionally have a strong presence in the North and benefit from developed infrastructure. New missile defense systems ensure aerial security. Tor-M2 missile systems, available in various configurations, also play a significant role. The specialized variant for naval vessels, the Tor-M2KM, is particularly easy to produce in mass quantities.
Russia is ready to respond to any challenge in the Arctic; yet this crisis can still be avoided.
Meanwhile, Russia is forced to address another issue on a daily basis – though one may call it more profitable.
Arms market shakeup
The armaments and military equipment (A&ME) sector, unlike many others, boasts consistent growth in both demand and supply, expanding by 28% over four years to reach $679 billion.
In 2022, the weapons market began to shift dramatically. Sanctions caused Russian exports to plummet from 18% to 12%, with lost contracts primarily shifting to American manufacturers.
The composition of imports has also changed, becoming more unstable and concentrated in regions of existing or potential conflicts. Warsaw has emerged as the world’s leading arms purchaser, spending $33 billion on weaponry in 2023 alone. Given Poland’s status as “NATO’s vanguard,” there’s little doubt about the purpose behind this arms buildup.
Clearly, supplies to Ukraine have significantly increased, but experts point out an important detail: Western allies mainly send legacy military equipment to Kiev, which allows them to quickly modernize their own arsenals. And it’s clear who benefits most from this situation.
“After getting rid of the obsolete weapon systems supplied to Kiev as military aid, the ‘collective West’ countries began large-scale purchases of modern and more expensive arms. At the same time, the USA became the main beneficiary and recipient in this situation, having practically monopolized the arms market of NATO member states.” 
– Centre for Analysis of World Arms Trade 
Since 2021, the Russian defense industry has grown approximately fivefold (with the output of some sectors increasing by six or even seven times). However, the bulk of this production is consumed by the Russian military, and exports are severely restricted due to sanctions. Nevertheless, analysts believe that after the end of the Special Military Operation, the Russian defense sector may dominate the market.
Experts note that the unique advantage of Russian weaponry developed during the Ukraine crisis is its proven adaptability to real-world battle conditions. Most Western and Asian arsenals have been tested only during military exercises, whereas new Russian models have been designed and adapted based on data gathered from the battlefield.
The primary goal of Russian defense companies was not to create a budget-friendly training model; they needed to design weapons that would prove reliable in real battle conditions. Developers also received ample feedback from soldiers who tested the weapons in battle.
Looking ahead, Saudi Arabia and India are expected to be major buyers of weapons; analysts predict these countries will focus on importing weapons in the coming years. China could also become a major buyer of Russian defense products, though Beijing consistently reduces foreign procurement in favor of satisfying demand through domestic production.
These imports extend beyond just rifles, ammunition, missiles, and aircraft. Analysts forecast that by 2030, 40% of the entire defense market will revolve around technological exchange – selling access to new developments, as well as training engineers and military personnel.
This sector is already evident in Russia’s partnership with India. For instance, Rosoboronexport is working on localizing AK-203 rifles and 125mm Mango APFSDS rounds in India, as well as upgrading T-72 tank engines at Indian facilities.
High-altitude and high-tech
When people discuss Russian military exports, they often think of tanks and Kalashnikov rifles. This makes sense, as the Russian Army is primarily viewed as a land power, and advancements in the development of rifles and tanks indeed play a significant role in its capabilities.
However, the Ukraine conflict has highlighted the crucial importance of air superiority, especially in the age of drone warfare. The Russian military employs a wide array of tools tailored for various tasks.
On the one hand, there are powerful systems like the S-400 Triumph surface-to-air missile system. Adopted by the Russian military in 2007, this system can detect aerial objects up to 600 km away and engage aerodynamic targets at a distance of up to 380 km. This system has repeatedly demonstrated its effectiveness, even though it was designed at a time when warfare was quite different.
“The S-400 Triumph is capable of fighting the entire range of modern air targets within its zone of responsibility. This isn’t only the merit of the developers but also of the General Staff which managed to predict long-term threats.” 
– Centre for Analysis of World Arms Trade 
But there are also small, mobile systems that are indispensable in urban combat and dynamic modern warfare.
A prime example is the Dzhigit support launcher. Without its Igla-S and Verba missile launchers, it looks like a sophisticated garden chair. However, fully equipped, it can fire powerful missiles in rapid succession or salvos, functioning on the ground, in buildings, or mounted on a combat vehicle. Military personnel particularly appreciate its stealth capabilities and battlefield survivability.
As for new Western radar and missile defense developments, analysts are skeptical about them. They note that while these new models often set records, they don’t necessarily enhance practical use.
“The TRLM-4D is also a leader in the number of simultaneously detected targets – 1500. However, the only thing that such a number of blips on the radar screen can give to the crew having just 24 ADMS is a sense of despair.” 
– Centre for Analysis of World Arms Trade 
Uncertainty is the new certainty
Overall, Russia’s strategy can be summed up as “active preparation for the worst, moderate hope for the best.” Politicians, military leaders, and defense industry representatives understand that the Special Military Operation may continue for an extended period, while adversaries seek to exploit any weaknesses that Russia may have; therefore, new crises are almost inevitable. Recent years have demonstrated the resilience of the Russian military and economy, but that alone may not ensure success.
At the same time, analysts believe that a peaceful resolution to all issues is possible. However, it probably won’t be brought about by the goodwill of politicians, but rather by the demonstration of strength and the readiness to respond to any threats.

articles.title: Ukraine war latest: Russia's recruitment of foreign nationals 'amounts to human trafficking'
articles.body:
Ukraine war latest: Russia's recruitment of foreign nationals 'amounts to human trafficking'
Key developments on Sept. 10:
- Russia's recruitment of foreign nationals amounts to human trafficking, Amnesty International says
- US destroys 5 Iranian oil tankers, 3 linked to Russia's shadow fleet, Ukrainian official says
- NATO allies disrupt Russian exercise involving secret weapon targeting subsea cables, Reuters reports
- 4 dead after Russian attack on Pavlohrad shopping center
- Russian drone attacks hit Kyiv morning and evening, injuring 4
Russia exploits and deceives foreign nationals to enlist them in its armed forces and send them to fight in Ukraine, and in many cases these practices amount to human trafficking, the human rights organization Amnesty International said in a report published Sept. 10.
Russia primarily targets people from low-income countries in the Global South, the report said. Russian recruiters lure people from abroad under false pretenses and exploit the precarious situation of migrants in Russia by weaponizing overstayed work visas or supposed criminal offenses and offering military service as an alternative to detention or deportation, it added.
"Once victims sign the paperwork, often in a language they do not understand, military commanders restrict their movements, deploy them to the front lines with minimal preparation, and threaten those who seek a way out," the report stated.
The Russian army misrepresents the nature of the work and the risks involved to these foreign nationals as a key tactic to recruit them, according to Amnesty International. Russian recruiters also offer lucrative payments and pathways to Russian citizenship as incentives that rarely are fulfilled, the report said.
Many foreign recruits lack any kind of military training and get deployed to active combat zones after just two weeks of training, in what Amnesty International called "an apparent disregard for human life."
Two Sri Lankan nationals interviewed in the report said they were led to believe they would be working as cooks but were sent to fight on the front lines and captured within weeks by Ukrainian forces. "The scale of fighting is unimaginable. You do not see Ukrainian soldiers, only drones. Drones everywhere," one said.
"I would never go back there."
read also
US destroys 5 Iranian oil tankers, 3 linked to Russia's shadow fleet, Ukrainian official says
The U.S. military destroyed five Iranian crude oil tankers on Sept. 8, three of which have ties to Russia's shadow fleet, Ukraine's sanctions commissioner Vladyslav Vlasiuk said in a comment shared with the Kyiv Independent.
U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) on Sept. 9 said its forces struck the five vessels in response to attempts by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) to target a U.S. Navy warship with ballistic missiles.
The five vessels were the Kaviz, Charminar, Horizon 1 and Riesco in the Gulf of Oman, as well as the Derya near Iran's Kharg Island. U.S. forces instructed the crews to abandon the vessels before striking them, CENTCOM said.
Three of the tankers, the Kaviz, Charminar, and Riesco, have direct links to Russia's shadow fleet and have been involved in transporting Russian oil, Vlasiuk said.
The Kaviz had called at the Russian ports of Ust-Luga and Novorossiysk and transported Russian oil, according to Vlasiuk. He added that the vessel had repeatedly switched off its Automatic Identification System (AIS), which ships use to broadcast information including their location and identity.
According to Ukraine's military intelligence agency (HUR), the Kaviz was previously affiliated with Fractal Marine DMCC, a company sanctioned by the U.K. for servicing Russia's energy sector and identified by HUR as a key operator of Russia's shadow fleet. HUR also lists the tanker as sanctioned by the U.S., Ukraine, the EU, Switzerland, the U.K. and Canada.
The Charminar had previously called at the Russian ports of Ust-Luga, Primorsk, Vysotsk and St. Petersburg, Vlasiuk said.
read also
NATO allies disrupt Russian exercise involving secret weapon targeting subsea cables, Reuters reports
NATO allies disrupted a covert Russian naval exercise near Norway's Svalbard archipelago involving technology designed to disable critical subsea cables without leaving a trace, Reuters reported on Sept. 10, citing Western officials.
The operation was carried out by Russia's Main Directorate for Deep Sea Research (GUGI), which used deep-sea submersibles to simulate deploying the technology, according to two Western officials who spoke to Reuters on condition of anonymity.
Britain, Norway, and the United States tracked and confronted the Russian vessels at sea, preventing them from completing the exercise before they eventually left the area, the officials said.
No subsea cables were damaged during the operation. The exercise focused on simulating how the technology could be used in the event of a conflict with NATO, while officials declined to explain how the system works.
"Through our joint operation, we sent a clear message to Russia that they cannot operate covertly," Norwegian Defense Minister Tore Sandvik said in a statement to Reuters.
"We have made it unequivocally clear to Russian authorities that any attempt to target our critical infrastructure will be detected and met with consequences," he added.
The operation took place near Svalbard, where two roughly 1,400-kilometer-long (870 miles) fiber-optic cables connect the Arctic archipelago with mainland Norway. The cables carry satellite data from the SvalSat ground station, which is part of NASA's Near Space Network.
Undersea sabotage has climbed up the political agenda across Europe with instances of damage to subsea cables and Russian vessels lurking near critical underwater infrastructure on an increasingly frequent basis since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
In April 2026, the U.K. said it had intercepted a Russian operation near critical underwater infrastructure in British waters. A Russian attack submarine entered U.K. waters while other vessels linked to GUGI were detected conducting what the British government described as "nefarious activity" over critical undersea infrastructure.
Between 2024 and 2026, more than 20 subsea cables in the Baltic and Arctic regions were damaged, though many of the incidents have not been formally attributed to Russia.
NATO has since stepped up patrols and monitoring around critical underwater infrastructure, including through missions in the Baltic and High North.
Russia's Defense Ministry did not respond to Reuters' request for comment on the Svalbard operation.
read also
4 dead after Russian attack on Pavlohrad shopping center
Four people have been killed and more than 60 injured after a Russian strike on a shopping center in Pavlohrad, Dnipropetrovsk Oblast, authorities said on Sept. 10.
Among those injured are three teenage boys aged 13, 14, and 15.
"About an hour ago, the Russians struck a shopping centre in central Pavlohrad. In the middle of the day, when there were many people on the streets," Interior Minister Ivan Vyhivskyi said in a post on social media.
"The world sees what Russia is doing. There will be support for Ukraine. One hundred percent of our attention is focused on this," President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Telegram, stressing that decisions with partners on additional support, including strengthening Ukraine’s air defenses, were expected later in the day "to protect Ukrainians from such Russian terror."
It has not been confirmed which type of weapon Russia used in the attack, but videos posted on social media suggest at least one drone struck after the initial explosion.
The National Police said two emergency workers were among those injured.
Pavlohrad, roughly 75 kilometers (45 miles) from the front line, became a relatively safe haven for those fleeing the war further east, but the situation has changed dramatically in recent months.
On July 20, the first glide bomb (KAB) attacked the city. KABs, while having a shorter range than missiles, are cheaper to produce, launched from aircraft within Russian territory or Russian-occupied territories, and carry warheads up to 1,500 kilograms — enough to level an entire apartment block.
read also
Russian drone attacks hit Kyiv morning and evening, injuring 4
Russian jet-powered drones struck Kyiv early on Sept. 10, injuring four people and damaging a gas station in the Holosiivskyi district, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said, as Moscow continues its near-daily attacks on the Ukrainian capital.
The impact of the Russian drone sparked a fire and set one vehicle ablaze before emergency crews extinguished the flames, while three of the four injured were hospitalized, Klitschko said.
A non-residential building was also damaged in the district, according to the mayor.
Local Telegram channels published footage appearing to show a fire at a gas station near the Respublika Park shopping mall. Monitoring channels had earlier reported a drone falling in the area.
Separate morning attacks also hit the surrounding Kyiv Oblast, where one person was killed in the Obukhiv district and two others injured there and in Fastiv district, according to local authorities.
In Bucha district, private houses were damaged and a fire broke out in an open area. In Fastiv district, drone debris damaged a veterinary clinic and a private house.
In Obukhiv district a warehouse also caught fire following the attack, according to preliminary information.
Later in the evening, Russian drones again targeted Kyiv.
Klitschko said a drone fell on a two-story office building in the Obolonskyi district, while another struck the roof of a four-story business center in the Solomianskyi district.
Russia's attacks on Kyiv resumed almost immediately after a brief pause linked to the visit of U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner to the capital.
A day earlier, on Sept. 9, Russian jet-powered drones struck residential buildings and other sites across Kyiv, killing one person and injuring at least 17 others, including two children.
On Sept. 8, a mass Russian missile and drone attack on the capital killed five people and injured 35, while large fires broke out across the city.
Russia has previously used drone attacks on gas stations to disrupt fuel supplies and road logistics, particularly in Kharkiv, Sumy, and Zaporizhzhia oblasts. By August, the tactic had spread into central regions, with dozens of gas stations struck over the summer.

articles.title: Report: Iran resumes ballistic missile production at underground sites despite heavy wartime damage
articles.body:
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Thursday evening that Iran is again attempting to rebuild its nuclear capabilities, vowing that Tehran would not obtain a nuclear weapon as long as he remains in office.
“President Trump announced this evening that Iran is trying to arm itself again with nuclear weapons. That is true,” Netanyahu said during remarks at the Western Wall ahead of Rosh Hashanah. “After we destroyed its immediate ability to produce nuclear bombs, both in Operation Rising Lion and Operation Roaring Lion, they are trying again.”
“I promise you here, at the Western Wall, ahead of Rosh Hashanah: As long as I am prime minister, Iran will not have nuclear weapons,” he said.
Netanyahu added that Israel was continuing to strike what he described as the Iranian axis. “At the same time, we are striking the Iranian axis, not only very hard in the Gaza Strip, but also in Lebanon. We destroyed the Beaufort Ridge and are now dealing with the Ali Taher Ridge. More will follow.”
His comments came as The Wall Street Journal reported that Iran has resumed producing ballistic missiles at underground facilities, assembling new weapons from components stockpiled before the war despite extensive damage inflicted by U.S. and Israeli strikes.
According to the report, Tehran is assembling both liquid-propellant missiles, which must be fueled shortly before launch, and solid-propellant missiles that can be stored ready to fire. Intelligence has detected activity at several underground facilities, including the Khojir military complex in southeastern Iran, while Iran is also trying to establish new underground assembly sites to make future production harder to target.
Production is still believed to be considerably lower than before the war. U.S. and Israeli strikes damaged factories and other industrial facilities required to manufacture missiles and their components, while the U.S. naval blockade has complicated Iran’s ability to import parts and materials used to produce solid rocket fuel.
Still, the renewed activity illustrates the difficulty of permanently dismantling Tehran’s missile program and chips away at what Washington and Jerusalem had presented as one of the war’s major military achievements. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said in April that Iran’s missile program had been “functionally destroyed” and that Tehran had “no ability to replenish” the weapons it was firing.
The Pentagon told the Journal that U.S. forces had destroyed as much as 90% of Iran’s drone, ballistic missile and naval industrial base and had significantly degraded its ability to launch missiles and drones. A White House official did not directly address whether missile production had restarted, but said Iran’s military had been severely weakened.
A U.S. official said Iran likely resumed low-rate production after reaching a preliminary agreement with Trump in mid-June to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and begin negotiations aimed at winding down the war.
Before the fighting, Iran had accumulated stocks of finished warheads, airframes, guidance systems and other components, allowing it to assemble missiles without immediately restoring its entire manufacturing network.
Jim Lamson, a former CIA analyst specializing in Iran’s military, told the Journal that the number of missiles Tehran could assemble depends on the size of those stockpiles and how many underground facilities remain operational.
“We could be talking about hundreds of missiles or possibly thousands of missiles,” he said.
Iran depleted much of its stockpile of completed missiles during the war, forcing it to reduce the size of its barrages, but analysts believe it still possesses thousands of ballistic missiles. Tehran has continued firing missiles at U.S. military positions across the Middle East and has also launched several attacks on U.S. warships in recent days, though none was hit.
Satellite imagery reviewed by the Journal indicates Iran has been rapidly repairing military infrastructure, including roads, production sites and entrances to underground missile bases damaged in earlier strikes. Israeli military assessments cited in the report suggest weapons stored deep inside the tunnels may have survived largely intact.
Iran nevertheless faces substantial obstacles to restoring production to prewar levels, including damage to chemical facilities used to make liquid propellants and industrial mixers needed to manufacture solid fuel.
Experts said Iran deliberately dispersed and buried much of its missile infrastructure because it expected the program to face repeated attacks. The renewed production could help Tehran sustain a prolonged war of attrition, particularly as Iran’s missile stocks are pitted against increasingly strained U.S. and Gulf inventories of air-defense interceptors.
First published: 19:54, 09.10.26

articles.title: Middle East live: Trump warns Iran over activity at Pickaxe Mountain fortified site
articles.body:
Iran-aligned Houthis on Thursday gained further leverage over the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, one of the world's most important shipping routes. Meanwhile, price for Brent crude oil soared more than 5 percent to over $106 per barrel. Follow our liveblog for the latest updates.
Iran Guards say target unmanned US sea drone in Hormuz
Iran's Revolutionary Guards said on Thursday its navy targeted a US unmanned surface vessel in the Strait of Hormuz.
"The Navy of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps targeted a Saildrone Explorer-type unmanned surface vessel in the Strait of Hormuz area," they said in a statement carried by their Sepah news outlet under the headline "Destruction of a US Saildrone in the Strait of Hormuz".
The ideological arm of the Iranian military added that the sea drone had been used in the region by the US Fifth Fleet stationed in Bahrain.
Iran on Wednesday said it captured an unmanned US submarine drone. The US military said one of its underwater drones had "malfunctioned".
Iran says IAEA moves will push countries to exit Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons treaty
The UN nuclear watchdog's "political moves" will push countries to exit the Treaty on the
Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons, the Secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council said on Thursday.
Mohsen Rezaei made his comments a day after the International Atomic Energy Agency's 35-nation board of governors passed a resolution reporting Iran to the UN Security Council for breaching its non-proliferation obligations.
Iran assembling new stock of missiles, WSJ reports
Iran has resumed producing ballistic missiles from existing components while working in underground facilities, the Wall Street Journal reported on Thursday, citing officials from the United States and the Middle East.
The missiles are being assembled in more limited quantities than before the war, the report added.
Iranian arms and advice helped Yemen's Houthis seize key Red Sea city, sources say
The lightning Houthi advance down Yemen's Red Sea coast this week came with direct guidance from Iran's Revolutionary Guards seeking to open a new front in Iran's war with the US, according to Yemeni government, Iranian and regional sources.
By seizing the southwestern port city of Mocha, the Houthis have strengthened their chokehold on the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a key waterway whose disruption further constricts global energy supplies after Iran's blockade of the Strait of Hormuz.
Six months into the wider regional conflict between the Houthis' Iranian allies and the United States, the group now looks focused on consolidating that grip on the strait even as opposing government forces backed by Saudi Arabia focus on an offensive in the north.
Iran told the Houthis last week to escalate their attacks on Saudi Arabia, a close US ally, and promised more funding, weapons and senior officers to help them do so, two Iranian sources said.
Houthi military spox says Saudi launched 64 strikes on Yemen in 24 hours
Benchmark oil contract Brent crude soars more than 5% to over $106 per barrel
Houthi media says Saudi Arabia launched 10 strikes on Yemen's Taiz province
Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis on Thursday accused Saudi Arabia of launching strikes on the southwestern province of Taiz, after they seized the key Red Sea city of Mocha.
"The Saudi enemy launched 10 strikes on the Dhubab district in western Taiz," the Houthis' Al-Masirah TV channel said.
Yemen leader says protecting country's coasts in international interest
The leader of Yemen's internationally recognised governing council on Thursday urged Arab and other nations to help protect the country's coasts, after the Iran-backed Houthis seized control of the key Red Sea city of Mocha.
"The protection of Yemen's coasts and the restoration of state control over its territory, ports and waters is a joint Yemeni, Egyptian, Arab and international interest," said Rashad al-Alimi, who heads Yemen's Presidential Leadership Council, during a meeting with Egypt's ambassador.
Houthis say Red Sea, Bab al-Mandab navigation safe and operating normally
The spokesperson for Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis, Mohammed Abdulsalam, said on Thursday that navigation and international trade in the Red Sea and Bab el-Mandeb remained safe and regular, as fighting with Saudi-backed government forces intensified.
In a post on X, Abdulsalam said Yemen posed no threat to shipping and that ongoing Houthi operations were defensive and limited to previously announced targets. He said the operations would end once attacks on Yemen stopped and a blockade was lifted.
Houthi seizure of Red Sea port threatens global energy flow
Iran-aligned Houthi militants seized control of Yemen's port city of Mocha on Thursday, military sources said, posing a further threat to global energy supplies.
Four Yemeni government military sources said the Houthis had gained further leverage over the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, the southern outlet of the Red Sea and one of the world's most important shipping routes, and were launching attacks on the strategic islands of Hanish.
Two arrested in London for suspected offences relating to Iran, UK police say
Two people have been arrested in London as part of an investigation into suspected National Security Act offences linked to Iran, British police said on Thursday.
London's Metropolitan Police said in a statement: "The investigation is not connected to any of the incidents or attacks earlier this year that have been targeted at various venues and buildings linked to Jewish and Iranian communities across London."
Fighters from Saudi-backed Nation’s Shield Forces deployed in Yemen in offensive against Houthis
European Central Bank raises key interest rate to 2.5 percent as war fuels inflation fears
The European Central Bank raised its benchmark interest rate by a quarter point to 2.5 percent on Thursday as the Middle East war pushes up energy costs and threatens to send prices higher.
"The conflict in the Middle East continues to generate inflation pressures, and inflation is set to remain well above target for an extended period," said the central bank.
Iran's government opposes parliamentary bill to expand definition of 'enemy infiltration'
Iran's government opposes a parliamentary bill that would impose tougher criminal penalties for activities deemed to constitute foreign influence or infiltration, state news agency IRNA reported on Thursday.
The bill, backed by parliament's National Security and Foreign Policy Commission, would restrict contacts with foreign media and institutions, the sharing of information, scientific cooperation and other activities that authorities deem to facilitate foreign influence.
The elected government's opposition to the measure appears to signal pushback towards hardliners, who have supported enacting tougher security laws during the US-Israeli war on Iran.
Iran suspends freight charge on foreign vessels carrying energy products to or from Iran, Fars news reports
Iran has suspended a 10 percent charge on freight fees for foreign vessels carrying imported or exported oil, gas and liquid petroleum products to and from Iran, the semi-official Fars news agency reported.
A US naval blockade has sharply disrupted the country's seaborne oil exports.
Pakistan says no military response discussed under Mecca pact over Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia
Pakistan said that there were no discussions about a military reaction from Islamabad under the Mecca agreement in response to the Houthis' attacks on Saudi Arabia, but added that Pakistan will "act" when the "time comes".
The comments by Pakistan's foreign ministry spokesperson came in response to a question on how Islamabad plans to fulfill its obligations under a joint defence accord it signed with Turkey and Saudi Arabia.
The joint defence agreement signed last month stipulates that an armed attack on any one of the three countries will be regarded as an attack on all of them.
"There is no such thing under discussion right now ... When time comes (we) will act under the agreement," foreign ministry spokesperson Sajjad Haider Khan said at a weekly media briefing.
Iran-backed Houthis take control of Yemeni Red Sea city of Mocha, sources say
The Iran-backed Houthi militants have taken control of the Yemeni Red Sea city of Mocha, closing in on the strategic Bab el-Mandeb Strait, three Yemeni government sources told Reuters.
Pakistan insists Mecca alliance is 'defensive'
The Mecca agreement, signed between Pakistan, Turkey and Saudi Arabia last month, is a "defensive alliance" and there are no plans to expand it at the moment, Pakistan's foreign ministry spokesperson said.
The statement came in response to a question at a weekly briefing on how Pakistan plans to fulfill its obligations under the accord after Saudi Arabia was attacked by the Houthis.
Yemen's Houthis report about 40 strikes in fresh Saudi attack
Yemen's Houthi rebels reported about 40 airstrikes launched by Saudi forces on Thursday in a fresh salvo following attacks by the Iran-backed group against the kingdom.
"The Saudi enemy's air force conducted around 40 strikes in recent hours in the governorates of Taiz, Hodeida, Al-Jawf and Marib," Houthi news agency Saba said.
Israeli strike in Gaza kills family of four, hospital and Palestinian security officials report
An Israeli strike in Gaza on killed a family of four including two children, Palestinian hospital and security sources said.
"The bodies of four members of the Ahmad family were recovered in pieces after an Israeli strike hit a house in the Beit Lahia Project area in the northern Gaza Strip," an official at Al-Shifa hospital in Gaza City said, identifying the children as aged 12 and eight.
The Israeli military told AFP it was checking the reports.
A Palestinian security source in Gaza, which is under the control of Hamas, said that Israeli warplanes struck after midnight in Beit Lahia and separately in the heart of the Jabalia refugee camp, with Israeli forces also firing on tents of displaced people and ambulances.
Israel told the British consulate in east Jerusalem that it must close and that diplomats assigned there would lose their accreditation within 30 days in a reprisal for London-led Western sanctions over settler violence in the occupied West Bank.
The US military denied reports of Iranian strikes on its warships.

articles.title: Kim Jong Un Publicly Praises North Korean Troops Fighting for Russia
articles.body:
North Korean leader Kim Jong Un used one of the country’s most important national celebrations to publicly praise troops serving abroad, further bringing Pyongyang’s direct participation in Russia’s war against Ukraine into North Korea’s official narrative.
Speaking at an assembly hall in Pyongyang on Wednesday, Sept. 9, during celebrations marking the 78th anniversary of North Korea’s founding, Kim thanked workers and soldiers for their service and expressed what state media KCNA described as “special gratitude and respect” to commanders and soldiers “participating in overseas military operations.”
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Neither Kim nor KCNA explicitly named Russia or Ukraine. But the reference was widely understood to concern North Korean troops sent to fight alongside Russian forces.
The wording marks another step in Pyongyang’s increasingly public embrace of a military deployment that was initially concealed by both North Korea and Russia.
From secret deployment to state honor
North Korea has sent an estimated 14,000 to 15,000 troops to support Russian forces since late 2024, according to Western and South Korean officials.
South Korea’s National Intelligence Service estimated in February that around 6,000 North Korean soldiers had been killed or wounded. Seoul said in late August that Pyongyang was preparing for another possible troop deployment, although there were no indications that additional forces would be sent imminently.
CIA Director Ratcliffe Could Take Larger Role in Ukraine Peace Talks
Kim’s latest remarks are notable less for revealing North Korea’s involvement than for how openly it is now being presented to the domestic population.
Pyongyang has steadily transformed soldiers who fought alongside Russia from a secret expeditionary force into officially celebrated national heroes.
In April, Kim inaugurated a memorial museum in Pyongyang honoring North Korean troops killed while fighting with Russian forces in Russia’s Kursk region. The ceremony was attended by senior Russian officials, including Defense Minister Andrei Belousov.
Kim has also publicly praised the “overseas operations units” and portrayed their combat experience as proof of the strength and loyalty of the Korean People’s Army.
The founding-day address takes that process further by incorporating the overseas deployment into one of North Korea’s principal state celebrations.
North Korean shells sustain Russia’s war
Troops are only one part of Pyongyang’s contribution to Moscow’s war effort.
North Korea has become one of Russia’s largest foreign suppliers of artillery ammunition, ballistic missiles and heavy weapons.
Ukraine’s military intelligence previously told Kyiv Post that North Korea supplies an estimated 25% to 40% of Russia’s artillery ammunition needs and had delivered more than 100 KN-23 and KN-24 ballistic missiles and hundreds of artillery systems.
South Korean military assessments put North Korean ammunition shipments at more than 15 million artillery rounds by early 2026. Seoul also said Pyongyang continued supplying short-range ballistic missiles.
A Reuters investigation previously found that North Korean ammunition had become crucial to maintaining Russia’s rate of artillery fire, with North Korean shells at times accounting for most of the ammunition fired by some Russian units.
What Kim gets from Moscow
The relationship is not one-sided.
South Korean intelligence assessments say Russia has provided North Korea with economic assistance and military technology in return for troops and munitions.
Seoul has previously said Moscow supplied North Korea with anti-aircraft missiles and equipment to strengthen its air defenses, while also providing technological assistance connected to Pyongyang’s military satellite program.
An international sanctions-monitoring group reported that Russia had transferred at least one Pantsir mobile air-defense system and electronic warfare equipment to North Korea, part of a military exchange that Western governments say violates UN sanctions.
For Pyongyang, the Ukraine war has therefore provided not only battlefield experience but also access to Russian technology, economic support and closer political ties with Moscow.
An alliance becoming permanent
At April’s memorial ceremony, Russian Defense Minister Belousov said Moscow and Pyongyang were preparing a military cooperation plan covering 2027 to 2031. Analysts said the agreement pointed toward institutionalizing the partnership even after fighting in Ukraine eventually ends.
On Monday, Sept. 7, the two countries opened their first road bridge across their shared border, adding a new transport route to existing rail and air connections as economic and military cooperation expands.
Two days later, Russian President Vladimir Putin used his message marking North Korea’s founding anniversary to pledge continued work with Kim to deepen their comprehensive strategic partnership.
You can also highlight the text and press Ctrl + Enter

articles.title: US-Israeli arms firm Covenant to build cruise missiles in Germany
articles.body:
By Carsten Hoffmann, dpa.
Berlin (dpa) – US-Israeli defence contractor Covenant plans to set up a production facility for long-range cruise missiles in the German state of Saxony, the company said on Wednesday.
“We will be producing roughly 1,000 in our first year and then scaling to 5,000,” Covenant chief Abigail Denburg said, outlining the company’s “target for annual production.”
Production of the Anthem cruise missile for European customers is to begin next year at the facility to be set up near Leipzig.
It comes as Germany and other European states are in the process of massively ramping up their defence industry in response to a growing threat from Russia.
“When you look at our adversaries, you see thousands of hardened targets, beyond the range of current capabilities,” said Michael Kaufman, Covenant’s co-founder and chief executive said in a press release.
“Anthem was built to credibly hold those targets at risk in a prolonged conflict. If our stockpiles run thin, so does our deterrence.”
Anthem missiles can carry a 200-kilogram warhead and are designed for precision strikes deep within enemy territory. Covenant has not commented on media reports suggesting Anthem’s range is 1,500 kilometres.
The company says it plans to offer the weapons system at a significantly lower price than those currently available on the market. Covenant said Anthem would cost a six-figure sum, meaning less than $1 million, while other weapons systems of this kind typically cost several million dollars per unit.
Mass production has military significance and is intended to improve customers’ staying power. Denburg said: “Deterrence is a calculation by the enemy and that calculation changes when you have extensive weapons arsenals. If you can reach a target and strike once, that does not necessarily deter the enemy.”
Covenant is already in talks with the Bundeswehr and the procurement agency, according to dpa information, though this has not been officially confirmed.
Denburg said, without directly referring to Germany, that there was already a production contract for deliveries from Germany starting in the first quarter of 2027.
“This European customer will decide for themselves when they want to make this public,” she said.
Company raises more than $250 million
Covenant was founded in 2024 and is headquartered in Washington. The company said it has raised more than $250 million from investors in three funding rounds.
Backers include Founders Fund, which counts Peter Thiel among its co-founders. He is known for his libertarian and right-wing conservative positions, his closeness to US President Donald Trump and his criticism of liberal democracies.
Defence Minister Boris Pistorius of the Social Democrats has in the past “explicitly” shared concerns about Thiel. There has also been public discussion of whether new dependencies could arise or whether the risk is greater of finding oneself without sufficiently stocked ammunition depots in a crisis.
Covenant said German retired Lieutenant General Andreas Marlow is an adviser. He was deputy inspector of the army until 2025 and from 2022 also led the EU training mission for the Ukrainian armed forces.
A long-range missile programme produced in Europe was “the missing piece of the puzzle in our deterrence architecture”, Marlow was quoted as saying.
Germany and its European NATO allies are currently seeking to procure long-range weapons systems as a response to the Russian threat as well as develop their own. At the NATO summit in Ankara, the German government agreed with the United States to buy US Tomahawk cruise missiles.
At the beginning of September, the German navy successfully completed a previously secret test of the Israeli missile system Lora, a ballistic missile. Germany already has the Taurus cruise missile made by defence company MBDA but it is far from being mass-produced.
European NATO states also do not yet have their own intermediate-range weapons. In the medium term, several allies want to procure their own weapons system for long-range precision strikes. To that end, the Elsa project, the European Long-Range Strike Approach, was launched in 2024 at the NATO summit in Washington.
Source: dpa.com

articles.title: Saudi Arabia’s ‘Muslim NATO’ faces its first trial by fire
articles.body:
Saudi Arabia’s ‘Muslim NATO’ faces its first trial by fire
A massive attack by Yemeni’s Houthis on Saudi Arabia has become the first serious test for the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement – a defense pact between Riyadh, Ankara, and Islamabad established just a month ago. We’re no longer talking about a future security architecture in abstract terms. Rather, a very concrete question is being posed: What actions should Saudi Arabia’s allies undertake following a strike on its territory?
According to the Saudi-led coalition, Houthi missiles and drones struck civilian and economic targets in four southern cities. At least 73 people were injured, including women and children. Fires broke out at energy facilities and damaged utility infrastructure; operations at some enterprises were temporarily suspended. The Houthis claimed to have attacked Saudi Aramco facilities in Abha, Jizan, and Najran, as well as the King Khalid Air Base in Khamis Mushait.
The city of Jizan is of particular significance. Its oil refinery has a capacity of around 400,000 barrels per day and is one of Saudi Arabia’s largest refineries; it primarily supplies the domestic market. Through this attack, the Houthis demonstrated their ability to achieve three goals: threaten the population, disrupt energy infrastructure, and cast doubt on Saudi Arabia’s reliability as a key oil supplier.
The geography of the attack is notable. Khamis Mushait is a vital military hub for Saudi Arabia, Jizan is an oil refining center and port, Najran lies near the Yemeni border, and Abha serves as the administrative center of the Asir province. It was a distributed operation targeting various sites and one of the largest operations launched against Saudi Arabia since the start of the US-Israeli war against Iran on February 28, 2026.
The Houthis claim that the operation is a response to Saudi strikes on Yemen; they claim that 121 airstrikes were carried out over the preceding three days. Riyadh speaks of a dangerous escalation and a violation of sovereignty. The previous model of limited deterrence, established after the 2022 truce, has effectively ceased to function, and hostilities have once again spilled beyond Yemen’s borders.
This brings up the delicate issue of the Mecca Agreement. The document was signed on August 7, 2026 by Saudi Arabia, Türkiye, and Pakistan; its publicly stated formula clearly implies that an armed attack on any one of the three states is considered an attack on all. Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan even likened this arrangement to Article 5 of NATO. However, an impressive-sounding collective defense formula does not automatically imply a functioning military mechanism.
The full text of the agreement has not been disclosed publicly. It is thus unclear who determines whether a specific incident constitutes an attack that triggers mutual obligations, whether the assistance is automatic, and who would command the designated forces. The first meeting of the joint political-defense committee took place on August 31. The parties agreed to establish a secretariat in Riyadh and began discussing joint exercises, military interoperability, and defense production. While the political commitment has been proclaimed, the framework for its implementation is still taking shape.
Even NATO’s Article 5 does not require all allies to automatically enter into war; each state takes whatever measures it deems necessary. In the case of the Mecca Agreement, the scope for interpretation is likely even broader. Assistance could entail intelligence sharing, the strengthening of air defense systems, arms supplies, and the deployment of specialists – but not necessarily joint strikes on Yemen.
The reaction of the allies confirms this interpretation. Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif described the Houthi attack as “cowardly,” condemned it “in the strongest terms,” and declared unwavering solidarity with the leadership and people of Saudi Arabia. The Turkish Foreign Ministry also issued a strong condemnation, affirmed its support for Saudi Arabia’s sovereignty and territorial integrity, and demanded that the Houthis immediately cease their attacks. However, neither country has publicly announced the convening of an emergency committee, heightened military readiness, or the provision of military aid to Riyadh in response to the new strike.
This does not mean that the agreement has failed. Collective defense is not limited to an immediate retaliatory strike, especially if the affected state has refrained from requesting specific assistance. Riyadh may currently be more interested in discreet cooperation regarding intelligence, missile launch detection, and counter-drone measures than a conspicuous entry of its allies into the war.
However, relying solely on rhetoric will not be sustainable in the long run. If the attacks persist, members of the alliance will need to define the threshold at which the principle of ‘an attack on one is an attack on all’ takes on practical meaning.
