articles.title: Putin dismisses rumors of another mobilization as ‘nonsense.’ But can Russia keep fighting without another draft?
articles.body:
Putin dismisses rumors of another mobilization as ‘nonsense.’ But can Russia keep fighting without another draft?
Vladimir Putin and his subordinates have recently been actively denying rumors of an impending mobilization. This has only made many people more anxious: trust in official statements is low, and speculation about plans to forcibly draft hundreds of thousands of recruits into the army shows no sign of letting up. Meduza’s Razbor (“Explainer”) desk has tried to answer the main questions surrounding mobilization. Why has the frenzy picked up specifically toward fall? Is it true that Ukrainian authorities are waging an information attack on the Kremlin with these rumors? And are there objective grounds for mobilization?
Why fall is the predicted timing for mobilization, and how the rumors snowballed
One fact is worth remembering up front: the “partial” mobilization Vladimir Putin announced on September 21, 2022, technically remains in effect. He never signed a decree ending it. The forced draft that sent hundreds of thousands of Russians into the army has ended only in name. Even today, authorities could legally issue someone a mobilization summons.
In practice, though, no one has been drafted that way since late fall 2022. But rumors of a “new wave” of mobilization keep resurfacing with striking regularity. Rather than catalog every failed forecast from 2023 through 2025, this piece focuses on the current “wave.”
Russian officials routinely accuse Ukraine of fueling these rumors to destabilize the country. Kyiv’s motive isn’t hard to explain: Ukrainian military strikes on oil refineries and market warehouses appear, at least in part, to serve the same purpose. The more Russians feel the war’s practical consequences — and the anxiety over a possible draft — the greater the odds of a social explosion and public pressure to end the fighting.
Public opinion polling shows no sign of a “pacifist” trend: data from the Levada Center shows the share of Russians who favor peace talks has been falling since February and March, while the share favoring continued war has been climbing. Still, polling conducted in a country under wartime censorship deserves considerable skepticism.
Either way, Ukrainian officials have genuinely kept the mobilization talk alive. The most prominent voice is President Volodymyr Zelensky, who has made more than a dozen public predictions over the past six months about an impending forced draft into the Russian armed forces. Sources in Western intelligence agencies and government bodies have repeatedly echoed him behind closed doors.
- In mid-April 2026, Zelensky linked the Kremlin’s decision to block Telegram in Russia to an anticipated forced draft of hundreds of thousands of Russians. He later repeated the point publicly: internet blackouts, he said, are a tool for preventing a “revolt” over the coming mobilization.
- Later that same month, Zelensky said the head of Ukraine’s Main Intelligence Directorate (HUR) had briefed him on Russia’s mobilization plans.
- In mid-May, Zelensky cited HUR figures putting Russia’s mobilization need at 100,000 people. European intelligence services lent support to the rumors around the same time: sources told The Wall Street Journal the move reflected the Kremlin’s desire to expand the conflict beyond Ukraine. EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas told the outlet: “If you just mobilize for this war, then you would send a signal that you are not really winning this war. So […] they need to escalate in order to justify the mobilization. And that’s a very dangerous point.”
- Later that month, Zelensky clarified that additional mobilization in Russia would affect “at least tens of thousands of people” and said Russian authorities had stepped up issuing mobilization notices. Around the same time, the first leaks surfaced suggesting the Kremlin might take the unpopular step in the fall, after elections to the State Duma, the lower house of Russia’s parliament, according to European officials who told The Washington Post as much on condition of anonymity.
- Zelensky’s next reference to mobilization in Russia came in early June, in his widely covered open letter to Putin, where he described his opponent’s intention to “launch a second wave” of forced conscription.
- In mid-July, Zelensky offered another forecast, this time about the possibility of “increased mobilization” after the State Duma elections.
- By the end of the month, Zelensky made a statement saying a faction within Putin’s inner circle was pushing him toward expanding mobilization, then followed up with another prediction of “a fairly significant wave” of recruitment into the Russian armed forces.
- A few days later, Zelensky added details, saying mobilization could happen in October and that the number mobilized could reach half a million people, or amount to at least 300,000. Soon afterward, sources in Washington backed the rumors for the first time: anonymous American officials told The Wall Street Journal they didn’t rule out the Kremlin soon having no way to reach its battlefield goals except through forced conscription.
- In early August, Zelensky again repeated his estimate that Putin needs half a million troops at the front, though he allowed that there might be no official mobilization announcement at all: recruitment could instead happen through “shadow” contracts. He followed that with a clarification: the information, he said, came from certain “internal Russian documents” obtained by Ukrainian intelligence.
- By the end of the month, the Ukrainian president gave a more detailed picture: “peripheral” mobilization in Russia “will not take place in major cities” and will be capped at 300,000 recruits in 2026 before continuing into 2027. Around the same time, The Wall Street Journal, citing Western intelligence sources, reported that Russia’s armed forces were intensifying drills for mobilization procedures.
- Zelensky’s last remark came on September 8: he continues to forecast 300,000 mobilized “after the elections,” whether in “covert or overt” form.
How justified are these forecasts, and does Russia’s military actually need mobilization?
One caveat upfront: we don’t have clear answers to either question, and in all likelihood, neither do the people making these forecasts.
Let’s start with the official denials. Since roughly midsummer, Russian lawmakers, diplomats, and top officials have regularly accused Ukraine of “planting” disinformation, waging “information attacks,” and otherwise trying to “destabilize” the country. Members of the State Duma’s defense committee have said as much, as has Russia’s U.N. envoy, Vasily Nebenzya; presidential spokesperson Dmitry Peskov; the deputy chairman of Russia’s Security Council, Dmitry Medvedev (more than once); and, of course, Vladimir Putin himself.
But these denials shouldn’t be taken as reassuring. Nebenzya, for one, said mobilization isn’t needed “at this moment.” Putin, in his last statement, ruled out the scenario only “for today.” Hedges like these would let the authorities walk back their assurances after the State Duma elections — exactly what happened in 2022, when State Duma defense committee chairman Andrey Kartapolov assured Russians two days before the “partial” mobilization was announced that they had no reason to fear “general” mobilization. “General” mobilization indeed never happened, only because the authorities hid it behind the euphemism “partial.”
There are other, indirect reasons to suspect that mobilization plans are being concealed.
- Since 2022, Russia has passed numerous laws closing loopholes for potential draft dodgers ahead of any future wave of forced conscription — though that alone doesn’t mean specific plans exist.
- Many observers have viewed this summer’s roundups of men in the Penza region as a testing ground for a coming “peripheral” mobilization. Local authorities there detained potential recruits under all sorts of pretexts and, through various methods — including violent ones — forced them to sign contracts and go to war. But an equally or even more likely explanation is that local officials were simply trying to catch up on contract-soldier quotas handed down from Moscow: sources who spoke to the Financial Times put the overall recruitment target at 409,000 people for 2026. What happened in Penza may reflect “excesses on the ground” by a region falling behind on its quota, rather than a model to be replicated nationwide. (In fairness, similar detentions have occurred in other Russian regions as well.)
- Possible mobilization preparations have also been linked to drills for mobilization procedures in the Kaliningrad region, an increase in job postings for military registration specialists, the distribution of mobilization notices Zelensky mentioned, and other developments. As with the laws above, none of this directly indicates whether mobilization will actually happen.
One argument deserves closer scrutiny: the central case Ukraine has been making for months. Zelensky and other Ukrainian military and political leaders have insisted that Russia needs mobilization not to expand its force at the front, but simply to replace its losses there. According to Kyiv’s account, that’s tied to the Ukrainian military’s success inflicting casualties on Russian forces. In this telling, the Ukrainian army has learned to kill or severely wound more Russian soldiers each month than Russia’s military can recruit.
Is that actually true? Probably not, though we can’t say for certain. There’s no reliable estimate of Russian military losses for 2026. The dispute centers on a benchmark figure of 30,000 people a month; Ukraine claims Russia loses more troops than that. This fall, we’ll test that estimate as part of a new round of our research into Russian military losses, drawing on data from the Registry of Inheritance Cases and named lists of the dead. But none of our previous rounds have come anywhere close to that level.
In August, German economist Janis Kluge wrote that the influx of new recruits into Russia’s armed forces in the second quarter stood at roughly a thousand people a day — the same 30,000-a-month figure. Kluge draws on regional budget data, which fund the large lump-sum payments made to contract soldiers and offer one of the most reliable metrics for tracking Russian army recruitment. In his view, the need for a new mobilization isn’t as acute as Ukrainian and Western sources claim.
But Putin may not be guided solely by “objective” criteria for maintaining the status quo. To reach the “victory” he envisions in the war, he could well opt for a “proactive” buildup of the army through mobilization.
We’ve already described the problems with this step in a recent series of answers to readers’ questions about the war.
- Formations and larger units — brigades, divisions, corps, armies — need support elements: air defense, electronic warfare, logistics, artillery, and so on. Contract-soldier recruitment quotas are set at their current level because that’s how many people the army can actually “absorb,” meaning train and equip. Units fight, not individual soldiers, and those units need officers — both combat and staff officers. There are now also drone-operator units numbering in the thousands.
- The Kremlin has already seen forced mobilization spark public discontent and drive people to flee the country. The social and political risks are real. There’s a financial dimension too: for, say, 300,000 newly mobilized troops, the federal budget alone would have to pay out more than a trillion rubles in the first year alone, by a conservative estimate, in signing bonuses, salaries, supplemental payments, and death and injury benefits.
Despite those risks, Russia’s Defense Ministry may well have a clear interest in mobilization: it appears dissatisfied with the recruits it’s currently getting. It’s hard to build the high-tech units of the “army of the future” out of people who risked their lives for money out of financial desperation, and without mobilization, there’s no alternative to them.
- Over the past year, Russia’s military has tried to recruit several tens of thousands of drone operators from among students and other young people, promising a guaranteed short-term contract with no possibility of transfer to other branches of service. Students apparently didn’t trust the military, and the campaign fell flat.
- The Defense Ministry has similarly tried to recruit people for mobile firing teams that combat drones in the rear, this time prioritizing cost. It tried to staff the teams with reservists — people who receive small payments from the army in exchange for short annual training stints. That campaign hasn’t shown signs of success either, though some reservists do turn up in mobile firing teams.
The Kremlin could well conclude — especially if Putin himself favors the idea — that mobilization would solve the recruit-quality problem. But that, too, remains purely speculative for now.
One last point: alarmism versus rationality.
The 2022 mobilization inflicted deep trauma on Russian society. Hundreds of thousands of people were sent to the front; hundreds of thousands of their family members lost loved ones (named lists alone show more than 20,000 mobilized soldiers have already died in the war, and the true toll is likely far higher); and hundreds of thousands fled the country in a hurry, with nowhere to go. Almost no one wants to relive that experience, save for a small camp of the war’s most die-hard supporters. Even reporting the news triggers irritation among Russians. We feel it every time we’re accused of alarmism after publishing an article, a YouTube show, or an Instagram post about mobilization.
Unfortunately, we can’t say for certain that this anxiety is entirely unfounded, if only because we don’t know what’s going on inside the head of Vladimir Putin, the main (and perhaps only) “decision-making center” on the Russian side. One can only assume he’d suffer serious reputational damage if, after soothing statements dismissing mobilization rumors as “utter nonsense,” he turned around and announced a forced draft of hundreds of thousands of recruits.
But does Putin actually care about his reputation? Is he guided by rational arguments in pursuing his goals, and what does he even want the war to achieve in the end? Only he knows the answers. And the vertical power structure he has built over the course of the war has done a great deal to ensure that any new mobilization goes as “seamlessly” as possible — for the authorities, if not for citizens.
At Meduza, we are committed to transparency about our use of artificial intelligence in the newsroom. The story you’re reading was written by one of our living, breathing journalists and translated from Russian using an AI model configured to follow our strict editorial standards. This translation process is the result of extensive testing and refinements to ensure our English-language coverage is timely and accurate. A Meduza editor reviews every draft before publication.
If you find any errors in this translation, please contact us at [email protected].
To read Meduza’s exclusive content in English, please subscribe to our newsletter.

articles.title: One Russian drone held up seven flights in Moldova, Zelenskyy’s trip to Norway for King Harald V’s funeral among them
articles.body:
Moldova closed its airspace on the afternoon of 8 September and delayed the plane carrying Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to Norway after a Russian drone crossed into the country, its government said in a statement to Reuters. The aircraft was cleared for takeoff once officials established that it had come down on Moldovan territory. Norway's prime minister described the episode as a near-miss, and neither government has said how close the drone came.
Russia runs three things at once along the EU's eastern frontier—mass drone attacks on Ukraine, drones crossing into Moldovan and Romanian airspace almost weekly, and strikes on the border checkpoints tying the three countries together—and states without interceptors can answer only by closing their skies.
What happened, and when
Moldova's National Army detected a Shahed-type drone entering from Ukraine at 16:20, the country's Defense Ministry reported. It flew toward Bender, a city in the Russian-backed breakaway region of Transnistria, then turned toward the capital, Chișinău, by 16:32. At 16:37, it left the country over western Moldova and headed into eastern Romania, across the Prut river border.
Controllers restricted the airspace over central Moldova at 16:30. The same drone came back from the Romanian side, crossed the north of the country, and came down outside a village in the northwest, near the Romanian border, setting dry vegetation alight, according to the log. Nobody was hurt, and the airspace reopened at 17:39, more than an hour after it closed. The BBC's Ukrainian service placed the crash near a different northern village, without naming a source, so the exact spot is unsettled.
The violation fell in the window when Zelenskyy's aircraft was preparing to take off, Militarnyi reported, citing the ministry. The civilian airport he was leaving from suspended operations and the border service closed the nearby crossings, the outlet added. Three departures and four arrivals were delayed in all, Reuters said.
A drone nearly hit Zelenskyy’s plane taking off from Moldova on his way to a king’s funeral, Norway’s PM says
How the plane and the drone crossed paths
Zelenskyy flies an Airbus A319 corporate jet, and the threat to it probably came from a jet-powered Geran drone that crossed Romanian and then Moldovan airspace at around 17:00 that day, Militarnyi wrote, publishing the drone's track from the monitoring channel Oko Hora. That fits the return leg in the army's log, though no authority has tied a specific aircraft to the delay.
Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre told the broadcaster NRK the plane was almost hit as it prepared to leave, without naming his source. His office later described a danger recorded in Moldovan airspace that forced the delay. Norway's Finance Minister Jens Stoltenberg said Zelenskyy recounted the details himself at a closed meeting in Oslo.
Zelenskyy and First Lady Olena Zelenska attended the farewell ceremony for King Harald V, who died on 28 August. Around it, the president worked on air defense, meeting Støre and then executives of defense companies from partner countries about the FREYJA anti-ballistic missile program, which Norway's government casts as a cheaper alternative to the Patriot.
Trending Now
The next night, the border crossing
Overnight on 9 September, Russian drones struck the Starokozache crossing on Ukraine's border with Moldova, killing two people and injuring three. The dead were Ukrainians, and a Moldovan citizen was among the injured, Moldova's Foreign Ministry told the broadcaster TV8. Border guards reopened the crossing that afternoon.
Russia claimed it had struck the crossing because it was used for military logistics. Moldova's Foreign Ministry rejected that outright, saying no weapons move through its territory, and that the people crossing there are families, children with their mothers, and the elderly. It is one of the working crossings on the Odesa Oblast stretch of the Ukrainian-Moldovan border, where the heaviest traffic runs through Palanca and Giurgiulești.
Moldova's President Maia Sandu condemned both the strike and the Geran-type drone that had forced her country to close its airspace the day before, and said the events show Ukraine needs more air defense.
Moldova is investing in air defense against the Russian drones crossing from Ukraine—Romania shoots down the ones that reach it
The pattern, and Moldova's empty sky
Russia has hit at least five checkpoints on Ukraine's western borders since late August, four of them facing Moldova and one facing Romania, and the drone that struck the Kotlovyna crossing on 20 August flew in through Moldovan airspace. Euromaidan Press has covered part of that campaign, including burned food cargo near the Giurgiulești crossing in August. The State Border Guard Service has called such strikes an act of terrorism, because people are present at the crossings when they are hit.
In the air, Moldova can do little. It is still buying its first serious air defenses, so it restricts airspace and waits while Romania scrambles jets against the drones that reach its side. It logged three airspace breaches in nine days in August, and more than 100 drones were detected near Romania in four days that month.

articles.title: General Atomics Offers First Glimpse of Wildfire Drone, Eyed as MQ-9 Successor
articles.body:
General Atomics has unveiled the first renderings of its Wildfire drone, which it plans to pitch for the Air Force’s hunt for a new, low-cost Massed Modular Aircraft.
Wildfire was unveiled in a sizzle reel-type video General Atomics Aeronautical Systems Inc. posted on social media Sept. 9. The video touts more than three decades of the company’s unmanned aerial vehicle development, starting with the Gnat and Predator drones flown in the 1990s up to and including its latest FQ-42A Dark Merlin, before revealing the first three images of Wildfire in short succession.
The images provide hints of the drone’s expected capabilities. One image shows Wildfire carrying four Joint Strike Missiles, which are stealthy cruise missiles, and another shows it with two Long Range Anti-Ship Missiles, or LRASMs.
“The whole point of a flying weapons truck is to come heavy,” General Atomics spokesman C. Mark Brinkley said in response to Air & Space Forces Magazine questions. “Wildfire will be able to carry a minimum of two LRASMs, four JSMs, or some similar configuration of heavy stand-off weapons, across meaningful combat distances.”
Brinkley said the MQ-9A is not be able to carry those payloads, and that they’re twice as much as the Pentagon originally envisioned for MMA. Brinkley said it’s too soon to sat how many Hellfire missiles—which the MQ-9A frequently employs—the Wildfire drone will be able to carry.
A third image shows a swarm of nearly a dozen Wildfire drones bearing down on a group of enemy ships and firing a barrage of missiles at them.
The Air Force envisions Massed Modular Aircraft, or MMA, as a low-cost drone to take on missions now done by General Atomics’ MQ-9A, and wants MMA to be semi-autonomous and able to be sent in groups to overwhelm enemy defenses.
Top Air Force officials told reporters Sept. 3 that they want the MMA’s air vehicle—not counting sensors or other capabilities—to cost no more than $10 million apiece. This would allow MMA to be “attritable,” meaning they would be inexpensive enough to be fielded in large numbers and easily replaced if lost in combat.
The Air Force and the Defense Innovation Unit, when unveiling the MMA concept in July, said losing $30 million drones in battle against an enemy would be unsustainable in a large-scale conflict, and a less expensive option is needed.
The conflict with Iran has cost the Air Force about 45 of its MQ-9 drones. In the Sept. 3 briefing, Air Force officials said the MQ-9 losses were concerning enough to push the service to accelerate its MMA effort. The Air Force and DIU want to have a prototype MMA a year after is contract is awarded and to start fielding it at scale within three years, or as early as 2029.
General Atomics created Wildfire as a clean-sheet design, and said it will be able to achieve all the Air Force’s MMA requirements at a high quality and an affordable price.
Brinkley said Wildfire will be able to exceed the Air Force and DIU’s 8,000 nautical mile ferry range requirement for MMA.
It will be modular, which will allow the Air Force to rapidly add or swap out different capabilities. When asked about Wildfire’s sensing capabilities, Brinkley said it will have “certain features available right out of the box,” but it will be up to the Air Force to decide what modular capabilities it wants to add.
“Modularity is key,” Brinkley said. “We’re showing that now with our Gambit series of uncrewed jets, which includes the XQ-67A Off-Board Sensing Station and FQ-42A Collaborative Combat Aircraft. One design, seamlessly pivoting to various missions. Wildfire will be able to do much the same from an [intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance]/strike lane.”
Brinkley said General Atomics will use its experience on autonomy, artificial intelligence, and machine learning from its work on programs like CCA and the MQ-20 Avenger, “to network dozens of Wildfires together on Day One.”
Brinkley said General Atomics has more than 5 million square feet of manufacturing space it could leverage to build Wildfire, and that the company has produced up to 100 aircraft per year, including MQ-9s.
“We have said from the beginning that we can deliver Wildfires years earlier than the [Air Force and DIU’s original] fiscal 2031 timeline,” Brinkley said. “We can deliver more than twice as many aircraft as originally asked for in the same amount of time. We’re not worried about scaling at all.”

articles.title: Kyiv couple marries after Russian strike ruins their home
articles.body:
A Russian strike hit a warehouse across the street from Liudmyla and Leonid Ryzhak's Kyiv apartment overnight into 8 September, sending a blast wave through their home hours before they were due to get married, the Associated Press reported. Leonid, 43, a soldier on leave from the front, had come back for the wedding.
Ukrainians keep marrying and rebuilding through a war that keeps interrupting both. More than 79,000 couples registered their marriages in the first half of 2026, 16% more than in the same period last year, nearly 40% of them online, according to Ukraine's Ministry of Justice figures. In July alone, the UN counted 437 civilians killed across the country, the deadliest month since May 2022.
The explosion blew out the windows, scattered furniture, and left the apartment uninhabitable. The couple fled to a shelter with Liudmyla's 6-year-old daughter and two guinea pigs. Their cat hid and could not be found. A second strike hit after they reached the shelter.
Neighbors clearing debris stopped to congratulate them.
“We should all be celebrated, that we survived,” Liudmyla replied.
They dug their wedding clothes out of the debris. Liudmyla, 33, shook broken glass from her white tulle skirt, which had small holes. Leonid could not find his dress trousers, so he wore army trousers with his embroidered shirt and sneakers.
The strike was part of a mass Russian attack on Kyiv that came once US peace envoys left the capital, ending a lull that had held for three days. Russia launched 166 drones and 32 cruise missiles at Ukraine overnight, along with ballistic and anti-ship missiles, and air defenses downed 142 drones, 31 cruise missiles, and two ballistic missiles, the Air Force said. Three people were killed in Kyiv, Kyiv Mayor Vitalii Klitschko said.
The couple arrived at the registry office on time, at 10:40, but another air-raid siren sounded soon after and the office closed. They waited in the courtyard for almost three hours as explosions hit the surrounding districts.
Eventually, the alert ended, and the couple went inside.
"If God gave me a continuation of life, then why should I put it off?" Liudmyla said. "At least for now, I have the right to be happy," she added.
They got married.

articles.title: Iran nuclear file is back at the UN Security Council. What now?
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Iran's nuclear file is back at the UN Security Council. What will happen next?
The International Atomic Energy Agency's Board of Governors has referred Iran to the UN Security Council over its alleged failure to comply with nuclear non-proliferation obligations, marking the first such referral in 20 years.
The 35-member board adopted the resolution on Wednesday by 23 votes in favour, with Russia, China and Niger voting against and eight countries abstaining.
Submitted by the United States, Britain, France and Germany, the resolution follows an earlier decision in June 2025 that found Iran to be in "non-compliance" with its obligations.
The latest move represents a significant diplomatic escalation between Tehran and Western powers, but with Russia and China holding veto power at the Security Council, it remains unclear whether it will result in any concrete action against Iran.
So why has Iran been referred, what could happen next, and what does it mean for Tehran's nuclear programme?
Why has Iran been referred to the Security Council?
The referral stems from the IAEA's previous finding that Iran had failed to comply with its nuclear non-proliferation obligations.
The agency's concerns predate the latest US-Iran war and centre partly on Tehran's failure to provide satisfactory explanations for traces of uranium found at undeclared Iranian sites that the IAEA had spent years investigating.
The Board of Governors ruled in June 2025 that Iran was in "non-compliance", but referring the matter to the Security Council on that basis required a separate resolution.
Wednesday's resolution also builds on a more recent decision calling on Iran to declare its remaining enriched uranium stockpile and allow IAEA inspectors to verify it.
What exactly does the new resolution do?
The resolution asks IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi to report on the latest decision and previous resolutions to all IAEA members, as well as to the UN Security Council and General Assembly.
Unlike a consensus decision, the resolution was put to a vote. Twenty-three countries backed it; Russia, China and Niger opposed it; and eight abstained.
It was submitted by four Western states: the US, Britain, France and Germany.
The referral itself does not impose new sanctions or other penalties on Iran. Instead, it formally brings the issue before the Security Council and increases diplomatic pressure on Tehran.
Why is the decision significant?
It is the first time Iran's nuclear file has been referred to the Security Council on non-compliance grounds in two decades.
It also comes during a vastly different political and military environment.
The June 2025 non-compliance finding was adopted just one day before Israel began bombing Iranian nuclear facilities, with the United States subsequently joining the attacks.
Iranian nuclear sites have also been targeted during the latest US-Israel war with Iran, while the IAEA has been unable to regain access to key facilities that were struck.
That has left the agency facing significant gaps in its knowledge about Iran's nuclear activities, including the fate of its highly enriched uranium.
How has Iran responded?
Iran has rejected the resolution as politically motivated.
Its mission to the IAEA said that "once again, a political resolution on Iran was adopted without consensus" by the agency's Board of Governors.
Tehran blamed the current situation entirely on what it described as the "criminal acts of aggression" committed by the United States and Israel, adding that Washington's objective of forcing Iran to surrender "will never be achieved".
Iran had warned before the vote that it would respond if the resolution was adopted, although its initial reaction did not specify what measures it might take.
Could the UN Security Council impose new measures on Iran?
In theory, bringing the issue before the Security Council opens another arena for international action against Tehran.
In practice, however, significant measures are considered unlikely.
Russia and China, both allies of Iran, are permanent members of the Security Council and possess veto power.
Both countries voted against Wednesday's IAEA resolution, meaning they could block attempts to impose measures against Tehran at the UN.
The immediate significance of the referral is therefore largely diplomatic: it further escalates the confrontation between Iran and Western powers and places the nuclear dispute formally before the Security Council.
What happened to Iran's enriched uranium?
This remains one of the biggest unanswered questions surrounding Iran's nuclear programme.
Iran has not allowed IAEA inspectors to return to bombed nuclear facilities, including the country's three uranium enrichment sites, which were destroyed or severely damaged in US-Israeli attacks.
Tehran has also not provided an account of its enriched uranium stockpile.
Before the strikes, the IAEA estimated that Iran possessed 440.9kg of uranium enriched to as much as 60 percent purity.
That is significantly above the levels normally associated with civilian nuclear energy and relatively close to the roughly 90 percent enrichment associated with weapons-grade material.
According to the IAEA's benchmark, the stockpile would have been sufficient, if further enriched, for around 10 nuclear weapons.
The agency believes more than 200kg of the stockpile remains at one site, although it is unclear how much survived the attacks undamaged.
Grossi has described the uncertainty surrounding the material as a "serious proliferation concern" and called for the situation to be addressed urgently.
Does this mean Iran is building a nuclear weapon?
No. The IAEA's non-compliance finding and the referral to the Security Council do not in themselves establish that Iran is building a nuclear weapon.
The dispute concerns Iran's compliance with its safeguards and reporting obligations, unanswered questions surrounding nuclear material and the IAEA's inability to verify the status of its enriched uranium stockpile.
Iran has consistently maintained that its nuclear programme is intended for peaceful purposes.
The immediate question is therefore not whether the Security Council will determine that Iran has decided to build a bomb, but whether the referral can increase pressure on Tehran to restore cooperation with inspectors and account for its nuclear material.
With Russia and China likely to oppose punitive Security Council action, the referral may ultimately have greater diplomatic significance than immediate practical consequences.

articles.title: Ukraine Hits Key Russia-Iran Shipping Hub on Caspian Sea in First Makhachkala Port Strike
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine Hits Key Russia-Iran Shipping Hub on Caspian Sea in First Makhachkala Port Strike
Ukrainian drones struck the Makhachkala International Commercial Seaport on Russia’s Caspian coast overnight on September 10, hitting a strategically important transport hub linked to maritime traffic with Iran roughly 1,000 kilometers from Ukraine’s border, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy confirmed.
The Ukrainian OSINT community Exilenova+ published footage of the operation.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Residents of Makhachkala reported explosions around the port during the overnight raid, marking the first known Ukrainian strike on port infrastructure in the city.
The target is particularly significant because Makhachkala serves as one of Russia’s principal maritime gateways on the Caspian Sea and maintains extensive shipping links with Iran.
The port has been used by vessels traveling between Russia and Iranian ports, including routes associated with the movement of military cargo and components for Iranian-designed drones supplied to Moscow.
Cargo arriving through Makhachkala can then move farther into Russia by road, rail and air, making the port part of a broader logistics network connecting Iranian suppliers with Russian military infrastructure.
Makhachkala is also Russia’s only ice-free deepwater commercial port on the Caspian Sea, allowing it to operate year-round.
The facility handles both liquid and dry cargo, with oil and petroleum products playing an increasingly important role in its operations.
Cargo volumes have surged during Russia’s war against Ukraine. During the first eight months of 2026, the port handled more than 2.9 million metric tons of cargo, an increase of 42.5% compared with the same period last year.
Oil accounted for more than 2.08 million tons of that total, rising nearly 50% year over year.
The acceleration was already evident earlier in 2026. Cargo turnover reached 1.4 million metric tons during the first four months of the year and climbed to 2.11 million tons by the end of June, roughly 50% above the same period in 2025.
Liquid cargo drove most of that expansion. During the first half of the year alone, the port handled nearly 1.57 million metric tons of oil and other liquid cargo.
Previously, Ukraine’s Security Service used long-range drones to strike multiple military and logistical targets across Russia overnight on July 25, including maritime targets in the Caspian Sea.
Ukrainian drones struck several targets in the Caspian Sea, including the Filanovsky offshore oil platform, the sanctioned cargo vessel Port Olya 2, the dry cargo ship Begey, and a Russian Project 12418 Molniya missile boat.
Ukrainian military intelligence further reported that Begey had been used to transport ammunition, artillery shells, body armor, and helmets from Iran across the Caspian Sea. During voyages between Iranian and Russian ports, the vessel’s crew allegedly switched off its Automatic Identification System (AIS), according to Ukrainian authorities.
Earlier, reports emerged that Ukraine carried out a drone attack against a sanctioned Russian cargo ship in the Mediterranean Sea, striking the vessel 12 times as it allegedly transported Iranian weapons and armored vehicles to Russia.

articles.title: Trump says Iran war will end ‘immediately’ after US midterms
articles.body:
U.S. President Donald Trump said Wednesday that he expects the war with Iran to end “immediately after the election,” arguing that Tehran is trying to hold out until the November 3 midterms in hopes that Democrats will regain control of Congress.
Trump made the remarks while speaking to reporters before departing for a Republican conference in Dallas, as crude oil prices climbed above $100 a barrel amid renewed escalation with Iran. “I think the war is going to end immediately after the election,” he said. Asked why, Trump replied: “Because they can't hold out any longer. They're desperate to try and affect the election so that we can get a nice weak group of people in there and leave them alone and let them have their nuclear weapon. All they want is a nuclear weapon. And if they had a nuclear weapon, the whole world is in deep trouble.”
Trump also took responsibility for recent U.S. attacks on Iranian vessels and suggested more strikes were coming. “Well, the attacks are made by us. We've knocked out nine of their ships,” he said. “And you're going to see a lot more.” At the same time, he signaled that Washington’s objectives go beyond another nuclear agreement, saying the U.S. was “not looking for a deal” and was seeking “much more than a nuclear deal,” while adding that negotiations could still take place.
The president also said he would speak with Israel about sanctions imposed on Israeli settlements in the West Bank. Britain announced new economic measures this week targeting companies and individuals involved in settlement activity, while Canada and France have also moved against settlement goods as part of coordinated pressure on Israel. The British move has sparked a diplomatic row with Jerusalem and criticism from leading Jewish communal figures in the UK.
Trump’s remarks came as Tehran faced a separate escalation on the diplomatic front. For the first time in 20 years, the International Atomic Energy Agency’s Board of Governors voted Wednesday to refer Iran to the UN Security Council after determining that Tehran had violated its obligations under the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty. The resolution was backed by 23 of the board’s 35 member states, with Russia, China and Niger voting against, eight abstaining and one not participating.
The referral is not expected to produce immediate sanctions because Russia and China, both Iranian allies and permanent members of the Security Council, could block such measures. Still, sending the issue to the UN’s most powerful body marks a significant diplomatic escalation and follows an IAEA resolution adopted on June 12, 2025, one day before Israel launched its war against Iran, which found Tehran in violation of its nonproliferation commitments.
The dispute centers in part on long-running IAEA investigations into uranium traces found at undeclared Iranian sites and Tehran’s refusal to allow inspectors full access to facilities damaged in the war. Iran has consistently denied pursuing nuclear weapons, but since its nuclear sites were bombed in June 2025 it has sharply restricted cooperation with the agency.
A central unresolved question is the fate of Iran’s stockpile of uranium enriched to 60%, close to the 90% level associated with weapons-grade material. Before the 2025 war, Iran possessed 440.9 kilograms of uranium enriched to 60%, an amount estimated to be sufficient for at least 10 nuclear weapons if enriched further. Much of the material was reportedly buried underground near the damaged Isfahan facility, while Iran has denied inspectors access to Isfahan, Natanz and Fordow.
The survival of that stockpile remains a major concern in Israel, where officials fear Tehran could eventually move the material to a secret facility and enrich it rapidly to weapons grade. One site that has drawn particular attention is a deeply buried complex known in Israel as “Pickaxe Mountain,” which Israeli officials fear could be difficult to destroy even with bunker-busting bombs.
Iran had threatened to respond if the IAEA referred the issue to the Security Council, though no concrete retaliatory step had been announced by Wednesday evening. Iranian Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi accused Western countries of exploiting conditions created by attacks on Iran’s nuclear facilities, while Iran’s mission to the IAEA denounced the decision as political and blamed the United States and Israel for the current crisis.

articles.title: Houthis seize key Yemen city near Bab el-Mandeb Strait
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Houthis seize key Yemen city near Bab el-Mandeb Strait
The Houthis have seized the strategic Yemeni port city of Mocha on the Red Sea coast, government sources said on Thursday, marking a major development in the renewed fighting as tens of thousands have been displaced across the country.
Three Yemeni government sources told Reuters that Houthi forces had entered Mocha and taken control of the coastal city, while local sources told The New Arab that large numbers of residents were fleeing towards the southern city of Aden.
The takeover comes after weeks of escalating Houthi attacks on Mocha and its port and amid a broader offensive by the Iran-backed group across western Yemen.
Mocha is strategically important because of its location on Yemen's western coast near the Bab al-Mandab Strait, the narrow waterway connecting the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden and one of the world's most important maritime trade routes.
The city's capture could therefore have wider implications for security around the strait and commercial shipping through the Red Sea, as fighting intensifies across Yemen's western coast.
The Houthis launched a major offensive in Hodeidah and Taiz provinces last week aimed at advancing towards Bab al-Mandab, prompting government-aligned forces to mount counterattacks and expand operations elsewhere in the country.
Mocha had already come under repeated Houthi missile, drone and explosive-laden boat attacks in recent weeks.
The city's port suspended all commercial and maritime operations in mid-August after it was struck by more than 25 Houthi missiles, according to information provided by sources.
The attacks caused civilian casualties and damaged facilities and property, with material losses estimated at around $16 million.
The takeover coincides with an escalation in fighting along Yemen's western coast, particularly in southern Hodeidah and western Taiz, where government and allied forces have been carrying out military movements and withdrawing from several positions.
Yemeni government forces withdrew overnight from Hays district in southern Hodeidah as military units operating around Hays and western Taiz began a process of reorganisation and redeployment, military and local sources said.
It remains unclear how many troops withdrew from Hays and Al-Wazi'iyah or where they have been redeployed. Military sources said the movements were part of preparations for a coordinated field operation.
Tareq Saleh orders western coast forces to regroup
Tareq Saleh, deputy chairman of Yemen's Presidential Leadership Council, said on Thursday that government forces on the western coast had suffered heavy losses in recent days while confronting the Houthi offensive.
Saleh said forces had been ordered to regroup and establish an alternative command centre in a secure location in consultation with the Saudi-led coalition and the Presidential Leadership Council.
Military media affiliated with Saleh's National Resistance said the joint forces had established a command centre south of Mocha following Houthi breakthroughs on several fronts under heavy fire.
The forces involved in the western coast fighting include the National Resistance, the Giants Brigades and Nation's Shield forces, alongside units from the Taiz military axis.
Saleh accused Iran of planning, supporting and participating in the Houthi offensive through what he described as its "various tools", without providing further details about Tehran's alleged involvement.
Iran has rejected accusations that it is interfering in Yemen, saying this week that it supports the country's unity and territorial integrity and a Yemeni-led dialogue based on a UN-backed roadmap.
Meanwhile, military media sources reported air strikes on Houthi positions in Al-Tuhayta, Al-Salif and Kamaran Island in Hodeidah province.
The National Resistance's military media also said the Houthis had targeted Zuqar Island with two ballistic missiles.
The latest developments come amid the most significant escalation on several Yemeni fronts following years of relative calm. Large-scale fighting largely subsided following a UN-brokered truce in 2022, but clashes resumed in July and have since widened.
Fighting has also spilled across the border into Saudi Arabia, with Riyadh accusing the Houthis of targeting Khamis Mushait, Abha and Jazan with ballistic missiles and drones. Saudi authorities said this week that recent Houthi attacks had wounded at least 73 people.

articles.title: North Korea has built new uranium facility to expand nuclear arsenal, UN agency says
articles.body:
The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) has voiced “serious concern” over evidence that North Korea has built a facility capable of enriching weapons-grade uranium to bolster its nuclear arsenal.
The new building, located at the the country’s main Yongbyon nuclear facility, can house up to 28 centrifuge cascades – machinery commonly used to enrich uranium – according to a report by the nuclear watchdog released this week.
The regime has also expanded operations at an enrichment site in Kangson, near the capital Pyongyang, according to the report, which was based on analysis of satellite imagery and open-source material, including photographs published by the country’s state media.
The IAEA, whose inspectors were expelled from North Korea in 2009, identified the Yongbyon building as the site’s second uranium enrichment facility after comparing satellite images taken during its construction with media photographs of a visit in early June by the country’s leader, Kim Jong-un.
During his visit, Kim claimed the North’s capacity to produce weapons-grade nuclear material had more than doubled over the past five years, according to state media, promising “vast future plans to exponentially strengthen the country’s nuclear forces”.
Citing a 2025 analysis by the James Martin Center for Nonproliferation Studies in the US, South Korea’s Chosun Daily said the potential 28 cascades comprising 4,592 centrifuges at the Yongbyon facility could yield about 85 kg of weapons-grade highly enriched uranium a year – enough to build three or four additional warheads.
In a statement released this week, the IAEA’s director general, Rafael Grossi, said: “The ongoing operation of enrichment facilities at Kangson and Yongbyon and the reported further expansion of [North Korea’s] production of weapons-grade nuclear material is a cause for serious concern.”
“The continuation and further development” of North Korea’s nuclear programme are “clear violations of relevant UN security council resolutions and are deeply regrettable”, he added.
South Korea’s defence minister, Ahn Gyu-back, said in August that the North possessed between 80 and 120 nuclear warheads – a much higher number than the 57 cited by Donald Trump the same month. The South Korean figure was based on estimates by private research organisations, Ahn told lawmakers, adding that the country’s military could not confirm the numbers.
North Korea has made rapid progress in its ballistic missile and nuclear programmes in recent years, as it demands international recognition as a legitimate nuclear state.
North Korea has conducted multiple long-range missile tests since 2017, the year it last tested a nuclear weapon. In a report submitted to the UN security council in 2020, international experts said the North had “probably developed nuclear devices to fit into the warheads of its ballistic missiles”.

articles.title: Iran strikes ships, expands no-go zone outside Hormuz strait
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Iran strikes ships, expands no-go zone outside Hormuz strait
Iran said it attacked more than a dozen vessels trying to pass through the Strait of Hormuz on Wednesday, as it announced an expansion of a no-go zone outside the strategic waterway it has blockaded for months.
The fresh attacks and fighting with the United States sent oil prices above $100 per barrel again as Tehran chokes off the strait and Washington presses a counter-blockade of Iranian ports. Brent oil closed at $101.21.
Iran's Revolutionary Guards said on Wednesday they attacked two US vessels, eight oil tankers, and 10 "non-compliant vessels" that were trying to pass through the route crucial for oil and gas trade, Iranian state media reported.
The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) said "several" vessels in the Gulf of Oman and the Gulf were "subject to disabling fire as part of ongoing military activity in the region".
The Gulf of Oman lies on the Indian Ocean side of the narrow Hormuz strait, a vital energy conduit that normally carries around a fifth of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas.
Iran's Guards also for the first time added parts of the Gulf of Oman and the Arabian Sea to a new "prohibited zone" on Wednesday, saying exact coordinates will be announced later.
"If a vessel enters that area without coordination, it will be subject to our sanctions," Guards spokesman Hossein Mohebi told state television.
The Guards also said they struck a US military base in Jordan in response to US forces destroying five Iranian oil tankers a day earlier.
Jordan's army shot down 18 missiles fired at the kingdom, it said.
Iran's foreign ministry condemned the attack on its oil tankers as "an overt threat to regional and international peace and security," saying the strikes "increase the dangers of tensions in the region".
It said the targeting of US military facilities in the region was "self-defence".
The US military for its part had said it was responding to an Iranian attack targeting an American warship, the second such incident in less than a week.
Nuclear referral
Iran's Guards, the ideological arm of the military, said the war could be brought to an end if Washington met its conditions, which included demands on the wars in Lebanon and Yemen.
"It must... refrain from renewed threats, withdraw the Israeli regime's army from Lebanon, end the blockade of Yemen, release $24 billion in Iran's frozen assets and refrain from any interference in the country's nuclear and missile capabilities," Mohebi said, according to Fars news agency.
Donald Trump, an unpopular president eager to end an unpopular war, asserted Wednesday the conflict will conclude right after the mid-term US elections in November. Polls show his Republican Party could face a drubbing and lose control of one or both houses of Congress.
"I think the war will end immediately after the election" because Iran "can't hold out any longer," Trump told journalists, accusing Tehran of being "desperate to try and affect" the vote.
But as Washington tries to choke off Iran economically, the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) board of governors on Wednesday voted to refer Iran to the UN Security Council over its nuclear "non-compliance", in a diplomatic move that piles pressure on Tehran.
The resolution was adopted by a 23-3 vote with eight abstentions, they said. Russia, China and Niger voted against it.
Iran's representative to the UN nuclear watchdog said the resolution was passed under US pressure, saying it "has no basis and will not bring any results".
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu also repeated his claim Iran was on the verge of collapse.
"The main task is to bring down the terror regime in Iran. We are very close to that," he said Wednesday on a troop visit in southern Syria, where Israel has occupied what it calls a "security zone".
The latest round of US-Iran fighting was triggered after American forces destroyed five Iranian oil tankers Tuesday, with the US military saying it "directed the crews to abandon ship" before hitting the vessels.
"Iran continues to try to hit US naval ships, and for every time they do that or try to do that, they're going to lose tankers, and I think you'll see that again today," US Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters Tuesday on a visit to Colombia.
Iran has asserted control of the Strait of Hormuz since US-Israeli strikes began the war in February, with traffic through the waterway virtually paralysed.
Tehran requires vessels to obtain permission and pay transit fees before using the strait.

articles.title: Ukrainian FP-1 Drones Fly Record 3,200 km to Strike Russian Gas Processing Plant
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukrainian FP-1 Drones Fly Record 3,200 km to Strike Russian Gas Processing Plant
Ukrainian FP-1 long-range drones traveled more than 3,200 kilometers to strike a gas condensate processing facility in Russia’s Yamalo-Nenets Autonomous Okrug, setting a new reported distance record for the drone, according to Ukrainian defense company Fire Point and the CyberBoroshno OSINT project.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Fire Point said the target was the Novy Urengoy Condensate Preparation for Transport Plant, one of Russia’s largest facilities for processing gas condensate.
The strike also marks a significant increase in the FP-1’s reported reach. The drone initially had a maximum range of about 700 kilometers, compared with the more than 3,200 kilometers covered in the latest operation, substantially expanding the depth at which targets inside Russia can potentially be reached.
“We are erasing the deep rear doctrine from the Russian military vocabulary,” Fire Point CEO Iryna Terekh said at MSPO 2026 according to a UNITED24 Media correspondent.
CyberBoroshno reported that the drones specifically struck a de-ethanization gas treatment unit at the facility, operated by Gazprom Pererabotka and located about 18 kilometers from Novy Urengoy.
According to the OSINT project, FP-1 drones reached the Yamalo-Nenets region for the first time, making the facility the most distant target from Ukraine’s state border to have been struck since the beginning of Russia’s full-scale invasion.
Unlike oil refineries frequently targeted in Ukrainian long-range operations, the Novy Urengoy facility is part of Russia’s gas-processing industry. It handles the initial processing of unstable gas condensate into marketable products and receives feedstock from fields in the Nadym-Pur-Taz region, Russia’s largest gas-condensate basin. The plant has a design capacity of approximately 19.5 million tons of feedstock annually.
The unit targeted in the strike processes gases released during the de-ethanization of condensate. These gases contain ethane, a key feedstock for producing ethylene and polyethylene, and are intended to supply the Novy Urengoy Gas Chemical Complex.
The gas chemical complex has a planned production capacity of up to 400,000 tons of low-density polyethylene per year. CyberBoroshno estimated that this represents roughly 10% of Russia’s combined polyethylene and polypropylene production capacity.
According to the OSINT project, damage to the de-ethanization gas treatment unit could disrupt the broader production chain from gas condensate to polyethylene. Without gas treatment, ethane supplies to the Novy Urengoy Gas Chemical Complex could be interrupted, potentially affecting the production of ethylene and polyethylene.
CyberBoroshno noted that even if the plant’s condensate de-ethanization units remain operational, disruption to the gas treatment infrastructure could prevent the resulting gases from being processed and transferred further along the production chain.
The record-range FP-1 strike comes as Fire Point continues to expand its portfolio of domestically developed long-range weapons. The company has also advanced its FP-7 ballistic missile to military trials after completing two earlier rounds of testing, moving the system closer to potential operational deployment.

articles.title: BRICS 2026: Putin and Modi have high expectations going into key summit
articles.body:
BRICS 2026: Putin and Modi have high expectations going into key summit
Russian President Vladimir Putin is due to arrive in India for the BRICS summit in New Delhi, where he is meeting Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Friday.
The meeting is expected to build on the warm spirit and progress made in bilateral relations based around the personal relations between the two leaders.
India and Russia also have kept up high-level diplomatic and economic contacts, amid geopolitical turbulence. Putin and Modi most recently met last week in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, at the Shanghai Cooperation Organization summit.
Three Russian IL-76 planes, carrying advance teams and military officials, reportedly landed in the Indian city of Greater Noida on Thursday morning. The teams are reviewing preparations and security arrangements as Delhi gears up to host world leaders for the BRICS summit on September 12-13.
Energy the bedrock of the relationship
India has become the second biggest importer of Russian oil as New Delhi seeks to secure the energy needs of its 1.4 billion population. Russia sold around 2.1 million barrels per day of oil to India, or 45% of the country’s total imports, in August – even as New Delhi has widened its crude basket.
But it is not a simple buyer-seller relationship, with both sides invested in each other’s energy ecosystem. India’s state-run ONGC Videsh holds a 20% stake in Russia’s Sakhalin-1 oil field project. A consortium of state-run Indian oil majors have sizable stakes in Russian oil company Rosneft’s subsidiaries, Vankorneft and Taas-Yuryakh Neftegazodobycha.
Rosneft holds nearly half of India’s Nayara Energy, which owns a refinery in Gujarat and a wide downstream network.
The implications of India’s Russian oil purchases are global. Indian refiners play a major role in preventing crude prices from surging out of control as the Middle East conflict chokes off a large chunk of global supply. More specifically, Europe buys about 60% of its diesel and 15% of its jet fuel from Indian refiners, which it has – counterintuitively – tried to sanction over Russian oil.
Moscow has repeatedly said it is ready to supply “as much oil as India needs,” despite the threat of Western sanctions on New Delhi.
Nuclear energy is another key dimension of the relationship, with India setting itself an ambitious nuclear power target to generate 100 gigawatts by 2047. Two of the six units of the Koodankulam nuclear power plant, built in collaboration with Russia’s Rosatom in south India, are generating electricity, and four more are under construction.
Putin and Modi agreed in December to further discuss a second nuclear power plant and finalize the site for it – reportedly in Tirunelveli district in Tamil Nadu.
India also is eyeing Russia’s small modular reactors, or SMRs, to achieve its energy targets.
Expanding economic ties is imperative
Bilateral trade has jumped in volume since Putin’s last visit to India, when a $100 billion target was set to be achieved by 2030. However, India has run up a massive trade deficit against Russia through its oil purchases. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said on Tuesday that Russian businesses are looking to buy more Indian goods and establish joint projects to address the trade gap.
The same geopolitical tensions that have pushed India to buy more Russian oil are also opening up avenues to expand bilateral economic ties to new areas.
Russian aviation companies could lead the charge. The CEO of Russia’s United Aircraft Corporation, Vadim Badekha, said a licensing agreement with Hindustan Aeronautics Limited for producing the SJ-100 regional jet is being finalized and the contract could be signed soon.
The first localized version of the Superjet could be made in India in three years, with the company looking at selling 100-200 planes. Indian airlines have also expressed interest in buying up to 100 Il 114-300 planes from Russia.
The Northern Sea Route, or the Arctic Route that skirts thousands of miles of Russia's coastline is high on the agenda this year. India plans to send its first ship along the route next year to take advantage of the time and cost efficiencies.
In addition, India is looking to Russia for its requirements of rare-earth minerals, which go into key components such as magnets needed for green energy transition. New Delhi is also exploring options to buy coking coal assets and import more nickel from Russia to boost steel production.
The two countries signed a labor mobility and migration agreement in December. First Deputy Prime Minister Denis Manturov said in February that Russia can accept an “unlimited” number of Indian workers. Tourism is another area that saw progress during Putin’s December visit, with both countries agreeing to provide 30-day e-tourist visas to travelers.
Both countries now settle the bulk of their transactions in local currencies, smoothing out frustrations over payment bottlenecks. It is a topic other BRICS leaders will also be interested in.
Defense and space ties bind India to Russia
India remains the top customer of Russian military hardware, inking deals to buy and manufacture many top-end Russian systems.
Joint production of the Russian fifth-generation Su-57 fighter aircraft is expected to feature prominently in the Putin-Modi talks. A Russian offer for full licensed production of the Su-57 in India, along with unrestricted transfer of technology, is already on the table, and talks are reportedly ongoing.
“We are ready to supply India with this aircraft, to keep developing it. We don’t have any issues or limitations,” Putin said in June.
Other weapons such as the S-500 missile system could also be discussed.
New Delhi and Moscow have partnered in the space sector since the early 1960s. Russia is collaborating on India’s manned spaceflight program, Gaganyaan, by providing crew training and supplying spacesuits. The collaboration will include engine building, rocket fuel, and the development of national orbital stations, Russian space agency Roscosmos has said.
Why India’s farmers need Putin’s helping hand
The Middle East conflict has disrupted fertilizer supplies from the Gulf countries, with implications for food production and food security in the world’s most populous nation – pushing the item to the top of the agenda for Modi and Putin.
Russia increased fertilizer exports to India by 20% in the first half of this year, and is ready to continue deliveries, First Deputy Prime Minister Manturov said in a recent interview.
Putin also reiterated this to Indian Foreign Minister S. Jaishankar in Moscow last month, saying “we’re doing everything to close this issue for Indian farmers, for agriculture.”
Why the Modi-Putin personal chemistry matters
Putin’s visit comes as the threat of steep US tariffs looms over India for buying Russian oil. The challenge before the two leaders is to deepen the relationship while keeping their respective national interests front and center amid Western coercion.
Kremlin spokesman Peskov said on Tuesday that both leaders are in close personal contact and able to discuss sensitive matters in open and constructive ways.
It’s a moment in history when the rapport Putin and Modi share will matter more than ever.

articles.title: Ukraine’s Bulava drone can now hunt in the dark—one camera handles day and night
articles.body:
Ukraine's Bulava strike drone can now hunt around the clock, its crews no longer switching optics between day and night. Its maker, DeViRo, showed the upgraded drone at a defense exhibition in Poland, the Military news outlet Militarnyi reported. The overhaul brings a new camera and lengthens the drone's flight time, and the developers say they substantially improved its flight characteristics. The company said every future production batch will carry the new optics.
Ukraine's war effort increasingly runs on small private firms that keep sharpening cheap drones in months, reworking weapons already in the fight rather than waiting years for a new model. A drone that sees in the dark can work the same targets after sunset that it hunts by day.
One camera for day and night
The updated loitering munition carries a multispectral optical station that lets it operate at any hour, a company representative told Militarnyi at the MSPO defense exhibition in Poland. The station packs a daytime channel and a thermal-imaging channel into one body, so crews no longer swap in different camera modules depending on the time of day. Operators flip between the two modes in the control station's software while the drone is already in the air.
Ukraine shows a home-built missile designed to hit ballistic targets for the first time, the Koral, at Poland’s MSPO
Longer in the air, 120 to 130 km out
Bulava now stays aloft for up to 110 minutes, and its guaranteed working range runs from 120 to 130 km, with room to grow depending on conditions and crew training.
DeViRo tied the drone to a summer campaign against Russian logistics, in which it says Bulava crews cleared the way for deeper strikes.
"We knocked out enemy radars and air defenses so that deep strikes could fly as deep as possible," the company representative said.
The company says its crews took a very active part in that campaign, which hit Russian supply routes across the south.
An interceptor in the same family
DeViRo builds more than strike drones. In March, it introduced the Sokyra interceptor, a prototype built to shoot down Russian attack drones. The prototype was listed at 240 km/h, a 45 km range, 30 minutes aloft, and a 750-gram warhead at the alpha-testing stage.

articles.title: Ukraine seeks 300 Patriot missiles from allies
articles.body:
Ukraine has asked allied countries to provide 300 Patriot interceptor missiles from their existing stocks as Kyiv attempts to strengthen its air defences before another winter of Russian missile and drone attacks.
Ukrainian Defence Minister Evgeniy Khmara set out the requirement during his first appearance at the Ukraine Defence Contact Group, alongside requests for 500 air-to-air interceptors capable of engaging cruise missiles and $2 billion in funding for drones.
Khmara said a recent Russian attack had involved cruise missiles, ballistic missiles and jet-powered Shahed-type drones. Ukrainian air defences had intercepted 31 of 32 cruise missiles, he said, but ballistic missiles were proving more difficult to counter because of shortages of Patriot ammunition.
He said: “Our air defence managed, among other things, to intercept 31 of the 32 cruise missiles, but the situation with ballistics is much more difficult, and that difficulty is precisely down to the lack of Patriot missiles.”
Ukraine is already contracting around 1,000 Patriot missiles with support from partner countries and through European Union financing, according to Khmara, but most of those weapons are not expected to arrive immediately.
He therefore appealed to countries to transfer missiles currently held in their own inventories, saying: “we ask that you supply us the missiles from your stockpiles today, in exchange for future improved missiles from our contracts.”
Khmara also warned that Ukraine faces a substantial defence funding gap. He said €70 billion in security assistance had been promised this year, with around €62 billion currently expected from bilateral assistance and European funding.
That leaves €8 billion of the earlier commitment outstanding, while Khmara put the wider Ukrainian defence funding shortfall at €23 billion, equivalent to around $27 billion. He asked partners to take the necessary funding decisions by November so that equipment could reach the battlefield during the winter.
Drones also featured prominently in the Ukrainian presentation. Khmara said: “Up to 90 percent of our success in the battlefield is down to drones.”
He said Ukrainian companies were developing lower-cost methods of intercepting jet-powered Shahed-type drones, with some interceptor systems already being tested in combat. Khmara also said Ukrainian assessments indicated that Russia was planning to mobilise around 300,000 additional personnel on top of existing recruitment and could seek a similar mobilisation effort in 2027.
He argued that Moscow was attempting to turn the conflict into a competition over manpower and resources, while Ukraine intended to rely increasingly on technology, drones and rapid battlefield adaptation.

articles.title: US destroys 5 Iranian oil tankers, 3 linked to Russia's shadow fleet, Ukrainian official says
articles.body:
US destroys 5 Iranian oil tankers, 3 linked to Russia's shadow fleet, Ukrainian official says
The U.S. military destroyed five Iranian crude oil tankers on Sept. 8, three of which have ties to Russia's shadow fleet, Ukraine's sanctions commissioner Vladyslav Vlasiuk said in a comment shared with the Kyiv Independent.
U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) on Sept. 9 said its forces struck the five vessels in response to attempts by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) to target a U.S. Navy warship with ballistic missiles.
The five vessels were the Kaviz, Charminar, Horizon 1 and Riesco in the Gulf of Oman, as well as the Derya near Iran's Kharg Island. U.S. forces instructed the crews to abandon the vessels before striking them, CENTCOM said.
Three of the tankers, the Kaviz, Charminar, and Riesco, have direct links to Russia's shadow fleet and have been involved in transporting Russian oil, Vlasiuk said.
The Kaviz had called at the Russian ports of Ust-Luga and Novorossiysk and transported Russian oil, according to Vlasiuk. He added that the vessel had repeatedly switched off its Automatic Identification System (AIS), which ships use to broadcast information including their location and identity.
According to Ukraine's military intelligence agency (HUR), the Kaviz was previously affiliated with Fractal Marine DMCC, a company sanctioned by the U.K. for servicing Russia's energy sector and identified by HUR as a key operator of Russia's shadow fleet. HUR also lists the tanker as sanctioned by the U.S., Ukraine, the EU, Switzerland, the U.K. and Canada.
The Charminar had previously called at the Russian ports of Ust-Luga, Primorsk, Vysotsk and St. Petersburg, Vlasiuk said.
HUR lists the Charminar as having been involved in exports of Russian crude and petroleum products and links the vessel to Fractal Marine DMCC. The vessel has also been linked to a shipping network associated with Iranian oil trader Mohammad Hossein Shamkhani, who trades in both Russian and Iranian oil, Vlasiuk said.
The third vessel, the Riesco, has likewise transported Russian and Iranian crude and petroleum products, including through ship-to-ship transfers with sanctioned vessels, according to HUR. The tanker has been under U.S. sanctions since November 2025 and Ukrainian sanctions since February 2026.
CENTCOM published footage showing the Riesco sinking in the Gulf of Oman following the strike.
Russia's shadow fleet is a network of vessels used to move sanctioned Russian oil around the world, at the same time obscuring ownership to avoid Western restrictions. HUR's register had identified more than 1,400 such vessels as of May 2026, many of them aging ships sailing under third-country flags.
The fleet has become a crucial source of revenue for Moscow, with estimates suggesting it carries about 75% of Russia's sanctioned oil and helps generate income used to fund the Kremlin's war against Ukraine.
