articles.title: Ukrainian drones strike Makhachkala port and Sochi waterfront, satellite data points to new damage in Russia’s Arctic gas region
articles.body:
Ukrainian drones attacked the commercial seaport in the city of Makhachkala in Russia’s Dagestan overnight into Sept. 10. At around 3 a.m., local residents began reporting explosions and air defense activity near the port. Before the authorities issued any official statements, the independent outlet Astra analyzed witness footage and determined that the commercial seaport was the likely target.
Astra also geolocated one of the explosions to the area of Pushkin Street where the Avar Theater is located.
Ukrainian monitoring channels Exilenova+ and Supernova+ published several videos showing drones flying overhead and exploding. Other footage showed smoke rising in the port area and damage in the city. Exilenova+ also published what it said was the apparent moment of a strike on the port’s infrastructure.
Acting Dagestan head Fyodor Shchukin confirmed that fires broke out at the port and at the Avarsky Theater. He said all aerial targets had been destroyed and that the fires were caused by falling debris. However, the theater’s director, Magomed Bisavaliyev, reported that a drone fell directly onto the building’s roof, blowing out windows before a fire started. Shchukin said the fires had been extinguished, no one was killed or injured, and the theater’s damaged roof would be repaired. Airports in Makhachkala, Vladikavkaz, and Grozny suspended operations for three and a half hours.
The Makhachkala Commercial Seaport is Russia’s only ice-free, deep-water port on the Caspian Sea. It is used for the shipment of oil, petroleum products, grain, containers, and other cargo moving between Russia, Iran, and countries in Central Asia and the South Caucasus. From January through August 2026, it handled a record 2.9 million metric tons of cargo, according to its own data, up 42.5% from a year earlier. More than 2 million metric tons of that volume was oil.
In addition to the strikes on Makhachkala, the Russian Black Sea city of Sochi was attacked by maritime drones on the evening of Sept. 9. Supernova+ published a full video of one part of the attack, while another clip captured a strike on a pier. Footage posted on social media also appeared to show a cafe building burning near a beach.
Twenty-eight people were injured in the attack, including two children.
Beach infrastructure and a nearby section of the Primorskaya Embankment were damaged. A concert by Russian singer Tatyana Bulanova at the Festivalny concert hall was also interrupted due to the threat of an attack, and performers and audience members were sent to shelter.
Russia’s Defense Ministry reported that it had intercepted more than 440 fixed-wing drones in the south of the country and over the Black Sea.
New data also emerged about the consequences of yesterday’s Ukrainian drone attack on gas infrastructure in the Yamalo-Nenets Autonomous District, located more than 2,000 kilometers from the border between the two countries.
The open-source intelligence channel Falcon Insight noted that NASA’s Fire Information for Resource Management System (FIRMS) detected several thermal anomalies at the Urengoyskaya compressor station near the Novy Urengoy Condensate Preparation Plant, which was attacked on Sept. 9.
Falcon Insight said such heat signatures are not typical for the compressor station.
The station supports several major gas pipelines, including the Urengoy-Center and Urengoy-Novopskov systems, which transport gas from the Yamalo-Nenets Autonomous District to other parts of Russia. There had been no previous reports of an attack on the compressor station, and there is still no separate confirmation that the facility was damaged. Satellite monitoring data only shows sources of intense heat and cannot by itself establish what caused them.
Ukraine’s Special Operations Forces claimed responsibility for strikes on two other facilities in the region: the Novy Urengoy and Purovsky gas condensate processing plants. The Novy Urengoy plant has a design capacity of 19.5 million metric tons of feedstock a year, while the Purovsky plant processed 13.4 million metric tons in 2025. Ukraine’s military did not list the Urengoyskaya compressor station among the targets it said had been hit.

articles.title: Ukraine almost ran out of F-16 missiles — Zelensky’s former spokeswoman
articles.body:
MOSCOW, September 10. /TASS/. The armed forces of Ukraine have almost run out of AIM-120 and AIM-9 air-to-air missiles for F-16 fighter jets, Vladimir Zelensky’s former press secretary Yulia Mendel said.
"In Ukraine, the missiles F-16s use <…> are almost gone. AIM-120s and AIM-9s are running out. Patriot batteries are also critically short of PAC-3 interceptors needed to stop ballistic missiles," she wrote on the X social network.
"І keep coming back to the same thought: without a move toward peace, there is just no way to stop the destruction and keep people alive," Mendel added.

articles.title: Zaluzhny: lack of technology, funding prevents Ukraine from seizing initiative from Russia
articles.body:
Ukrainian companies are capable of promptly responding to battlefield needs and developing new types of weaponry based on real combat experience, but state funding for defense innovation in Ukraine is limited, which is why private investment can and must become a mutually beneficial solution for both sides, Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary of Ukraine to the UK and former Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces of Ukraine (2021–2024) Valeriy Zaluzhny notes.
"Ukrainian companies are capable of promptly responding to battlefield needs and developing new types of weaponry based on real combat experience. No other country can offer more relevant experience for developing new arms, modernization, and tactics for their application. However, the lack of technology and funding prevents seizing the initiative from Russia and its partners," Zaluzhnyi said during a speech at the Defence & Resilience Tech Scale Up Showcase in London, the text of which was published in his column on the Interfax-Ukraine agency's website on Thursday.
He called on Ukraine's partners to increase financial and technological investments in arms production in Ukraine, not only to reduce Russia's military potential, but also to strengthen their own defense capabilities.
"State funding for defense innovation in Ukraine is limited. Therefore, private investments can and must become a beneficial solution for both sides. Creating clear mechanisms for cooperation with Great Britain at the institutional level will help attract private capital, technologies, and ultimately create new markets and develop long-term cooperation between the defense industries of Ukraine and its partners," the diplomat said.
Zaluzhnyi stated that Ukraine has gained significant experience in drone production, but the component base, and especially its production, currently remains outside Ukraine, which precludes possibilities for scaling and modernization in the long term, "where marketing gives way to strategy and the outline of victory finally becomes visible." "Even now, these investments are vital in countering urgent threats such as ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones," the former Commander-in-Chief emphasized.
He noted that achieving victory or a dignified peace requires systemic impact on Russia's ability to continue the war, rather than isolated technological solutions.
"Systemic impact means implementing strategies to achieve the main goal: victory over the enemy. Naturally, building such a systemic impact is possible only with appropriate strategies. These strategies must be based on implementing financial and technological policies that enable producing today what is needed tomorrow, or better yet, the day after tomorrow. And what is needed today should be taken from storage facilities as something produced yesterday. Defense production must be part of a war strategy, not the other way around, where war is made to justify someone's promises and profits. Only in this way is it possible to seize the initiative, impose one's will on the enemy, and demand terms from them," Zaluzhny concluded.

articles.title: Defense Forces destroy 128 Russian UAVs – Air Force
articles.body:
On the night of September 10, Russian occupiers attacked the territory of Ukraine with 149 strike UAVs of the Shahed, Herbera, and Parodiya-type decoy drone types, the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported.
"According to preliminary data, as of 08:00, air defense forces shot down/suppressed 128 Russian UAVs of the Shahed, Herbera, and other types," the report on the Telegram channel says.
In addition, hits by enemy air attack weapons were recorded at 13 locations, and falling debris from shot-down drones was recorded at nine locations.
The air attack was repelled by aviation, anti-aircraft missile troops, electronic warfare units, unmanned systems units, and mobile fire groups of the Defense Forces of Ukraine.
The attack is ongoing, with enemy UAVs remaining in the airspace.

articles.title: This Is What Ukraine’s Novorossiysk Strike Did to Russia’s Kalibr Fleet
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
This Is What Ukraine’s Novorossiysk Strike Did to Russia’s Kalibr Fleet
Satellite imagery and new visual evidence are revealing the aftermath of Ukraine’s September 9 strike on Novorossiysk, with at least three Russian Black Sea Fleet vessels now confirmed hit and additional missile-carrying warships appearing to have sustained damage.
Ukraine has confirmed that at least three Russian Black Sea Fleet vessels were hit during the September 9 missile-and-drone strike on Novorossiysk, with new imagery providing a clearer picture of the damage inflicted inside one of Russia’s most important naval hubs.
Ukraine’s General Staff said on September 10 that additional analysis confirmed strikes on the minesweeper Zheleznyakov, the missile frigate Admiral Essen and the Project 11711 large landing ship Pyotr Morgunov.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The updated assessment significantly expands the confirmed results of the overnight operation, which targeted both military and port infrastructure in Novorossiysk.
Fuel-oil storage facilities at the port were also confirmed hit.
The most striking evidence, however, comes from imagery showing the vessels after the attack, published by the OSINT community Exilenova+.
Visual analysis indicates that Admiral Essen, a Russian missile-carrying frigate capable of launching Kalibr cruise missiles, was struck in its superstructure. A fire subsequently broke out on the ship, an effect also reported by Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence.
Separate imagery also appears to show another strike on the superstructure of the missile frigate Admiral Makarov. The full extent of damage to that vessel is still being assessed.
A Buyan-M-class small missile ship was also identified among the vessels apparently hit during the operation. Ships of this class are used by Russia as platforms for long-range cruise missiles and have participated in strikes against Ukraine.
One Buyan-M vessel linked to the latest visual evidence had reportedly taken part in a recent Russian missile strike on Kyiv before subsequently coming under Ukrainian attack in Novorossiysk, Exilenova+ noted.
The September 9 operation combined missiles and drones against the port, where Russia has concentrated significant elements of its Black Sea Fleet after Ukrainian strikes made operations from occupied Crimea increasingly dangerous.
Novorossiysk has consequently become particularly important for Moscow as both a naval base and a logistical hub.
Damage assessments remain underway, and Ukrainian authorities have not yet disclosed the full results of every strike recorded during the operation.
Earlier, Ukrainian forces struck a Russian high-speed Mangust patrol boat in temporarily occupied Crimea, along with drone facilities, reconnaissance systems, and ammunition depots across several temporarily occupied regions.

articles.title: Iran Damages US A-10, F-15s with Missile Attack on Air Base in Jordan
articles.body:
A U.S. Air Force A-10 Thunderbolt II aircraft flies in the U.S. Central Command area of responsibility Aug. 30, 2026. U.S. Air Force photo by Tech. Sgt. Tiffany A. Emery
Audio of this article is brought to you by the Air & Space Forces Association, honoring and supporting our Airmen, Guardians, and their families. Find out more at afa.org
An Iranian ballistic missile attack on a key U.S. air base in Jordan damaged multiple U.S. warplanes, people familiar with the matter confirmed to Air & Space Forces Magazine.
One A-10 Thunderbolt II attack aircraft suffered a severely damaged wing and about eight F-15E Strike Eagle fighters were lightly damaged but are considered serviceable after Iran attacked Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Jordan on Sept. 8 Eastern Time.
The damage to U.S. aircraft was first reported by CBS News.
A spokesman for U.S. Central Command did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The attack on the base, known as MSAB, came after the U.S. struck five Iranian tankers Sept. 8, and Iran retaliated by lobbing scores of ballistic missiles at the installation. U.S. and Jordanian forces launched dozens of interceptors at the Iranian missiles. U.S. officials said no American personnel were killed. But Iran was able to harm American materiel. In the hours after the attack, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps claimed it damaged U.S. aircraft at the base.
The U.S. has dozens of warplanes operating from the base, which acts as a key airpower hub for operations against Iran. Tehran has targeted the facility, near the Jordanian town of Azraq, numerous times since the conflict began in February. Three Army Soldiers were killed in a missile attack on the base in July.

For Staff Sgt. Francisco Estrada, the hardest part of the job isn’t the possibility of ground combat,…
Startups Anduril Industries and Heremus have agreed to integrate Anduril’s autonomy software onto Hermeus’ hypersonic demonstrator aircraft “Quarterhorse”—uniting two technologies that have drawn keen interest and investment from the Air Force.
In a dramatic flare-up in the hostilities between the U.S. and Iran, American forces struck and destroyed five Iranian oil tankers Sept. 8, U.S. Central Command said. Iran retaliated by lobbing ballistic missiles toward a major U.S. base in Jordan.
After months of delays, the first F-15EX fighter jet the U.S. Air Force will permanently base overseas left Boeing’s facilities in St. Louis on Aug. 28. Eventually, the aircraft will fly to Kadena Air Base in Japan and join the 18th Wing there, but for now it is going to…
The Air Force is accelerating its plans to field an MQ-9A replacement in the wake of heavy Reaper losses in operations against Iran, top officials said Sept. 3, and they’re targeting a price point of just $10 million per aircraft.

articles.title: Zelensky says Canada has agreed to a big air defence package for Ukraine
articles.body:
Zelensky says Canada has agreed to a big air defence package for Ukraine
- Canada will provide Ukraine with a significant air defence package and support for its energy sector, as confirmed by President Volodymyr Zelensky ahead of talks with Prime Minister Mark Carney.
- Canada has committed over C$25.5 billion in aid since Russia's invasion in 2022, including C$8.5 billion in military assistance, addressing Ukraine's critical shortage of US-made Patriot interceptors.
- Prime Minister Carney pledged further support to help Ukraine defend against Russian attacks and aid its efforts to join NATO and the EU, highlighting Canada's strong Ukrainian diaspora and future reconstruction plans.
AI generated
CALGARY, Alberta - Canada will give Ukraine a “very important package of air defence” as well as support for the energy industry, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Sept 10 ahead of a meeting with Prime Minister Mark Carney.
Canada, one of Ukraine’s most vocal defenders, has committed more than C$25.5 billion (S$23.3 billion) in overall aid since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022, including C$8.5 billion in military assistance.
Kyiv is running critically low on US-made Patriot interceptors capable of stopping Russia’s ballistic missiles at a time when Moscow is stepping up its attacks.
“This is a very important package of air defence. This is crucial,” Zelensky told reporters.
He did not give details about the package, or speak about what Canada would do to back the energy industry.
He and Carney were due to address the media at around 10.30am Mountain Time (12.30am on Sept 11 in Singapore).
Canada is home to an estimated 1.3 to 1.4 million people of Ukrainian descent, forming one of the largest Ukrainian diasporas in the world.
In his own remarks to reporters, Carney promised Canada would offer Kyiv more aid to help it fend off Russian attacks as well as back its efforts to join NATO and the European Union.
“Ukrainians help build this province, this country. Canada will help rebuild Ukraine when peace comes,” he said.
On arrival in Canada, Zelensky had said support for Ukraine’s air defences and winter preparation would be the main focus of his visit. REUTERS

articles.title: At least three killed in Russian strikes on Ukraine while Zelenskyy is in Canada for talks
articles.body:
Ukraine's Special Operations Forces said they had carried out their deepest strike inside Russia, with drones travelling 3,000 km to target two gas condensate plants, the Novy Urengoy and Purovsky plants, located in the Yamalo-Nenets Autonomous Okrug, one of Russia's key oil and gas regions.
As Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy arrives in Canada for talks with leader Mark Carney, Russia and Ukraine continue to exchange fire.
At least three people were killed in Russian overnight attacks. Ukraine's Armed Forces reported that Moscow attacked Ukraine with 149 drones overnight from Wednesday into Thursday, 128 of which were intercepted. The statement added that they had been launched from Russian cities including Kursk, Millerovo and from the temporarily occupied region of Donetsk and Hvardiiske in Crimea, striking 13 locations.
A late Russian attack on a shopping center car park in Sumy killed at least three people and injured 14 including a teenager, on Wednesday, Oleh Hryhorov, Head of Sumy Oblast Military Administration said on Telegram.
Attacks on the eastern city of Kharkiv have left at least two people injured, after a residential buildings were damaged by drones, according to the city's mayor Ihor Terekhov.
Another large scale attack hitting residential building in the central city of Kryvyi Rih left two people in critical condition, its Head of Kryvyi Rih Defence Council, Oleksandr Vilkul said on Telegram.
Four firefighters have been hospitalised after responding to a blaze on a market in the Western city of Khmelnytskyi, sparked by fallen debris from a Russian drone attack. The firefighters were injured in a secondary explosion, officials reported.
Meanwhile, Ukraine's Special Operations Forces said that they had managed their deepest strike inside Russia, as their drones travelled 3,000 km to strike two gas condensate plants, the Novy Urengoy and Purovsky, located in one of Russia's key oil and gas regions; the Yamalo-Nenets Autonomous Okrug region.
Ukrainian media reported that Russian Telegram media channels had said Ukraine launched a drone attack on the Republic of Dagestan.
The southern coastal city of Sochi also reportedly came under attack by Ukrainian uncrewed surface vessels sparking multiple fires, according to Russian authorities. Russian media said residents also reported explosions on the port Caspian sea city of Makhachkala, it is known for its handling of dry and liquid cargo, residents also reported a lack of air raid warnings.
Zelenskyy travels to Canada
As Russia and Ukraine trade fire, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy travelled to Canada on Wednesday to hold talks with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney as he hopes to build a closer relationship with his allies.
According to a statement by Carney, Zelenskyy's visit "will focus on shared priorities between Canada and Ukraine, including deepening defence, economic, and energy cooperation."
Carney added:"It will also address the human cost of Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine and build on the strong people-to-people ties that connect our countries," and that Canada "remains steadfast in our commitment to support Ukraine's defence, recovery, and reconstruction."
Zelenskyy and his wife, Olena Zelenska, are scheduled to stay in Canada until Friday, with events in Calgary, Toronto and North Bay on the agenda, as well as a meeting with Cabinet members in Banff, Alberta.

As Russia and Ukraine trade fire, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy travelled to Canada on Wednesday to hold talks with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney as he hopes to build a closer relationship with his allies.
According to a statement by Carney, Zelenskyy's visit "will focus on shared priorities between Canada and Ukraine, including deepening defence, economic, and energy cooperation."
Carney added:"It will also address the human cost of Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine and build on the strong people-to-people ties that connect our countries," and that Canada "remains steadfast in our commitment to support Ukraine's defence, recovery, and reconstruction."
Zelenskyy and his wife, Olena Zelenska, are scheduled to stay in Canada until Friday, with events in Calgary, Toronto and North Bay on the agenda, as well as a meeting with Cabinet members in Banff, Alberta.

articles.title: New record set: Ukrainian drones strike Russian gas facility over 3,000 km away in Siberia
articles.body:
New record set: Ukrainian drones strike Russian gas facility over 3,000 km away in Siberia
Ukraine's Special Operations Forces (SSO) carried out Kyiv's deepest strike into Russia so far in the full-scale war, attacking a natural gas facility 3,200 kilometers (1,988 miles) from the Ukrainian border on Sept. 9, the military said. 
Ukraine's General Staff announced a successful strike on the Novy Urengoy Gas Condensate Treatment Plant (GCTP) in the Yamalo-Nenets Autonomous Okrug. 
Novy Urengoy is located in northwestern Siberia, over 3,000 kilometers from Ukraine's border. The attack marks the first time Ukrainian forces have struck Russia's Yamalo-Nenets region.
"Until today, this area was considered completely safe territory for the aggressor," the SSO wrote on Telegram.
The GCTP facility processes 19.5 million tons of crude oil and natural gas annually and produces diesel fuel and other petroleum products for Russia's military. The record-breaking strike also targeted the nearby Purovsky Gas Condensate Processing Plant.
Ukrainian weapons manufacturer Fire Point, producer of the Flamingo missile, said that its FP-1 drone model was used to carry out the strike.
Fires and smoke billowing from the plant were visible in footage shot by residents of Novy Urengoy. Monitoring channel Exilenova-Plus posted footage of the facility releasing excess gas through flare stacks to prevent explosions.
The attack was confirmed by Dmitry Artyukhov, governor of the Yamalo-Nenets Autonomous Okrug.
The strike on the GCTP facility was 600 kilometers (about 372 miles) from a major Russian liquefied national gas (LNG) site: the Yamal LNG project, located on Russia's Arctic Yamal Peninsula.
Yamal LNG is one of the country's largest LNG projects, accounting for over 60% of its total LNG exports — most of which flow to the European Union.
Alexander Kirk, sanctions campaigner at the German environmental and human rights organization Urgewald, said Ukraine's attack should serve as a wake-up call to Europe.
"The war has reached Russia's Arctic gas heartland, close to Yamal LNG, just days before this weekend's European Arctic Summit," Kirk said in a statement.
"The EU needs to get a grip. It should use the upcoming 22nd sanctions package to sanction all 14 Arc7 tankers sustaining Yamal LNG and close the sanctions gap around the European maritime and maintenance services keeping them operational."
Kirk urged EU countries to impose economic penalties against Russian LNG "before potential kinetic sanctions are applied to the Russian gas infrastructure supplying the European market."
The Yamalo-Nenets strikes demonstrate how Ukraine has increasingly extended the range of its unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) in a campaign against Russia's energy infrastructure. 
In one of its previous farthest-reaching strikes, Ukrainian forces struck an oil refinery in Omsk, nearly 2,500 kilometers (around 1,550 miles) from Ukraine's border, the General Staff said on July 6. Ukrainian long-range drones also recently targeted oil refineries in Russia's Perm Oblast, located more than 1,500 kilometers (930 miles) from Ukraine, on Sept. 7.
Emphasizing Ukraine's success with long-range UAVs, President Volodymyr Zelensky warned airlines, insurers, and foreign governments that Russian airspace "will be de facto closed" because of Ukrainian drone strikes.

articles.title: Trump says Iran war to end after US midterm elections, threatens to attack Pickaxe Mountain
articles.body:
Trump says Iran war to end after US midterm vote, Houthis close in on key Strait, sources say
CAIRO/WASHINGTON/DUBAI, Sept 10 - President Donald Trump said he expected the war with Iran to end after the November U.S. midterm elections and threatened again to attack a site associated with the Islamic Republic's nuclear programme after the two sides launched their biggest wave of attacks on shipping since the start of the six-month-old war.
Tensions in the region were high, with Saudi civil defence authorities on Thursday issuing emergency alerts in the southwestern city of Khamis Mushait for the fourth time in 24 hours, as clashes flared with Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis.
The Houthis were edging closer on Thursday to gaining more leverage over the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, the southern outlet of the Red Sea and one of the world's most important routes for shipping, four Yemeni government military sources said.
Brent crude prices hovered above $100 a barrel as supply routes through both the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea remained heavily disrupted.
Iran said it had attacked 10 ships near the waterway on Wednesday after the U.S. sank five Iranian oil tankers, the latest in a series of tit-for-tat strikes that have signalled scant chance of an imminent end to hostilities.
DEADLINES TO END WAR
The war and subsequent increase in fuel prices have helped drive Trump's popularity to record lows. The president said Tehran was trying to influence the November U.S. midterm elections, which will determine whether his Republican Party retains control of Congress.
"I think war is going to end immediately after the election because they can't hold out any longer. They're desperate to try and affect the election," Trump told reporters on Wednesday.
Trump has previously set deadlines for the war to end.
The Wall Street Journal reported later that top White House advisers, including Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, have privately warned Trump that the conflict could extend through the remainder of his presidency, which ends in January 2029. Reuters could not immediately verify the report.
Trump also said the U.S. may hit Iran's Pickaxe Mountain, a heavily fortified site that hosts two deeply buried tunnel complexes near Iran's damaged Natanz uranium enrichment facility.
"We notice there's a little activity at Pickaxe. I would advise Iran not to get cute because we will have to hit them very hard," Trump said in a speech at the midterm Republican convention. Trump has been threatening strikes on Pickaxe Mountain since at least mid-July.
The U.S. and Israel launched military strikes on Iran in February partly due to concerns over Tehran's nuclear programme.
Iran says its nuclear activities are for peaceful purposes.
In recent weeks Washington had cited increasing success guiding tankers through the Strait of Hormuz, which carried about a fifth of global oil supplies before the war. But a resumption of fighting this month appears to have set back any such gradual reopening. Just seven vessels transited the strait on Wednesday, half the 10-day average, preliminary ship-tracking data showed on Thursday.
RED SEA CLASHES
Fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis in Yemen has also escalated in the past few days, a second theatre of war that threatens global energy supplies from the Middle East.
Houthi militants have taken control of the Yemeni Red Sea city of Mocha and are launching attacks on the strategic Red Sea islands of Hanish, the Yemeni sources told Reuters on Thursday.
Government forces and their allies are relocating south to Dhubab, which sits directly on the strait, across from the island of Perim. Control of Dhubab and the island is key to gaining hold of the strait, they said.
Bab el-Mandeb, or the Gate of Tears, named for its perilous navigation conditions, lies between Yemen on the Arabian Peninsula and Djibouti and Eritrea on the African coast, making it a major prize for the Houthis, who control Yemen's most populous areas and much of the north.
It is one of the world's most important routes for crude oil and fuel from the Gulf bound for the Mediterranean via the Suez Canal or the SUMED pipeline on Egypt's Red Sea coast, as well as commodities bound for Asia, including Russian oil.
Blocking the narrow passage would isolate Gulf oil-producing countries such as energy superpower Saudi Arabia from their main shipping routes after Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz — the primary maritime energy artery between Asia and Europe.
Earlier this week, at least 73 people were wounded in four southern Saudi cities, including Khamis Mushait, in recent Houthi strikes on the world's largest oil exporter.
The militant group said it attacked an air base in the southwestern city of Khamis Mushait and oil infrastructure in nearby cities in one of the biggest attacks on Saudi Arabia since the start of the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran in February.
Saudi civil defence authorities issued an all-clear on Thursday following another emergency alert declared in Khamis Mushait. REUTERS

articles.title: Trump predicts Iran war end, says Putin ready for Ukraine deal
articles.body:
U.S. President Donald Trump said Wednesday that the war with Iran could end immediately after the Nov. 3 midterm elections, while signaling possible diplomatic openings on both Tehran and the war in Ukraine.
Speaking to reporters before traveling to Dallas, Texas, for the Republican Party's first midterm convention, Trump claimed Iran was seeking to influence the elections and could not sustain the conflict much longer.
"I think the war will end immediately after the election because they can't hold out any longer," Trump said.
Asked about the possibility of renewed nuclear negotiations with Tehran, Trump said his administration was not actively pursuing talks but did not rule them out.
"We're not looking for it. Yes, a negotiation could possibly happen, but it's not something we're looking at," he said.
Trump said any potential agreement with Tehran would extend beyond its nuclear program, suggesting other issues would also be included in negotiations.
"There is a lot more than nuclear," he said.
He also said recent U.S. strikes in the Strait of Hormuz had incapacitated about nine Iranian tankers and suggested further military action could follow.
Trump separately struck an optimistic tone on efforts to end the Russia-Ukraine war following a phone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin, saying the Russian leader was "wanting to make a deal."
Trump described his conversation with Putin as "good" and said a trilateral meeting involving Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy "could happen."
"If Zelenskyy is wanting to make a deal, that'd be very nice," Trump said.
His comments followed visits to Moscow and Kyiv last weekend by U.S. mediators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, though no significant breakthrough toward ending the war has been announced.
The Kremlin said Putin told Trump that Moscow had no "aggressive plans" toward Europe and provided the U.S. president with an assessment of developments on the battlefield.
Putin also outlined what he believed Washington could do to help bring the fighting to an end, according to Kremlin foreign policy adviser Yuri Ushakov.
Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Washington has stepped up mediation efforts since Trump's return to the White House, including a meeting between Trump and Putin in Alaska last year.

articles.title: Rutte warns delays in Ukraine aid cost lives
articles.body:
NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte has urged allies to accelerate military support for Ukraine, warning that delays in delivering weapons and funding are costing lives.
Speaking at the latest Ukraine Defence Contact Group meeting, Rutte said Ukraine’s war against Russia was directly affecting the wider security environment across NATO and called on countries to increase their contributions.
Rutte said: “Ukraine’s fight shapes the entire Euro-Atlantic security environment. It directly impacts, as we all know, our own security, and as we work on modernising the alliance and building a stronger Europe and a stronger NATO, we must continue to support Ukraine’s security and help them defend from Russia’s brutal attacks.”
He added: “That means supporting Ukraine with the utmost urgency. And here, let me say that delays simply cost human lives.”
Rutte said the level of civilian deaths had reached its highest point since May 2022 and told members of the group that more military assistance was required. He said: “Nations must dig deeper. We do not have a choice, I believe.”
The NATO Secretary General identified air defence, drones and extended-range ammunition as priority requirements for Ukrainian forces. Rutte also said allies were seeing changes in the weapons employed by Russia, including greater use of North Korean missiles and jet-powered attack drones.
He stressed the continuing role of the PURL mechanism, under which NATO allies and partners finance the purchase of American weapons for Ukraine. According to Rutte, around $10 billion had been allocated over the previous year through PURL and US foreign military sales for Ukraine, including $3.5 billion originating from the Ukraine support loan.
He described those figures as evidence of European countries taking on a greater share of the effort to sustain Ukraine. Rutte said continued deliveries were particularly important for maintaining Ukrainian air defences and enabling forces to hold positions on the front line.

articles.title: IAEA exposes North Korea's secret nuclear enrichment facility, expansion of weapon infrastructure
articles.body:
North Korea has built a new uranium enrichment facility at its main Yongbyon nuclear complex that could house up to 28 centrifuge cascades, and started operating an expanded annex at its Kangson enrichment site, the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) said.
The Vienna-based nuclear watchdog said in a report that the findings pointed to a steady expansion of North Korea's nuclear infrastructure at multiple locations.
In the report, dated August 28, the IAEA said it relied on satellite imagery and open-source material, including photographs published by North Korean state media, to track Pyongyang's nuclear activities. The agency has had no inspectors in North Korea since 2009.
It identified a new two-story building at Yongbyon as the site's second uranium enrichment facility by comparing state media photographs of a June visit by North Korean leader Kim Jong Un with satellite images taken during the building's construction.
Photographs from the visit indicate gas centrifuge cascades are installed on both the upper and lower floors of the main building, the report said, adding the building could accommodate up to 28 of the cascades shown in the photographs.
Expansion of North Korea's production of weapons-grade nuclear material
The report also said there were indications that operations began in January at a uranium enrichment facility in Kangson, near the capital Pyongyang, within an annex that had been constructed in 2024.
The IAEA said the developments in North Korea's nuclear program violated UN Security Council resolutions.
"The ongoing operation of enrichment facilities at Kangson and Yongbyon and the reported further expansion of the DPRK’s production of weapons-grade nuclear material is a cause for serious concern," IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi said in a statement to the board of governors on Monday, referring to the North's official name, the Democratic People's Republic of Korea.
The report accompanied Grossi's statement.
Pyongyang has repeatedly rejected the agency's authority. North Korea's mission to the United Nations in Vienna said last September that North Korea's status as a nuclear weapons state had become irreversible and the IAEA had "no legal right… to interfere in the internal affairs of a nuclear weapons state which exists outside the NPT," referring to the Non-Proliferation Treaty.

articles.title: Iran arms, advice helped Yemen's Houthis seize key Red Sea city
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Iranian arms and advice helped Yemen's Houthis seize key Red Sea city, sources say
The lightning Houthi advance down Yemen's Red Sea coast this week came with direct guidance from Iran's Revolutionary Guards seeking to open a new front in Iran's war with the U.S., according to Yemeni government, Iranian and regional sources.
By seizing the southwestern port city of Mocha, the Houthis have strengthened their chokehold on the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a key waterway whose disruption further constricts global energy supplies after Iran's blockade of the Strait of Hormuz.
Six months into the wider regional conflict between the Houthis' Iranian allies and the United States, the group now looks focused on consolidating that grip on the strait even as opposing government forces backed by Saudi Arabia focus on an offensive in the north.
Iran told the Houthis last week to escalate their attacks on Saudi Arabia, a close U.S. ally, and promised more funding, weapons and senior officers to help them do so, two Iranian sources said.
While Iran describes the Houthis as an ally, it publicly denies giving them military direction, saying they are "not a proxy".
Several senior Revolutionary Guards commanders had already travelled to Yemen to oversee and command Houthi attacks directed against Saudi Arabia after weeks of discussions over military strategy, a regional diplomat briefed by Tehran said.
A third Iranian source, an official, said Iran had held several meetings with allies including the Houthis and that the move on Mocha was a Houthi rather than Iranian decision. However, it had helped Iran by putting upward pressure on oil prices and hurting the United States and Saudi Arabia, the official added.
Inside Yemen, five military sources from the Saudi-backed and internationally recognised government said the Revolutionary Guards had directed the new Houthi campaign along the Red Sea coast, a flat, narrow plain known as the Tihama, starting with a blitz of rocket fire.
Citing communications intercepts and the accounts of captured Houthi prisoners, the Yemeni military sources said they believed the Iranian effort was being directed by Abdolreza Shahlaei, a top Revolutionary Guards commander.
Iranian sources were not immediately able to confirm that, though they had previously described Shahlaei, who is in the Guards' specialist Quds Force unit, as having spent time in Yemen in recent years.
The Guards were still able to move weapons and personnel in and out of Yemen despite an aerial and maritime blockade of Houthi areas, the Iranian sources said without elaborating on how they did so.
"If we look at their offensive on the west coast, it's not something prepared just last week or last month," said Ahmed Nagi, Yemen analyst at International Crisis Group, describing the seizure of Mocha as a significant milestone in the war.
"The evolution of the Houthis was basically because of the new weapons they gained, either through the Iranians directly or through the different smuggling networks that they are counting on," Nagi said, pointing specifically at their use of drones in the latest offensive.
As the Houthis began an advance towards Mocha last week, Yemen's government requested more air support and other help from the Saudis, two more Yemeni officials said.
It was seeking a Saudi air campaign against Houthi targets in the Houthi heartland including Sanaa and key strategic assets such as oil depots, they said.
However, the kingdom stuck to providing logistical, armament and intelligence support with only limited air strikes that were focused on northern battlefronts in Jawf and Marib provinces, areas the government regarded as less important.
The officials' own assessment was that Riyadh was anxious to avoid a major escalation with the Houthis for fear of provoking heavier drone strikes on Saudi territory.
Saudi officials did not immediately respond to Reuters requests for comment on Riyadh's military focus on the northern front rather than the Red Sea coast and other big Houthi targets.
The overall military situation in Yemen is hard to gauge after a years-long pause in major warfare since a ceasefire was agreed in 2022. Both Iran and Saudi Arabia have invested in forces they back there. But the pro-government coalition has suffered from internal splits.
Although previous rounds of warfare in the Tihama had produced sudden advances and retreats, it remains unclear if Saudi-backed forces can easily dislodge the Houthis this time, Nagi said.
"Maybe we can see some advances from the government if they get the necessary support from the Saudis. But that could be a bit difficult this time," he said.

articles.title: Government again commits not to extend Dreadnought sub life
articles.body:
The Government has confirmed that it has accepted a Strategic Defence Review recommendation not to extend the service lives of the Royal Navy’s Dreadnought-class ballistic missile submarines beyond their intended end-of-service dates from the mid-2050s.
The position was confirmed in a written parliamentary answer to Conservative MP Ben Obese-Jecty, who asked whether ministers had committed to Recommendation 34 of the 2025 Strategic Defence Review.
Defence Minister Luke Pollard replied: “The Government accepted this 2025 Strategic Defence Review recommendation and is in the process of implementing it.”
Recommendation 34 explicitly calls on the Government to avoid repeating the costs associated with extending ageing submarine fleets and to begin planning for the system that will eventually replace Dreadnought.
The Strategic Defence Review stated: “To avoid the costs of the past, the Government must commit to not extending the life of the Dreadnought class submarines beyond their intended end-of-service dates from the mid-2050s. It should start to define the requirement for the post-Dreadnought nuclear deterrent within this Parliament.”
The Government has also confirmed separately that work to define Dreadnought’s eventual successor is beginning as part of wider investment in the Defence Nuclear Enterprise.
In a written answer in July, Obese-Jecty asked what plans the MOD had to define the requirement for the post-Dreadnought strategic deterrent.
Pollard said: “As announced in the Defence Investment Plan, this Government will invest over £20 billion more in the Defence Nuclear Enterprise over the next four years than the previous four years to modernise and sustain our nuclear deterrent, the cornerstone of our national security.”
He added: “This will fund our new deterrent submarines and warheads, establish a nuclear fuels programme, start defining the Dreadnought successor, and upgrade our infrastructure across the defence nuclear estate.”
Pollard said this would allow the Government to meet its commitment to begin defining the future system during the current Parliament, stating: “This will allow us to meet the Government’s commitment to start to define the requirement for the post-Dreadnought strategic deterrent within this Parliament.”
The Dreadnought class is being built to replace the Royal Navy’s existing Vanguard-class ballistic missile submarines and will carry the UK’s strategic nuclear deterrent through much of the middle of the century.
The Strategic Defence Review recommendation is intended to avoid the additional cost and complexity that can arise when major platforms remain in service significantly beyond their originally planned lives. Rather than relying on a later life-extension programme for Dreadnought, the review calls for work on its eventual successor to begin decades in advance, with the requirement-definition process now being funded through the wider Defence Nuclear Enterprise programme.

articles.title: Iran likely to reverse-engineer captured US underwater drone
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Iran likely to reverse-engineer captured US underwater drone
Iran's capture of a US military underwater drone gives Tehran an opportunity to study and potentially reverse engineer the vessel, delivering a setback for the Pentagon and drone maker Anduril.
The US military and Anduril have downplayed the significance of the drone falling into Iranian hands. The vessel, a Dive-LD autonomous underwater vehicle designed for long-range surveillance and other undersea missions, is among a new generation of military drones intended to operate for days with little human intervention. Washington has previously treated the loss of advanced drones to Iran as a serious matter.
After Iran captured an RQ-170 Sentinel stealth reconnaissance drone in 2011, then-President Barack Obama publicly asked Tehran to return the aircraft. Iran later claimed it had reverse-engineered the drone and subsequently unveiled domestically produced models that appeared to draw heavily on its design.
More recently, the U.S. military moved swiftly to prevent Iranian forces from taking possession of uncrewed maritime technology. In 2022, a US Navy patrol ship and MH-60S Seahawk helicopter were deployed after an Iranian naval vessel attempted to tow away a Saildrone surface vessel in the Gulf, according to the Navy.
Analysts say Iran is unlikely to gain a decisive military advantage from the captured drone, but the episode nonetheless represents a propaganda victory for Tehran and an awkward setback for Washington's efforts to project technological superiority.
Iranian embassies mock US
Iranian embassies around the world have mocked the US for losing its drone. Iran's embassy in Ghana, in a post on X, boasted about picking the submersible up in "a strait controlled by people who can hear a shrimp sneeze," adding that, "Our guys picked it up like a plastic bottle in a fishing net. Fully intact. Still blinking like an idiot. Condolences to whoever was holding the joystick."
US Navy Captain Tim Hawkins of US Central Command said the "defective drone was an older model that neither collected sensitive data nor carried any classified sonar or radar equipment." Anduril did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
"Of course Iran will take every opportunity as a propaganda win," said Farzin Nadimi, a senior fellow at the Washington Institute for Near East Policy. "It can help the (Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps) make better versions of their own designs."
Iran will almost certainly try to pry open the drone's hardware, but the drone's software carries built-in defenses, said Bryan Clark, a senior fellow and director of the Center for Defense Concepts and Technology at the Hudson Institute. Iranian engineers "could definitely reverse-engineer the mechanical systems," he said, pointing to Tehran's track record with captured American aircraft.
"Unboxing ceremony by our reverse engineers, tomorrow morning!" Iran's embassy in Hyderabad wrote on X.
The incident has also highlighted a disconnect between the messaging of Anduril and its customer, the US Navy.
Navy officials said the Dive-LD was an older-model vehicle that suffered a malfunction and was recovered by Iranian forces after being left "dead in the water."
Anduril has promoted the Dive-LD as "the most reliable and flexible" large autonomous underwater vehicle available, saying it is capable of operating for up to 10 days in demanding conditions. In addition to its use by the US Navy, the Dive-LD was the testbed vehicle for the development of Australia's new Ghost Shark large underwater drone.
"This is something that Iran has proven very adept at exploiting for its own benefit in terms of seeking to frame the narrative as one of US, in this case, ineptitude and their ability to sort of retain control over the Strait of Hormuz," said Mona Yacoubian, director of the Middle East program at the Center for Strategic and International Studies.

articles.title: Russia attacked Ukraine with more than a hundred drones: there were strikes at 13 locations
articles.body:
Russia attacked Ukraine with more than a hundred drones: there were strikes at 13 locations
Kyiv • UNN
The Russian Federation launched attack drones from the territory of the Russian Federation and the occupied Crimea and Donetsk regions. Air defense shot down or suppressed 128 UAVs; strikes were recorded at 13 locations.
During the night of September 10, the Russians attacked Ukraine with Shahed-type attack UAVs (half of them jet-powered), Gerbera drones, as well as decoy drones of the "Parody" type. This was reported by the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, UNN reports.
Details
The enemy launched drones from the Russian cities of Millerovo, Kursk, and Primorsko-Akhtarsk, as well as from the occupied Crimea and Donetsk.
The air attack was repelled by aviation, anti-aircraft missile forces, electronic warfare units and unmanned systems units, and mobile fire groups of Ukraine's Defense Forces.
Air defenses shot down/suppressed 128 enemy Shahed-type UAVs, Gerbera drones, and drones of other types.
Hits by the enemy's air attack weapons were recorded at 13 locations, as well as the falling of downed drones (debris) at 9 locations.

articles.title: Poland expects Russia to target border crossings as attacks on Ukraine escalate – Russia has already hit crossings with Moldova and Romania
articles.body:
Poland expects Russia to target border crossings with Ukraine as Moscow expands its strikes on trade and logistics routes far from the front line, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said on 10 September, according to Reuters.
The warning comes after Russia has already struck at least five Ukrainian border crossings with Moldova and NATO member Romania since late August. The attacks mark a significant escalation in Russia’s targeting of Ukraine’s civilian transport, trade, and logistics infrastructure, far from the front line.
“Last night, thanks to cooperation between our services and their Ukrainian counterparts, a direct threat to one of the border crossings was averted,” Tusk said at a press conference in Bratislava, according to Reuters.
He said Poland expected Russia to take similar action against border crossings in other countries, including Poland.
Russia has significantly ramped up its aerial attacks across Ukraine in recent months, increasingly striking civilian transport, energy, industrial, and logistics infrastructure while deploying newer and more capable weapons. The expanded use of drones and missiles has also made these attacks harder to stop, allowing Russia to hit targets farther from the front line with greater frequency and inflict more damage and casualties.
Russia is striking Ukraine’s civilian travel and logistics routes
The Russian attacks have targeted crossings in Ukraine’s southern Odesa Oblast, hundreds of kilometers from the front line.
Four of the crossings hit since late August are on Ukraine’s border with Moldova, while another is on the Romanian border. The sites handle civilian traffic, trade, and logistics that have become increasingly important to Ukraine as the war continues.
On 9 September, Russian drones struck the Starokozache crossing with Moldova, killing two civilians and injuring three others. During the attack, one Russian drone entered Moldovan airspace and flew toward Romania, prompting NATO aircraft conducting air-policing duties to scramble.
Russian drones also struck the Orlivka ferry crossing on the Romanian border twice in early September.
Far from any front line: Russia has hit at least five of Ukraine’s western border crossings with Moldova and NATO member since late August
Poland prepares for further escalation
Tusk said he had received a “fairly precise report” from the CIA about possible developments in the coming months, which he said aligned with warnings he had made previously.
“Poland and all of Europe need to be prepared for different possibilities,” Tusk said, including developments not only on the Russian-Ukrainian front but also along the EU’s eastern flank.
The warning comes as Russian strikes increasingly reach toward Ukraine’s borders with NATO and EU countries. The drone incursions into Moldovan and Romanian airspace during attacks on Ukrainian infrastructure have already brought NATO forces into the response.
The latest attacks represent a broader shift in Russia’s targeting: Moscow is not only striking Ukraine’s cities and military infrastructure, but increasingly hitting the trade, transport, and civilian logistics routes that keep the country functioning during the war.

articles.title: Australia declares its new air defense missile system combat ready
articles.body:
- Australia's Army declared Final Operational Capability for NASAMS on September 9, 2026, with 16th Regiment, Royal Australian Artillery as the first operational unit.
- The system, built under the SRGBAD project with Raytheon Australia and Norway's Kongsberg, uses Australian CEA Technologies radar and Hawkei-mounted launchers.
Australia’s Army has declared Final Operational Capability for its National Advanced Surface to Air Missile System, confirming the ground-based air defense system is ready to support Australian Defence Force operations. Defence announced the milestone on September 9, 2026.
NASAMS is built to detect, track and destroy cruise missiles, aircraft, helicopters and drones. The system was delivered under the Short Range Ground Based Air Defense project, known as SRGBAD, part of a broader air and missile defense setup that also draws on ships and fighter aircraft to protect ADF personnel and infrastructure.
Soldiers from Adelaide’s 16th Regiment, Royal Australian Artillery, are the first operational unit to field the system. The regiment, based at Woodside in South Australia, ran live-fire trials and qualification training as part of the phased rollout that led to this week’s declaration.
“The achievement of Final Operational Capability for NASAMS marks a significant milestone in strengthening Australia’s integrated air and missile defence capability,” said Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Defence Richard Marles. “NASAMS provides Army with a modern, highly capable air defence system that enhances our ability to protect Australian Defence Force personnel, critical assets and infrastructure from a range of airborne threats.”
Raytheon Australia is the prime contractor on SRGBAD, running under the Army’s long-standing LAND 19 Phase 7B program. NASAMS itself was co-developed by Norway’s Kongsberg Defence & Aerospace, and Kongsberg Defence Australia built the system’s Fire Distribution Centres locally before handing final units to Raytheon Australia last year. The SRGBAD program is valued at roughly A$2.5 billion.
The Australian version pairs the Norwegian NASAMS design with locally built CEA Technologies radar, the CEATAC and CEAOPS active electronically scanned array systems, mounted alongside launchers on Hawkei protected mobility vehicles. Raytheon’s AN/AAS-52 Multispectral Targeting System adds day and night optical tracking. The setup replaces the Army’s older RBS-70 man-portable air defense missiles.
“The achievement of Final Operational Capability delivers a world-leading capability for Defence and provides a major boost to Australia’s integrated air and missile defence,” said Minister for Defence Industry Pat Conroy. “Australian-designed radar technology is a key part of this capability, highlighting the important contribution local industry makes to Australia’s national security.”
NASAMS is in service with, or on order for, more than a dozen countries. Ukraine has used the system in combat against Russian cruise missiles and drones since 2022, giving the design an operational record beyond Australia’s own trials. Defence has not disclosed how many NASAMS batteries or launchers 16th Regiment will ultimately operate; the regiment is expected to field two batteries once full capability is reached.
Each NASAMS troop is built around a Fire Distribution Centre, a CEATAC radar, an optronic sensor vehicle and several launchers, with the Hawkei launchers and canisters carried on MAN/Rheinmetall HX77 trucks. The missile load is a mix of AIM-120 AMRAAM and Sidewinder missiles, the same interceptors used on Australian and allied fighter jets.
Sustainment of the system will run primarily through Australian-based support contracts already in place with CEA Technologies and Raytheon Australia.

articles.title: Ukraine Hits 8 Russian War Sites From Arctic to Caspian
articles.body:
Ukrainian forces struck eight Russian infrastructure facilities supporting Moscow’s war effort in a sweeping campaign stretching from the Arctic to the Caspian Sea, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Thursday, Sept. 10.
In a Telegram post, Zelensky said the targets included an oil refinery in the Yamalo-Nenets region and the Makhachkala Commercial Sea Port in Russia’s Republic of Dagestan.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Facilities in the Moscow, Voronezh, Astrakhan, and Bryansk regions also came under attack, according to the president.
“Russia continues its terror against Ukraine every day. And every day it receives a just response,” Zelensky said.
Shahed supply route hit on the Caspian
Ukrainian drone manufacturer Fire Point said its FP-1 long-range drones attacked the Makhachkala port, which Russia allegedly used to receive Iranian-made Shahed attack drones transported across the Caspian Sea.
A strike and subsequent fire were recorded within the port, RBC-Ukraine reported, adding that the full extent of the damage was still being assessed.
The Makhachkala facility is Russia’s only ice-free deep-water port on the Caspian Sea. It operates throughout the year and connects Russia with other countries in the region, including Iran.
Shahed drones delivered through the port were reportedly transported onward to deployment areas before being launched against Ukraine.
During the first eight months of 2026, the port handled more than 2.9 million metric tons (3.2 million tons) of cargo, including over 2.08 million tons of oil.
Russia Sets Eye on Zaporizhzhia's Orikhiv With 150,000-Troop Formations
Eight targets across six Russian regions
Along with the Makhachkala port, Zelensky confirmed that a refinery had been hit in the Yamalo-Nenets region of Russia’s Arctic. He did not identify the facility or describe the damage there, but the reported attacks covered six Russian federal subjects.
The president did not provide details about the sites attacked in the Moscow, Voronezh, Astrakhan, and Bryansk regions.
Ukraine has increasingly targeted Russian refineries, ports, logistics hubs, and other infrastructure Kyiv says supplies Moscow’s military or generates revenue used to finance Russia’s invasion.
Zelensky thanked the Ukrainian personnel involved in the latest operations and those supporting the country’s ability to conduct strikes deep inside Russia.
“I thank every warrior and everyone who ensures our long-range capability and precision,” he said.
