articles.title: Zelensky arrives in Canada to discuss Ukraine's air defense needs
articles.body:
Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional details.
President Volodymyr Zelensky held talks with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney on Sept. 10, as Ottawa is expected to provide Ukraine with a new aid package, Zelensky said.
Zelensky arrived in Canada on Sept. 9 as he seeks support for Ukraine's air defenses and preparations for the winter. He is also expected to hold "important meetings" aimed at strengthening the countries' strategic partnership for years to come.
"We're talking today about a winter support package and energy. This is very important. Today, Canada is making a significant decision — a very important aid package for air defense," the president said in a social media post.
"There is a major global shortage of such systems and the missiles for them."
Details of the new aid package remain unclear. Presidential spokesperson Serhii Nykyforov told reporters that Ukraine and Canada are also expected to sign a number of documents.
As part of the visit, the Ukrainian delegation, led by Zelensky, plans to attend an off-site meeting of the Canadian government. First Lady Olena Zelenska is also expected to meet with Canadian philanthropists supporting Ukraine.
The visit follows Zelensky's trip to Norway, where he and the first lady attended the Sept. 9 funeral of King Harald V.
In Oslo, Zelensky also met with Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store to discuss strengthening Ukraine's air defenses and advancing the Freyja anti-ballistic missile program.
Ukraine aims to have a working prototype of Freyja ready in the first half of 2027. The project brings together Ukraine and nine European countries, including Norway, as well as several European defense manufacturers.

articles.title: Over the past day, the Defense Forces struck eight infrastructure facilities in the Russian Federation, including an oil refinery and a commercial port, Zelenskyy says
articles.body:
Over the past day, the Defense Forces struck eight infrastructure facilities in the Russian Federation, including an oil refinery and a commercial port, Zelenskyy says
Kyiv • UNN
The Makhachkala Commercial Sea Port in Dagestan, through which Iranian Shaheds were delivered, came under attack.
Over the course of a day, Ukrainian forces struck eight Russian infrastructure facilities. In particular, they hit an oil refinery in the Yamalo-Nenets region and the Sea Trade Port in Dagestan. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy reported this, UNN writes.
Over the course of this day, our warriors struck eight Russian infrastructure facilities that support the war. An oil refinery in the Yamalo-Nenets region was hit, as was the Sea Trade Port in Dagestan. Facilities in the Moscow, Voronezh, Astrakhan and Bryansk regions were also targeted. Russia continues its terror against Ukraine every day. And every day it receives a just response
The president also thanked the warriors who ensure our long-range strike capability and accuracy.
As the manufacturer of the strike drones Fire Point reported, the Sea Trade Port in Dagestan was hit by FP-1 drones. Hits and a subsequent fire were recorded on the port’s premises.
Makhachkala Sea Trade Port is Russia’s only ice-free deep-water port on the Caspian Sea. It operates year-round and provides maritime connections between Russia and the countries of the Caspian region, including Iran. Makhachkala was also used as one of the delivery points for Iranian strike UAVs to Russia across the Caspian Sea, from where they were subsequently transported to areas of deployment against Ukraine.
During the first eight months of 2026, the port handled more than 2.9 million tonnes of cargo, of which more than 2.08 million tonnes was oil.

articles.title: AFU General Staff confirms strikes on Russia’s Makhachkala seaport and three ships in Novorossiysk
articles.body:
AFU General Staff confirms strikes on Russia’s Makhachkala seaport and three ships in Novorossiysk
As reported by Ukrinform, the press service of the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine said this on Telegram.
“Overnight on September 10, 2026, units of Ukraine’s Defense Forces struck the Makhachkala Commercial Seaport in the Republic of Dagestan, Russian Federation. A fire was recorded at the facility. The extent of the damage is being clarified,” the statement said.
In addition, based on an analysis of additional data, the General Staff confirmed that on September 9, 2026, fuel-oil storage facilities in Novorossiysk, Krasnodar Krai, Russian Federation, were struck, as well as at least three enemy vessels: the Zheleznyakov minesweeper, the Admiral Essen frigate, and the Project 11711 Pyotr Morgunov large landing ship, the General Staff noted.
The Makhachkala Commercial Seaport is the only ice-free deep-water port of the Russian Federation on the Caspian Sea and an important transport and logistics hub.
The port plays a key role in the Russia-Iran logistics corridor across the Caspian Sea, which is used to circumvent Western sanctions. Military-related supplies are transported in both directions along this route: components and Shahed-type attack UAVs from Iran to Russia, and explosives, drone components and ammunition from Russia to Iran. A base of the Russian Caspian Flotilla is located near the port.
As reported by Ukrinform, President Volodymyr Zelensky said that Ukraine’s Defense Forces struck an oil refinery in Russia’s Yamalo-Nenets region as well as a seaport in Dagestan during the night.

articles.title: Houthis seize strategic Red Sea port near key shipping route – media
articles.body:
Houthis seize strategic Red Sea port near key shipping route – media
Yemen’s Houthis have seized the crucial Red Sea city of al-Makha (Mocha) and are advancing toward the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, media reports claimed on Thursday.
According to Reuters, the Houthis pushed Saudi-backed government forces out of Mocha after several days of fierce fighting, capturing both the city and its port. Witnesses told AFP that they saw Houthi fighters entering on Thursday chanting “death to America, death to Israel.”
The Houthis have also reportedly attacked the strategic Hanish islands, pushing government forces further south. An unnamed military source claimed the group seized Zuqar Island after rocket attacks and an amphibious assault. Control of the area would strengthen the Houthis’ position on Yemen’s side of Bab al-Mandeb, potentially cutting government supply routes and depriving Saudi-backed forces of a key logistics hub, sources said.
Yemen’s internationally recognized government has not confirmed Mocha’s capture. However, Lt. Gen. Tareq Saleh, whose forces controlled the city, said earlier Thursday he had ordered them to “reorganize their ranks and establish an alternative command center in a secure location.”
The reported advance marks a sharp escalation after roughly four years of relative calm following a UN-brokered truce in 2022. The Houthis had previously fought Yemen’s internationally recognized government since seizing Sanaa in 2014, prompting a Saudi-led coalition to intervene.
Tensions flared again in July after, according to Yemen’s internationally recognized government, its forces struck Sanaa airport to prevent an Iranian aircraft carrying a Houthi delegation from landing. The Houthis blamed Saudi Arabia, declared the de-escalation phase over and subsequently announced a naval blockade of the kingdom. By mid-August, the group was launching coordinated missile and drone strikes on camps belonging to Yemen’s Saudi-backed government, which in turn launched counteroffensives across several provinces.
The fighting sharply escalated earlier this week. On Tuesday, the Houthis targeted energy and other infrastructure in Saudi Arabia’s south, including facilities belonging to Saudi Aramco, the country’s largest oil producer. The Houthis called the operation retaliation for Saudi strikes in Yemen, claiming Riyadh had carried out 121 airstrikes over the previous three days. Saudi aircraft carried out another 40 strikes across four Yemeni provinces on Thursday, according to the Houthi-run Saba news agency.
What is the significance of the Houthis’ advance?
The battle for Yemen’s Red Sea coast has implications far beyond the country. Bab al-Mandeb links the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden and Indian Ocean and carries roughly 10% of global seaborne trade. Its importance to energy markets has surged since the US-Israeli war on Iran erupted on February 28 and the Strait of Hormuz came under a de facto blockade, forcing Saudi Arabia, one of the world’s largest oil exporters, to rely more heavily on Red Sea exports.
Saudi Aramco has increasingly diverted crude through its cross-country pipeline to the Red Sea port of Yanbu. Loadings have averaged more than 4 million barrels per day since June, more than four times last year’s level. Saudi crude shipments through Bab al-Mandeb between March and mid-July were eight times higher than in the same period of 2025, making disruption to the strait a growing threat to the kingdom’s oil exports.
The Houthis have disrupted the waterway before, repeatedly attacking Red Sea shipping in 2023 in what they said was support for Palestinians during Israel’s war in Gaza.
Despite the renewed hostilities, Riyadh says diplomacy remains possible. Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan Al Saud earlier this week accused the Houthis of prioritizing “their narrow interests” over the interests of Yemen, but insisted that “the road to diplomacy is not closed.”

articles.title: Russia and Vietnam to strengthen military cooperation and intelligence sharing on “hostile” countries
articles.body:
Russia and Vietnam have agreed to deepen cooperation in defense, security, and military technology, as well as to exchange information on the activities of “hostile forces and foreign special agencies,” according to a joint statement issued following talks between Vladimir Putin and Vietnamese President To Lam in Moscow on Sept. 9. Additionally, Putin announced that Russia will soon introduce a visa-free regime for Vietnamese nationals.
The two sides agreed to “enhance cooperation between military branches” and cooperate in maritime security, military personnel training, science, technology, and engineering. After the talks, To Lam stated that Russia and Vietnam intend to “deepen defence, security, and military technical cooperation as a strategic pillar of our ties.”
A separate clause in the joint statement addresses cooperation in the field of information security. Russia and Vietnam agreed to intensify the exchange of information and expertise “in countering the conspiracies, intentions, and activities of hostile forces and foreign special agencies,” which, in the document’s wording, are aimed at interfering in internal affairs and influencing state, political, and legislative institutions. The two sides also stated their readiness to expand cooperation “in combating crime in all its forms and manifestations, including cybercrime” and to continue cooperation between law enforcement agencies.
In addition, Moscow and Hanoi intend to expand cooperation in the oil and gas sector. The joint statement describes energy and fossil fuels as areas of “strategic breakthrough in Vietnam-Russia relations.” The two sides agreed to speed up work on possible supplies of Russian oil and liquefied natural gas to Vietnam and on building infrastructure on the Vietnamese side for receiving, processing, and storing hydrocarbons.
Putin said the Russian side had even proposed creating strategic fuel reserves in Vietnam. “Our companies are also interested in establishing transit deliveries of energy resources through Vietnamese territory to neighboring states,” he said. During the visit, the two sides signed agreements on oil and gas projects on the Vietnamese shelf and a framework agreement between Zarubezhneft and Petrovietnam regarding the strategic oil reserve.
Nuclear energy remains another area of cooperation. This past March, Russia and Vietnam signed an intergovernmental agreement on building a Russian-designed nuclear power plant in Vietnam. Putin called the initiative “a truly flagship project.” The two sides also intend to build a Nuclear Science and Technology Center in Vietnam.
In the context of expanding political and security cooperation, Putin announced the potential liberalization of Russia’s visa regime for Vietnamese citizens. “For our part, we are working to introduce reciprocal visa-free travel for our Vietnamese friends in the near future,” he said. Russians no longer need a visa for short trips to Vietnam, and according to Putin, almost 700,000 Russians visited the country in 2025, and another 800,000 in the first half of 2026.
In the final statement, Moscow and Hanoi called their development a “long-term strategic choice and one of the priorities in the foreign policy of each country.” During the meeting with Putin, To Lam called the Russian leader “a great friend of our country and a close brother to the Vietnamese people.” The joint statement also says that Russia “highly appreciates” Vietnam’s position regarding the war in Ukraine.

articles.title: Zelensky’s plane nearly collides with drone during takeoff in Moldova, Norwegian PM states
articles.body:
The plane of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky nearly collided with a drone during takeoff on its way from Moldova to Norway, Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Stoere told the broadcaster NRK on Sept. 9, as quoted by Reuters. Stoere did not specify the source of this information nor how close the drone had come to Zelensky’s plane.
“His plane was nearly hit by a drone as it was about to take off from Moldova. That’s the reality he’s facing,” Stoere said.
On Sept. 8, Zelensky flew to Oslo for King Harald V’s funeral and met with Stoere that same evening. The Norwegian government’s official statement on the talks does not mention the drone incident.
Around the same time, a drone flew over Moldova and Romania; Moldovan authorities initially identified the object as a Shahed of the sort commonly used by Russian forces. According to Moldova’s Defense Ministry, the aircraft entered the country’s airspace from Ukraine at 4:20 p.m., headed through the Chisinau area toward Romania, and left Moldovan territory 17 minutes later.
Romania’s Ministry of Defense said that at 4:33 p.m. its radars detected an aerial target west of Chisinau, and at 4:37 p.m. it entered Romanian airspace roughly 30 kilometers southeast of Iasi. Two Spanish F-18s were scrambled to track the drone, which advanced further into Romania, reaching the vicinity of Roman before turning back. It was detected again over Moldova at 5:08 p.m. The aircraft eventually crashed near the village of Mihaileni Vechi, roughly 25 kilometers from the Romanian border.
On Sept. 9, Moldovan police said that the debris found at the site featured a turbojet engine and other elements characteristic of UAVs commonly used by Russia. The impact caused an explosion that left a large crater; at the scene, investigators found shrapnel in the form of metal balls. Experts are still determining the drone’s exact type and the size of its warhead. No casualties were reported.
The OSINT project Oko Hora (Eye of Horus) ✙ News and Analysis claims that the UAV was a jet-powered Geran-4 that had flown about 500 kilometers over Moldova and Romania at an altitude of 7,000-8,000 meters before it ran out of fuel and crashed.
Violations of Romanian airspace by Russian drones have happened before. Since the start of the full-scale war, the country’s Ministry of Defense has recorded 45 unauthorized drone incursions — 26 of them in 2026. In July, Romanian troops destroyed three drones over the course of three days, and in late May a Russian Geran-2 crashed into a residential building in Galati, injuring two people.

articles.title: Pakistan warns Iran to rein in Houthis amid Yemen conflict
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Pakistan warns Iran to rein in Houthis amid renewed Yemen conflict
Pakistan has delivered a Saudi warning to Iran to rein in its Yemeni Houthi allies after they stepped up attacks on the kingdom, in a coordinated effort to prevent the crisis from spiralling, Saudi, Pakistani and Iranian sources said.
The Houthis struck an airbase in Khamis Mushait and oil infrastructure in nearby cities on Tuesday, wounding 73 people, in one of the biggest attacks on Saudi Arabia since the start of the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran in February.
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said on Wednesday that Saudi warplanes carried out 54 airstrikes across various Yemeni provinces over the past 12 hours, adding that they would "not go unanswered and unpunished".
The escalating conflict, which represents a second theatre of war threatening global energy supplies, comes as Iran and the United States wage their biggest declared wave of tit-for-tat attacks on shipping in the Gulf region since their war began.
Pakistan's warning to Iran carries significant weight because of its recently signed Mecca Defence Agreement with Saudi Arabia and Turkey.
While officials in Islamabad stressed any military role would be confined to defending Saudi territory, Pakistani Defence Minister Khawaja Asif said attacks spilling into the kingdom could trigger a joint security arrangement involving Riyadh, Ankara and Islamabad.
"An aggression on one country will be considered an aggression on all three countries," Asif said on Pakistani TV.
"There is no ambiguity or doubt... Unprovoked aggression or spillover... into Saudi Arabia will definitely make this agreement operational."
The Pakistani defence ministry, foreign ministry and the military did not respond to a Reuters request for comment.
Fears of regional conflict
Pakistan’s intervention, after years of balancing ties with Saudi Arabia and Iran, has underscored the seriousness of the Houthi attacks. The message to Tehran is clear: rein in the Houthis or risk turning a proxy conflict into a broader regional security crisis, the sources said.
A senior regional diplomat said Pakistan had conveyed the message to Iran over the past 24 hours, urging Tehran to use its influence to halt Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia.
A senior Iranian official confirmed that Pakistan conveyed the message to Tehran on Tuesday and Tehran's response was that "Iran does not control the Houthis".
However, two Iranian sources said Tehran had told the Houthis last week to carry out attacks on Saudi Arabia. Tehran promised additional funding and weapons, they said, while several Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps commanders had travelled to Yemen to help coordinate the attacks.
The regional diplomat said Islamabad was seeking to restrain the Houthis before the escalation reached a point where Riyadh could press Pakistan to play a more active role in defending it.
"Pakistan has an agreement with Saudi Arabia, but I am hopeful the situation will not reach the point where Pakistan has to practically step in," the diplomat told Reuters. "It will pursue a diplomatic solution for now."
Pakistani support for Saudis
The Pakistani source said Saudi officials had met senior Pakistani and Turkish military representatives in Riyadh to coordinate their response. The three countries agreed that their troops would not enter Yemen and that any response would be launched from Saudi territory, the source added.
A second Pakistani source said no decision had been made to join retaliatory strikes, stressing that its military pact with Riyadh was defensive and limited to protecting Saudi territory. Pakistani forces could provide military, technical, ground or air support within Saudi Arabia, but would not take part in combat operations on foreign soil, the source said.
The pressure campaign waged by Iran and the Houthis could have the opposite effect to that intended by Tehran, the regional diplomat said.
By targeting Gulf security in a bid to pressure Washington over its blockade of Iranian ports, Tehran risks driving Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, Turkey and other U.S.-aligned states into closer security coordination rather than fracturing their ties.
Trump's blockade of Iran set to continue
Regional officials also see little sign that Washington is prepared to relent.
President Donald Trump appears committed to maintaining the US.blockade until Iran reaches an agreement with Washington, the diplomat said, while Qatar is quietly exploring new proposals aimed at bringing both sides back to negotiations.
Another regional source said Saudi Arabia's military response would remain focused on the Houthis rather than Iran itself. Nor do Saudi officials believe Houthi attacks will achieve Tehran's broader objective of ending the U.S. blockade.
Riyadh is not expected to press Washington to lift the blockade, that source said, stressing that Trump believes sustained economic coercion is the most effective pathway to negotiations.
"The question is how much pain Iran can absorb, and for how long," the source said. "Trump does not want a military solution. He wants to squeeze them through the blockade."

articles.title: Zelenskyy’s Plane Nearly Hit by Drone in Moldova as Russian Drones Violate Its Airspace the Same Day
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Zelenskyy’s Plane Nearly Hit by Drone in Moldova as Russian Drones Violate Its Airspace the Same Day
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s plane was nearly hit by a drone during takeoff from Moldova as he was traveling to Oslo, Norway, for the funeral of King Harald.
The aircraft safely arrived in Oslo on Tuesday evening, where Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre met with the Ukrainian leader the following morning, as reported by Reuters.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
During their meeting in his office on Wednesday, Støre inquired about Zelenskyy’s night. The Ukrainian leader mentioned that it was not a good night, as he spent time on the phone gathering updates regarding missile strike locations across Ukraine.
Commenting on the incident in an interview with NRK, Støre highlighted the constant danger surrounding the Ukrainian delegation, stating, "This is the reality he faces."
Støre emphasized the severity of the situation during the discussions, describing the current circumstances in Ukraine by noting, "It is a very dramatic situation."
He added that the continuous aerial threats and operational demands leave "a deep impression" on those witnessing the ongoing defense effort.
In addition to his meeting with Støre, Zelenskyy met with Norwegian Finance Minister Jens Stoltenberg and Foreign Minister Espen Barth Eide shortly after landing in Oslo on Tuesday evening.
The recent near-miss in Moldova is not the first time aerial threats have targeted the Ukrainian president's travels abroad.
On August 14, Romanian authorities issued three air alerts as Russian forces attacked Ukraine’s Odesa region, with another drone reported entering Romanian airspace, highlighting the recurring violations of both Romanian and Moldovan airspace during such attacks.
Four unidentified military-grade drones tracked the flight path of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and First Lady Olena Zelenska during their official visit to Ireland.
The presidential aircraft had touched down at Dublin Airport slightly ahead of schedule, but the drones arrived at the airspace where the plane was originally expected. Afterwards, the drones circled an Irish Navy vessel that had been secretly stationed in the Irish Sea.
Irish authorities chose not to engage the drones, which were believed to have been launched from northeast Dublin and had remained airborne for up to two hours. Law enforcement officials believed the intent had been to disrupt the president's arrival, as the drones had operated with visible lights turned on in a deliberate attempt to be seen.

articles.title: Almost 80% of Poles support helping Baltic states if Russia attacks
articles.body:
Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!
Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.
Almost 80% of Poles say that they would want their country to come to the aid of the Baltic states – Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania – if they were attacked by Russia.
The new poll follows a controversy over comments by a senior opposition figure, former defence minister Mariusz Błaszczak, in which he refused to confirm his support for Poland fulfilling its NATO obligations by coming to the aid of the Baltic states if they were invaded.
🔴Czy w razie ewentualnej agresji ze strony Rosji, Polska powinna pomóc Litwie, Łotwie i Estonii?
➡️tak – 77,8% 
➡️nie – 16,1%  #sondaż @IBRiS_PL dla @RadioZET_NEWS pic.twitter.com/6jiBgOW5v3
— IBRiS (@IBRiS_PL) September 9, 2026
In a survey for broadcaster Radio Zet, the IBRiS agency asked: “In the event of Russian aggression, should Poland help Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia?” In response, 77.8% of those polled said that it should, while only 16.1% were opposed.
Among respondents who identified as politically centrist, 92% were in favour. The figures were lower for those with left-wing (75%) or right-wing (73%) views, though in both cases a large majority still supported coming to the Baltic states’ aid.
Commenting on the findings, Radio Zet wrote that “the survey shows that Poles feel responsible for the military security of their NATO allies – contrary to what some politicians have said”.
That was a reference to remarks last week by Błaszczak, who is the head of the parliamentary caucus of the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), Poland’s largest opposition group. Between 2018 and 2023, Błaszczak served as defence minister in the former PiS-led government.
In an interview with Radio Zet, Błaszczak was asked if, in the event of a Russian attack on the Baltic states, Poland should come to their aid. “Polish soldiers should defend Poland,” he responded. “We need to be strong in our alliances…We should prioritise cooperation with the United States.”
The interviewer pointed out that Article 5 of the NATO treaty requires members of the alliance to come to the assistance of another member that is attacked, and again asked if Poland should help the Baltic states if such an attack occurred.
“We border Russia directly, and we border a Russia that has effectively taken over Belarusian territory. So we’re also on the front line,” replied Błaszczak. “This article, of course, speaks of solidarity, but the point is that the government that governs Poland should establish the best possible relations with the United States.”
With the interviewer continuing to press the question, Błaszczak simply said that “it all depends on the circumstances” and “it’s not a straightforward issue”.
🇵🇱🇺🇸🇪🇪🇱🇹🇱🇻@mblaszczak @pisorgpl o zobowiązaniach sojuszniczych wynikających z artykułu 5 @NATO 👇
Źródło: @BogRymanowski @Radio_ZET pic.twitter.com/gfQz4QyD1D
— WarNewsPL (@WarNewsPL1) September 1, 2026
Błaszczak’s comments were criticised by figures from Poland’s ruling coalition, which ranges from left to centre right. They accused him of calling into question the validity of Article 5, on which Poland would rely if it were attacked.
“A former defence minister who undermines the sanctity of Polish security, i.e. NATO’s Article 5, is a moron,” wrote deputy defence minister Cezary Tomczyk. Interior minister Marcin Kiewiński said that Błaszczak had “undermined the very purpose of NATO’s existence”.
In response to the criticism, Błaszczak wrote on social media that, during the PiS government’s time in power, it had significantly enhanced security ties with the Baltic states, including stationing Polish forces in Latvia and contributing Polish F-16s to NATO’s air policing mission.
“NATO’s Article 5 is activated collectively, and alliance commitments are binding, but every [Polish] defence minister’s priority should be the defence of Poland and ensuring the safety of Poles,” he added.
Błaszczak to stan umysłu. Mało im było niszczenia SAFE, to dziś były szef MON podważył sens istnienia NATO wskazując, że Wojsko Polskie nie powinno bronić Litwy, Łotwy czy Estonii. 
Przyjaźń tego skompromitowanego środowiska z Orbanem to nie był przypadek…
— Marcin Kierwiński (@MKierwinski) September 1, 2026
On Wednesday, Poland’s foreign minister, Radosław Sikorski, visited Latvia, including the base in Ādaži where a Polish military contingent has been based since 2017 as part of a multinational NATO brigade.
“Poland and Latvia face similar threats in the security domain,” said Sikorski. “We must speak with one voice and take our security seriously. Only such actions can guarantee effective protection against the threat from Russia.”
“We do not want an escalation of the conflict, but Putin must know that we are not going to sit idly by and wait for his next step,” he continued. “We understand that the defence of our allies also contributes to Polish security. We stand ready to share the burden of defending the eastern flank.”

Continuing visit to Latvia, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign Affairs @sikorskiradek visited the base of the Polish Military Contingent.
The Polish contingent in Latvia serves as part of NATO’s allied presence, strengthening deterrence and defence… pic.twitter.com/tKMIix2h9L

articles.title: Ukrainian security services face new scrutiny after Kiev gunfight – for speaking Russian
articles.body:
Ukrainian security agents probed for speaking Russian during Kiev gunfight
Ukrainian security operatives involved in a scandalous gunfight between two rival factions of Vladimir Zelensky's government in Kiev last week are facing a fresh probe – this time for speaking Russian during the clash.
The September 2 gang-warfare-style clash between the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) and the Ukrainian Military Intelligence Directorate (HUR), centred on an attempt to arrest white supremacist Stepan Kaplunov, a senior officer in the so-called Russian Volunteer Corps (RDK), a paramilitary unit operating under the HUR and thought to be in control of a number of Ukrainian scam-call centers.
Ukraine’s language ombudswoman, Elena Ivanovskaya, said Wednesday she had requested personal information on all those involved and demanded the two services provide an explanation as to why their officials “used a non-state language while performing their official duties.” The data was needed “to clarify the circumstances and make a balanced decision on response measures,” she said in a statement published by Ukrainian media.
Crackdown on Russian
Ukrainian is mandatory in the country's public sphere, including government, education, media and customer service. Violations can result in administrative fines of up to $270.
Ivanovskaya has suggested increasing the fines tenfold and has demanded Russian-speaking children and parents use Ukrainian during breaks and in conversations with teachers. According to the ombudswoman, both instances fall under the “public sphere” definition and the use of Russian in such cases could be punishable by fines.
Kiev announced plans in February to take all Russian and Russian-language books out of circulation in Ukraine. Ukraine expanded 2016 import restrictions to outright ban any commercial Russian and Belarusian book entries in 2023.
Kiev is also seeking to block access to Russian music on international streaming platforms inside Ukraine and prevent performers from the neighboring country from appearing in domestic popularity charts, according to Ukrainian Sanctions Policy Commissioner Vladislav Vlasiuk. More than 100 Russian performers have been blacklisted in Ukraine and the list will be expanded, according to the official.
Moscow has repeatedly denounced such measures as “Russophobic censorship,” warning that attempts to “cancel” Russian culture will ultimately fail.
Russian remains widespread
Despite the restrictions, Russian remains widely used in Ukraine. Ukrainian Culture Minister Tatyana Berezhnaya said earlier this year that 71% of Ukrainians regularly consume Russian-language content, with nearly a quarter doing so every day.
Ukrainian officials, especially those in Vladimir Zelensky's inner circle targeted by anti-corruption agents, have been repeatedly caught using Russian on surveillance audio.
The Western-backed Ukrainian anti-corruption agency (NABU) published audio recordings that showed that the chief cybercrime prosecutor accused of extorting protection money from Ukraine’s massive scam-call industry was predominantly using Russian in his communications.
Foreign Minister Andrey Sibiga also spoke Russian throughout a lengthy recent interview with a Kazakh outlet while acting in his official capacity.

articles.title: Russia: Recruitment of foreign nationals to fight in Ukraine amounts to human trafficking
articles.body:
Russia has used deceptive, coercive and exploitative practices to recruit foreign nationals into its military forces and send them to fight in Ukraine, Amnesty International said in a new briefing published today. In many cases this amounts to the human rights violation and crime of human trafficking, which remains widespread in Russia and which the international community should urgently address.
The research details how recruiters have lured individuals from abroad into the Russian Armed Forces under false pretences and exploited the precarious circumstances of migrants and refugees already present in Russia. Those targeted are primarily from low-income countries in the Global South.
“Amnesty’s research demonstrates how Russia’s Armed Forces are bolstering their ranks with economically vulnerable foreign nationals and using them as cannon fodder in the war of aggression against Ukraine. The level of exploitation and coercion involved led us to conclude that in many cases this amounts to human trafficking, as defined under the UN’s Palermo Protocol,” said Agnès Callamard, Amnesty International’s Secretary General.
“Building on pre-existing exploitative migration pathways and abusive practices towards migrants and refugees in Russia, recruiters have developed a system of coercion, fraud and deception, including false promises of civilian or non-combat employment, to enlist foreigners in the military. Once victims sign the paperwork, often in a language they do not understand, military commanders restrict their movements, deploy them to the front lines with minimal preparation, and threaten those who seek a way out.”
The briefing is based on interviews with individuals from Brazil, Colombia, Cuba, Egypt, Sierra Leone, Sri Lanka, Somalia and South Africa conducted at two Ukrainian prisoner of war camps between 2024 and 2026; and conversations with foreign nationals currently serving with Russian forces and members of their families as well as lawyers, human rights activists and journalists.
Among their primary tools to recruit foreign nationals, the Russian authorities have weaponized the irregular immigration status of those who overstay work-related visas and the precarious situation of foreigners accused of criminal offences, presenting enlistment as a favourable alternative to detention and deportation.
Amnesty’s research demonstrates how Russia’s Armed Forces are bolstering their ranks with economically vulnerable foreign nationals and using them as cannon fodder.
Agnès Callamard, Amnesty International’s Secretary General
Amnesty International interviewed two Sri Lankan men recruited after overstaying their work visas, as well as Cuban and Egyptian nationals who were jailed for alleged drug possession and offered the opportunity to sign military contracts instead of serving or completing their prison sentences. The organization also received testimony from a refugee from Central Africa who was detained after his temporary protection status expired and threatened with deportation unless he signed up with Russia’s Armed Forces.
Obscuring or misrepresenting the risks involved and the specific nature of the work on offer has become key to the Russian Army’s recruitment of migrants. The prospect of military service is typically presented as a non-combat support function, such as working in a military kitchen or as a driver far from the front line. The two Sri Lankans said they were led to believe they would be working as cooks but were sent to fight on the front lines and captured within weeks by Ukrainian forces. “The scale of fighting is unimaginable. You do not see Ukrainian soldiers, only drones. Drones everywhere,” one said. “I would never go back there.”
Local agents and misleading online job advertisements have been instrumental in deceiving foreign nationals in their home countries. Individuals from Brazil, Colombia, Sierra Leone, Somalia, South Africa and Sri Lanka who had been recruited from outside Russia said they were falsely promised civilian jobs in security, logistics, construction, IT and other sectors, often with assurances of high salaries and expedited access to Russian citizenship – only to be fraudulently drawn into the Armed Forces upon arrival.
A South African man who applied online for a driving job in Poland received instructions via an agent on WhatsApp to fly to Moscow to pick up a truck and drive it to Poland, his wife told Amnesty International. “Upon arrival to Moscow, everything was taken from him… He was told that he would not be going to Poland and that he is becoming a soldier.”
Many recruits were promised lucrative salaries and sign-up bonuses that were not fulfilled. While some received partial payments before being captured, many reported receiving nothing at all. Beyond financial remuneration, all those interviewed described promised pathways to Russian citizenship as a particular incentive.
All the interviewees alleged severe restrictions on their freedom of movement after signing military contracts. Recruits from Brazil and Sri Lanka said their passports and mobile phones were taken from them during training or prior to front line deployment. Others said they could not leave the facilities they were taken to after signing the paperwork, with all transportation conducted in a secretive and strictly controlled manner.
Pedro, a Brazilian IT professional recruited after signing what he thought was a contract for a well-paid tech job in Russia, said he asked his commander to leave but was told: “If you try to escape, you will either go to jail or we will kill you.”
Lack of military experience seems to be no barrier to recruitment, with most enlistees deployed to active combat zones after just two weeks of training. Many reported insufficient preparation, lack of equipment, and limited communication with commanders due to language barriers. This suggests that recruitment of foreign nationals is driven by a desire to increase the sheer numbers of Russia’s front line forces, with little or no concern for combat readiness and an apparent disregard for human life.
The patterns documented in this research raise serious concerns over Russia’s violations of its international law obligations, including apparent involvement in human trafficking, failure to criminalize and combat human trafficking; conduct prompt and effective investigations of all reported crimes and serious human rights violations and abuses; identify and protect victims and survivors; and bring to account anyone suspected of being responsible or complicit in such practices.
Amnesty International calls on Russia to immediately end all abusive practices involving the military recruitment of foreign nationals and their treatment in training centres and at the front line. This includes recruitment through coercion, deception and misinformation; the exploitation of economic, legal or other vulnerabilities of foreign nationals in Russia and individuals from economically disadvantaged communities in the rest of the world; and restrictions on their movement once in Russia or Russian-occupied Ukraine.
These recruitment networks reach far and wide, into vulnerable communities across the world, leaving a trail of exploitation, loss, and pain far beyond war-torn Ukraine.
Agnès Callamard, Amnesty International’s Secretary General
States whose nationals are at risk or have been affected by such practices should take proactive protective measures, including issuing clear public warnings and guidance on the risks of deceptive or fraudulent recruitment schemes linked to employment in Russia or third countries. They should also take active steps, at national, regional and global level, to end the crime of human trafficking and seek accountability for those responsible, as well as remedies for people subjected to coercion, exploitation or abuse.
The briefing also contains a series of calls to the Ukrainian authorities, including with regard to third-country nationals being held as prisoners of war.
“The human suffering caused by the trafficking of foreign nationals by Russia, or by those it has enabled and incentivized, is not restricted to the front line in Ukraine. These recruitment networks reach far and wide, into vulnerable communities across the world, leaving a trail of exploitation, loss, and pain far beyond war-torn Ukraine,” Agnès Callamard said.
“If Russia refuses to put an end to human trafficking and continues exploiting vulnerable communities globally, other states must do everything in their power to stop this crime. There must be full accountability for all those directly involved and all those complicit, whether as private recruiters or intermediaries, state officials or military commanders. Wherever human trafficking has occurred, its victims and survivors should be identified and treated as such, with all evidence collected and preserved in order to pursue those responsible.”
Background
In May 2025, the Russian authorities formally outlawed Amnesty International’s presence in Russia, criminalized its activities there, and denied it the opportunity to openly collect information in or from Russia. This has prevented the organization from freely investigating the stories of individuals there who, according to Russian government-controlled media, have alleged that Ukrainian recruiters have also sought to enlist foreigners through deception or exploitation of vulnerable circumstances.
For more information or to arrange an interview please contact Amnesty International’s press office: [email protected]

articles.title: Ukraine attacks port in Russia’s Dagestan with drones. One drone hits theater building.
articles.body:
Ukraine attacks port in Russia’s Dagestan with drones. One drone hits theater building.
Ukraine’s armed forces struck Dagestan with drones, according to Fyodor Shchukin, the region’s acting head, who said a fire broke out at the Makhachkala International Sea Trade Port after “drone fragments” fell there.
A drone also struck the Avar Musical Drama Theater, named after Gamzat Tsadasa, coming down on the roof, according to Theater Director Magomed Bisavaliev. The blast blew out windows and sparked a fire.
The fires have since been extinguished and no one was killed or injured, Shchukin said.
Ukrainian drones also struck Russia’s Voronezh region, Governor Alexander Gusev said, with one hitting a private home in Borisoglebsk. The strike killed a woman and injured two other people.
Russia’s Defense Ministry announced that air defenses shot down 448 Ukrainian drones overnight across various regions.

articles.title: Yemen's Houthis report dozens of new Saudi airstrikes
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Yemen's Houthis report dozens of new Saudi airstrikes as conflict exacerbates
Yemen's Houthi rebels reported dozens of Saudi airstrikes on Wednesday as daily attacks continued in a conflict that has reignited during the Middle East war, with hundreds of people killed in fighting near the Red Sea.
More than 50 attacks targeted several regions including Taiz and Hodeida, the scene of fierce clashes between the Houthis and the Saudi-backed internationally recognised government, the Houthis said.
"It's a catastrophe, and the attacks are ongoing," said Mohammed Khudairi, one of nearly 20,000 people who fled the fighting, according to the International Organization for Migration.
"We managed to leave, but others remain trapped there," he said at a displacement camp of wood-and-straw huts near Khokha, on the Red Sea coast.
The latest salvos in Yemen's previously dormant conflict come a day after the Iran-backed Houthis set oil sites ablaze and wounded 73 in their heaviest missile and drone attacks against Saudi Arabia in years.
The Houthis' Al-Masirah TV Channel reported on Wednesday the toll from Saudi strikes on a prison days earlier had climbed to 32 dead and seven injured as rescue and recovery efforts continued.
The fighting comes against the backdrop of the Middle East war, which erupted in late February with US-Israeli strikes on Iran.
Over 500 killed; Hodeida in Saudi crosshairs
The fighting in Yemen has killed more than 500 people since the Houthis launched a major offensive last week to seize territory around the Bab al-Mandeb strait, gateway to the Red Sea shipping route.
The Houthis have also been attacking Saudi oil tankers, and are trying to tighten their squeeze on the shipments, analysts say -- a lifeline for exports after Iran's blockade of the Strait of Hormuz.
"During the past 12 hours, the Saudi enemy's air force conducted 54 airstrikes targeting the provinces of Al-Jawf, Marib, Taiz, Hodeida and Saada," said Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree.
Footage released by the Iran-backed group showed what it said were attacks on Saudi-backed forces on Al-Jawf province's frontlines, with missiles heard flying overhead before impact, followed by flaming wreckage.
There was no official comment from Saudi Arabia.
Analysis by the Institute for the Study of War said the city of Hodeida, held by the Houthis, could be the "ultimate objective" of the Saudi backed forces.
The Red Sea port is "critical to both Houthi civilian and military goods, and its loss would be a significant setback for the Houthis", a report published by the institute said.
Saudi warnings
Saudi civil defence issued warnings twice for the southern governorate of Khamis Mushait, near Yemen, and once for Abha city, but quickly lifted the alerts without elaborating on the cause.
On Tuesday, Saudi authorities vowed to respond to the Houthi attacks, saying they caused fires and temporary shutdowns at oil sites.
The Houthis triggered the return to hostilities in July, when they let an Iranian plane land in defiance of Saudi control of Yemeni airspace.
Yemen's internationally recognised government, which controls Aden and the south of the country, retaliated by striking the airport, an attack the Houthis blamed on its sponsor, Saudi Arabia.
The ongoing exchanges risk returning Yemen to a conflict that left hundreds of thousands of people dead and sparked one of the world's worst humanitarian crises.
The Houthis, after seizing Yemen's capital Sanaaand forcing out the internationally recognised government, fought a Saudi-led coalition from 2015 until a United Nations-brokered ceasefire in 2022.

articles.title: “Weeks, Not Months”: Ukraine’s FP-7 Ballistic Missile Nears Battlefield Debut
articles.body:
- Category
- Defense Tech
“Weeks, Not Months”: Ukraine’s FP-7 Ballistic Missile Nears Battlefield Debut
Ukraine’s FP-7 ballistic missile is now in military trials and could enter operational use within weeks, while its longer-range FP-9 may ultimately have to prove itself the hard way—against real Russian targets.
Ukrainian defense company Fire Point has moved its FP-7 ballistic missile into military trials after successfully completing two earlier stages of testing, bringing the weapon potentially within weeks of operational use.
Fire Point CEO Iryna Terekh announced the milestone during the 34th International Defense Industry Exhibition MSPO, according to a UNITED24 Media correspondent on September 10.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Terekh, the FP-7 has already passed its first two testing phases and is now undergoing military evaluation, which is also part of the missile’s formal codification process.
The earlier stages included ground and laboratory testing, during which individual systems and subsystems were evaluated separately, including the rocket engine and navigation equipment.
“We are erasing the deep rear doctrine from the Russian military vocabulary,” said Terekh.
Flight testing followed, allowing engineers to collect data on the missile’s behavior in the air and determine how closely its actual performance matched design calculations.
The FP-7 has now advanced beyond those stages.
“We’re talking weeks, not months,” Terekh said when asked how soon the missile could move toward operational use.
Fire Point is simultaneously developing the longer-range FP-9 ballistic missile, which is currently undergoing flight testing and remains one stage behind the FP-7.
Testing the FP-9 presents a very different challenge because of its greater range.
According to the developers, the missile has a minimum distance required for ballistic flight. Once it passes a certain point in its trajectory, the test can no longer simply be terminated through software.
That makes conducting a complete test entirely within Ukrainian territory difficult.
As a result, once the current flight-testing phase is completed, the FP-9 could potentially move from testing into military evaluation through actual employment against Russian targets rather than following the same conventional test sequence as the shorter-range FP-7.
Earlier, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy expressed hope that the US will support implementing the FREYJA anti-ballistic missile program, with the interceptor missile being built based on the Fire Point FP-7 ballistic missile.
“We are preparing our own FREYJA program. We very much hope that the Americans will support this program as well. But nevertheless, with the Europeans we will definitely achieve the desired result,” Zelenskyy said.

articles.title: How Emmanuel Macron brought France’s AI darling to the world stage
articles.body:
It’s not every AI company that can count the French president as its top salesman.
On June 11, 2025, the founder of French AI company Mistral took to the stage alongside Jensen Huang, the powerful CEO of chip giant Nvidia, to announce a partnership between the two companies. As President Emmanuel Macron joined them, the Taiwanese-American executive turned to Mistral’s young CEO Arthur Mensch and said something just audible to the Parisian audience of techies and public officials: “Your president worked really hard for you.”
The Nvidia boss was referring to the deal his company had just sealed with Mistral to roll out AI infrastructure across Europe. “I told the president that Arthur and Mistral needed support from France’s biggest companies. Mr. President said to me: ‘Which ones? Let me call them!’” Huang said.
Advertisement
By the time the deal was official, the companies could announce that BNP Paribas, Orange, SNCF and Thales had all expressed interest in the partnership — boosting Mistral’s official entry into the global race for computing power.
Even for the head of Nvidia, the world’s most valuable company, such presidential proactivity was remarkable, illustrating the French government’s dedication to championing its homegrown startup and showing how Mistral has leveraged ties to the executive branch in Paris to try and reach the level of some of the biggest generative AI companies.
Mistral’s rise over the past three years, according to a dozen public officials and representatives of France’s tech ecosystem interviewed by POLITICO, owes much to the privileged relationship it built with Macron — enabling the company to secure both strong ties with the French state and a seat at the table with the world’s leading AI companies.
Now, with a French presidential election bringing to a close Macron’s two-term reign, details on the depth of that relationship — many of which are reported here for the first time — also raise questions about Mistral’s future under a different president.
The company on Tuesday announced a new €3 billion funding round including investments from the European Union and South Korea’s electronics giant Samsung, valuing Mistral at more than €21 billion. While that falls well short of the valuations of Anthropic and OpenAI, the news confirms the French startup as the only serious European player in the AI race.
As Europe questions its ability to challenge Chinese and American tech giants, Mensch and his team must now plan for life after Macron.
‘Fairy godmothers around the cradle’
Launched in 2023 by three co-founders — Mensch, Guillaume Lample and Timothée Lacroix — Mistral AI set out to build a full-fledged large-language model to compete with the likes of OpenAI and Anthropic. To do so, the Paris-based startup put forward a clear strategy from day one: cultivate a relationship with the French executive, and Macron in particular.
From its first funding round, the startup — which declined to respond to questions for this article — made a point of forging ties with the public sector. First among them was Bpifrance, France’s public investment bank and one of its earliest investors.
“We were aware of the sovereignty issues linked to AI,” recalls Arnaud Caudoux, deputy CEO of Bpifrance. “We had a good idea of the few — a few hundred in the world at the time — credible experts in the sector, among whom were Mistral’s founders.”
Advertisement
The BPI investment was part of a record €105 million total for a French seed round. But Caudoux noted: “There were a lot of fairy godmothers around the cradle.”
Those looking out for the startup came from the cream of French business and tech, playing crucial roles as matchmakers, patrons and fundraisers. They included telecom billionaire Xavier Niel, as well as Jean-Charles Samuelian-Werve and Charles Gorintin, co-founders of insurance startup Alan.
They were driven by the same goal: helping a European AI giant emerge. They tapped their networks to identify the most promising French AI researchers. These three businessmen were the ones who played matchmaker, bringing together Mensch, Lacroix and Lample.
When the Alan team struck a deal with the three young co-founders, it secured a strategic recruit to forge ties with the public sector: Cédric O, a former digital affairs secretary of state and early Macron supporter, would play a crucial role in the startup’s launch.
It was O who went into battle in Brussels to try to secure looser rules under the European Union’s AI Act, first proposed in April 2021. For Mistral, the burgeoning legislation posed a threat: How could Europe build a giant of its own if it stifled innovation?
In 2023, O intervened on Mistral’s behalf in EU talks in an effort to influence the negotiations — to the point that some lawmakers accused him of a conflict of interest. He also drew a rebuke from Thierry Breton, then European commissioner for the internal market.
Advertisement
Mistral “is lobbying, that’s normal,” French-born Breton said during the final weeks of negotiations over the AI Act. “But we are not fooled by anything. It is defending its business today, and not the general interest.”
“Cédric O’s role was, in a way, that of a lightning rod,” said a private-sector official who followed Mistral in its early days. By taking the hits, O allowed Mensch “to grow and develop as a CEO.”
Behind the scenes
From the outset, Mistral played the French and European card. The three co-founders may have built their careers in U.S.-based AI labs — Google DeepMind for Mensch and Facebook AI for Lample and Lacroix — but the first concept notes drafted for the startup’s launch put technological sovereignty at the heart of the project.
At the time, Mensch was a discreet 30-year-old engineer who needed to transform himself into the public face of Mistral on the international stage. Just a few months after launching the startup, the alum of the prestigious École Polytechnique made his first public appearance at VivaTech 2023 — Europe’s largest annual technology event — alongside Macron, who had already begun making the appeal for European technological autonomy.
The two were clearly in sync. “How do France and Europe intend to enable European champions to emerge, and how do we make sure that AI regulation does not hinder innovation?” the young sneaker-wearing entrepreneur asked the French president on the main stage.
Mensch would himself be tasked with helping come up with the answers. A few months later, the prime minister’s office formed a committee of experts to devise a French AI strategy. Alongside Mensch and O, its members included Gaël Varoquaux, a top researcher at France’s national digital research institute and Mensch’s former Ph.D. supervisor, as well as future Nobel economics laureate Philippe Aghion and Meta researcher and Turing Award recipient Yann LeCun.
By 2024, the committee delivered its report and Mistral unveiled Le Chat, its rival to OpenAI’s ChatGPT. But the AI landscape was already changing rapidly — and Europe was having second thoughts.
German rival Aleph Alpha, the continent’s other great hope in generative AI, announced it was moving away from developing its own models. Its CEO, Jonas Andrulis, offered a gloomy assessment: “Simply having a European LLM is not enough as a business model. It does not justify the investment.”
Advertisement
Mistral was not spared those doubts. Many observers feared its technology could fall behind American or Chinese rivals — even raising concerns that the startup might be acquired from abroad.
In 2025, reports of talks with Apple sparked panic at the highest levels of the French state. France’s embassy in the United States and the Elysée presidential palace asked Mistral whether the reports were true, according to two advisers who spoke to POLITICO. The company eventually reassured them: There had been no discussions “at the highest level.”
The French champion instead turned to a partner closer to home, and at the heart of Europe’s drive for technological sovereignty: the Netherlands’ microchip-printing giant ASML. The Dutch pioneer in the chips supply chain poured €1.3 billion of fresh investment into Mistral in September 2025 in a bid to speed up industrial AI development and keep Mistral’s know-how in European hands.
The deal was a boon for politicians — including Macron — seeking to keep the United States out of Europe’s most prized critical technology players.
Strategic partner
Three years into the company’s existence, the French government is no longer simply promoting a promising young startup. The state is now prepared to bend over backward to preserve a company whose technologies are being integrated across government.
After signing a strategic partnership with France’s national employment agency in early 2025, Mistral secured a deal with the French Armed Forces Ministry to develop AI for defense. Since 2025, Le Chat has also been in the process of being rolled out to 10,000 civil servants.
Advertisement
In public, Mensch has played down the importance of public subsidies and government support for his company. But Mistral’s teams in private conversations readily acknowledge that this privileged relationship is a major asset.
With Macron’s help, the French company has also opened the doors to the world’s biggest international summits — all the way up to the G7.
Mensch has been brought along on almost every presidential trip abroad in the past two years, giving him repeated opportunities to sharpen and spread his AI counter-narrative to contrast with the all-powerful Silicon Valley vision.
For several months, the Mistral boss — who readily appropriates the École Polytechnique motto, “For the Nation, Science and Glory” — has hammered home a position aligned with Macron’s: Europe must promote technological sovereignty and offer the rest of the world a model that is more sensitive to cultural and linguistic nuances than American and Chinese rivals.
In February, on stage at the New Delhi AI summit attended by Dario Amodei of Anthropic, Demis Hassabis of Google DeepMind and Sam Altman of OpenAI, Mensch defended AI as “a tool for empowerment, not domination.” He spoke about the importance of deciding who controls the deployment of AI, who benefits from it and how to ensure that it serves the general interest, not just a few powerful players.
That landed as countries across the world were scrambling to get insights from U.S. firms and the Trump administration into how new AI models were creating major new hacking risks.
Advertisement
And in June, in Evian-les-Bains at Lake Geneva, Mensch had lunch with G7 leaders and AI executives, including Altman. He once again took on the role of maverick to confront his American rivals, who were calling for technological standards to be drawn up under U.S. leadership.
“We still need to be very wary,” Mensch told POLITICO in an interview after the meeting. “It’s true that American actors tend to make that argument, which is, ‘Trust us—we’ll set standards here, and then we’ll export them to you.’”
Succession planning
As Mistral moves into infrastructure by building data centers and continues rolling out its solutions at major companies, some are beginning to doubt whether it can remain in the race to produce “frontier” models — the most powerful models available.
For Macron, the June G7 meeting was one of the last opportunities to leave his mark on the global AI debate before his presidency ends next spring. For Mistral, its relationship with Macron’s successor has yet to be built.
Gabriel Attal, former prime minister and presidential candidate for Macron’s pro-business bloc, readily showcases his ties to Mistral and has put AI at the heart of his campaign platform — even incorporating Le Chat into his communications toolkit. Attal’s centrist rival Edouard Philippe would also almost certainly continue backing Mensch.
Advertisement
While Mistral does not publicly associate itself with the far-right National Rally of Marine Le Pen, the nationalist party sees the company as a sovereign asset. On the left, the parties have unanimously backed the company — and called for sovereign AI — in response to the risk of American models being weaponized against European countries.
Yet Mistral relies on international funding and major partnerships with American giants including Amazon, Nvidia and Microsoft. While bringing in ASML as a key investor meant Mistral would remain firmly rooted in Europe, it also shifted some of the power to ASML’s headquarters in Veldhoven, the Netherlands.
This detail could undermine the French consensus in favor of Mistral, just as AI is emerging as a key campaign issue for the presidential election.
“We need to kill this very bar room idea that it would be feasible to own the capital, and therefore finance on our own, at French or European level, the hundreds of billions that AI infrastructure requires. It’s simply impossible,” said Bruno Bonnell, a French businessman who runs a major public investment program, France 2030, under the prime minister’s office.

articles.title: Trump touts $5,000 payout if Republicans win
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Trump touts $5,000 payout if Republicans win as Vance waits in wings
President Donald Trump capped the first day of his Republican Party's first-ever midterm convention by proposing to pay every US adult a $5,000 "Trump dividend" if his party wins November's congressional elections.
Trump delivered the extraordinary overture during a primetime speech that lasted nearly two hours and firmly placed him at the center of the midterm campaign at a time when his sagging approval ratings could weigh on Republicans' chances.
Vice President JD Vance will give the keynote address on Thursday night, though Trump is scheduled to make closing remarks to bring the made-for-television two-day event in Dallas to an end.
With Trump constitutionally barred from seeking a third term, Vance's speech could serve as an early audition for the 2028 presidential election and offer clues about how he would lead a party reshaped by Trump.
It was not immediately clear how the $5,000 payments would work or whether they would be legal. The proposal would likely cost more than $1 trillion, with approximately 270 million US adults, and could require the approval of Congress.
The convention's focus on Trump–some Republicans have dubbed it "Trumpapalooza"–amounts to a risky bet that he can mobilize the voters who carried him to the presidency two years ago, despite opinion polls showing his popularity is at an all-time low.
But it remains to be seen whether his campaign-style speech will appeal to the critical swing voters who have drifted away from Trump's party amid growing dissatisfaction with the cost of living and the war on Iran.
"I'm asking you to pretend that I'm on the ballot," Trump said, a line that may have pleased Democratic campaign strategists just as much as MAGA voters.
Republican efforts got a boost from an unlikely source on Wednesday, when Democratic U.S. Senator John Fetterman appeared in a pretaped video segment introducing his "great friend," fellow Pennsylvania Senator Dave McCormick, a Republican.
Fetterman said he would always "reject the extremes in socialism," a comment that is likely to bolster Republican attacks on Democrats as too left-wing. Fetterman, who has increasingly broken with his fellow Democrats, has nevertheless rejected speculation that he might leave the party.
Some vulnerable Republicans in tough races, perhaps mindful of tying themselves too closely to the unpopular Trump, elected to skip the affair, including Senator Dan Sullivan of Alaska and Senator Susan Collins of Maine.
While Republican officials had described the convention as an opportunity to tout Trump's policies, most speakers focused on attacking Democrats as extreme on topics such as transgender women in sports and border security—political red meat for core Trump supporters.
Alabama state Representative Ernie Yarbrough, a convention attendee, said Trump needs to give voters a clearer sense of how long the war in Iran could last.
"People want to feel like we're not getting stuck in an endless cycle," he said.
Trump defended his decision to attack Iran, saying he acted to prevent Tehran from developing a nuclear weapon. He also promised that oil prices would drop "as soon as we win the war with Iran," which he vowed would happen soon.
But the conflict shows little sign of ending more than six months after the U.S. and Israel launched strikes on Iran, and analysts have said Iran's nuclear program has not been eliminated. Iran denies seeking a nuclear weapon.
Before Trump took the stage, a parade of speakers called Democrats "socialists" and "communists," echoing one of Trump's favorite attack lines. Democrats are "dangerous, radical and weird," said Senator Tim Scott of South Carolina, the chairman of the party's Senate campaign arm.
The stakes are high for both parties in the United States. With the elections less than two months away, Republicans face the prospect of losing control of at least one chamber of Congress, with public polling showing Democrats more motivated to vote and Trump's approval ratings deeply underwater.

articles.title: He photographed Ukraine, then enlisted and died defending it at 27. Eleven years on, Viktor Hurniak’s story is still being told
articles.body:
Viktor Hurniak was a Ukrainian photojournalist who worked for UNIAN, a major Ukrainian news outlet, and for Reuters, and co-founded the LUFA photo agency, according to Ukrainska Pravda. He joined the fight in the Russo-Ukrainian war in September 2014. Russia killed him on 19 October that year near the village of Smile in Luhansk Oblast, as he helped evacuate wounded soldiers under mortar fire.
Since the Russo-Ukrainian war began in 2014, Ukrainian media workers have been killed while reporting, as civilians, and after joining the armed forces.
From photographer to volunteer
Hurniak had been photographing since he was 14. He started at the Ternopil newspaper 20 Khvylyn, and UNIAN picked up his work after he happened onto a fire on Crimea’s Ai-Petri in 2007.
By summer 2014, Viktor was raising money and finding helmets, body armor, clothing, and vehicles for Ukrainian troops, often delivering the supplies himself. His network and ability to source equipment earned him the callsign Oligarch among Aidar soldiers.
On one trip to Italy, Viktor, his father Petro, and friends returned with 550 helmets.
Friends, including Vitalii Derekh, tried to persuade him not to go further. They argued that he was more useful finding equipment than carrying a rifle.
Hurniak answered: “Well, I want to fight.”
In September 2014, he joined Aidar’s 24th territorial defense battalion.
His decision did not make him more distant from his family. Olesia Yedynak-Khoma recalled that after joining the battalion, he contacted them more often, sent photographs, and shared more about what was happening in Donbas. He told his sister Olia that there was “real life” in Donbas and that he had found sincere people and a strong sense of brotherhood there.
The day Russia killed him
On 19 October 2014, Hurniak was helping evacuate wounded soldiers from checkpoint 32 on the Bakhmutka road near the village of Smile in Luhansk Oblast when mortar fire hit. He was killed by shrapnel.
Viktor was 27. His daughter Yustyna was two.
Seven years later, Ukraine posthumously named Viktor Hurniak a Hero of Ukraine and awarded him the Golden Star.
His photographs were later exhibited in Poland, Estonia, Germany, and the United States, including at the European Parliament in an exhibition titled “Donbas: War and Peace.”
His story continues
Writer Iryna Vovk's Viktor Hurniak, published by Folio in its "True Heroes" series, was presented at a memorial festival in his home region in October 2025 and in Ternopil in January 2026, 11 years after his death. The book is built from the recollections of his family and friends.
Olesia Yedynak-Khoma, one of Hurniak’s friends, founded a scholarship in his memory at the Ukrainian Catholic University’s School of Journalism and Communications.
The question Hurniak once asked himself later became a guiding phrase for his sister Olia:
“What have you done for victory?”
He had already given his own answer. Urged to keep sourcing equipment rather than carry a rifle, he said he wanted to fight, and in September 2014 he went.
