articles.title: Zelensky hopes to meet with Trump after September 20 — media
articles.body:
ROME, September 10. /TASS/. Vladimir Zelensky hopes to meet with US President Donald Trump after September 20, Italy’s La Stampa said.
"I hope to meet with Trump around 20th of September and I want to raise the issue of supplies of American air defense systems," the newspaper quoted him as saying.
Ukrainian Foreign Ministry Spokesman Georgy Tikhy said on Tuesday that an in-person meeting between Zelensky and Trump had been preliminarily scheduled for September.
After their latest meeting in Washington in late July, The Financial Times reported, citing sources, that Trump had refused to provide Kiev with interceptor missiles for Patriot systems. Following those talks, The Atlantic reported, also citing sources, that Zelensky also did not get permission to use Starlink to strike deep into Russia. It noted, however, that Trump did not give a definitive no, while entrepreneur Elon Musk had refused to meet with Zelensky.

articles.title: US urges NATO allies to leave ICC
articles.body:
The US, further complicating already tense international relations, is pushing for a “systematic dismantling” of the International Criminal Court, urging NATO members to abandon the Rome Statute, writes Politico.
According to three anonymous NATO diplomats, at a closed meeting of ambassadors from 32 NATO member states in Brussels in July, US envoy Matthew Whitaker asked for the alliance’s help in dismantling the ICC and called for abandoning the Rome Statute. Whitaker reportedly concluded his speech by saying that Americans would be careful who supported them.
The pressure to leave the ICC is part of a broader campaign by US President Donald Trump’s administration against international institutions and rules that it sees as restricting US freedom of action. The campaign is driven by US concerns that its officials could be tried for war crimes. The White House is also moving to withdraw from the Paris Climate Agreement, has pulled the US out of the World Health Organization and the UN Human Rights Council, and has pressured companies to withdraw from the Space Summit in Paris. The White House has also launched a series of trade spats.
In addition to Whitaker’s comments, the US mission to NATO issued a statement saying the US would systematically dismantle the ICC’s capabilities and called for steps to withdraw from the Rome Statute. It also called on allies to assess the risks posed by the ICC to their countries, publicly condemn the court’s abuse of power and end support for the ICC. The document says the ICC’s charade must be ended immediately and permanently. Although NATO is not a signatory to the Rome Statute, all alliance members except Turkey and the US have ratified it.
Opposition to the ICC was launched this summer by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio,
who accused the court of undermining US sovereignty. He said on the 13th of July that the ICC and its friends were waging war on the US, not with bullets or missiles, but with the force of statutes and so-called international law. Rubio added that if the court believes it can take away US sovereignty, Americans will show the extent of their resolve.
The ICC was established in 2002 to try individuals accused of the most serious international crimes, including genocide and war crimes. The last investigation against US officials was launched in 2020, when the ICC opened a case into alleged war crimes committed by US soldiers in Afghanistan. The case lost priority a year later. The ICC is now facing calls to investigate US attacks on boats in the Caribbean, which the Americans say are part of a fight against drug trafficking.
The US campaign marks a sensitive moment for NATO. The alliance has been strained by the refusal of many European countries to join Trump’s war on Iran, drawing Trump’s ire. Washington also rattled the alliance when Trump threatened to take over the Danish territory of Greenland. The alliance managed to bridge the gap at an annual summit in Ankara, but just days later, the US demand to dissolve the ICC renewed tensions. One NATO diplomat said Whitaker’s comments were “quite shocking,” while another added that they were “disappointing.”
Diplomats said that in response to Whitaker’s remarks,
France and the Netherlands defended the ICC and made it clear that they opposed the court’s dissolution.
The US delegation to NATO did not respond to a request for comment. The French delegation declined to comment on the situation, but stressed its support for the ICC. The Dutch delegation referred to the country’s Foreign Minister Tom Berendsen as saying that the Netherlands fully supports the ICC.
American envoys also spoke of the dual position of European countries. The US State Department said it was determined to closely monitor countries that refuse to “reject the ICC’s false authority” while relying on US assistance. In August, Washington imposed sanctions on top officials of the ICC.
An ICC spokesman said the court remains focused on the independent and unbiased exercise of its mandate, as set out in the Rome Statute, to protect victims and ensure justice.
The campaign against the ICC comes against the backdrop of other US efforts. Washington is trying to get Canada and Europe to take greater responsibility for their own defense. A survey sent to NATO countries in August, asking for their opinions on US foreign policy, including in the Middle East, is being seen as an effort to force them to align with US views in exchange for defense assistance.
Read also: Trump puts Iceland under US flag; US ambassador summoned for talks

articles.title: Trump: Iran war will end immediately after midterm elections
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump announced on the 9th of September that the Iran War will end immediately after the midterm elections, and oil prices will plummet, writes Politico.
Trump said that Iranian leaders are deliberately escalating the conflict to undermine Republican positions in the upcoming midterm elections in November. On the way to the Texas Republican convention, the president told reporters that he thinks the war will end immediately after the elections. He argued that Iran will not be able to hold out much longer, and that Tehran is desperately trying to influence the midterm elections so that a nice, weak group of people can come to power in the United States, who will leave the Iranians alone and allow them to build nuclear weapons.
The prediction that the war will drag on for another two months means that Republican candidates will have to continue to deal with the political turmoil caused by the conflict and its impact on the cost of living.
Republicans have long worried that the economic impact of the Iran war could cost the party its majority
in the House of Representatives and possibly the Senate.
Trump’s comments came at a time when fuel prices have risen to record levels. The cost of energy has pushed up the prices of everyday goods, including food, and is increasing concerns about inflation and voter anger. The US president has promised that fuel prices will fall by half after the midterm elections.
The US and Iran have stepped up their attacks in recent days, and Trump has said he no longer intends to end the fighting through negotiations. He said he had initially wanted to make a deal, but now everything has gone too far and Tehran has too little left, so the path to negotiations is out of the question. Talks are still possible, but that is not what the Americans are planning.

articles.title: Pollard says he does not want kit that fails in Ukraine
articles.body:
Equipment that would not survive the war in Ukraine has no place in the British armed forces, the Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry has told an audience of financiers and defence firms at Mansion House, in a speech setting out how the government intends to bring private capital into defence.
Luke Pollard was speaking on Tuesday at an event hosted by the Lady Mayor, ahead of remarks by the Ukrainian Ambassador, and used the address to announce a Defence Finance Investment Strategy to follow the autumn budget along with a defence investment summit in December.
Warning that Britain must “discard the warm comfort blanket that we are used to, of polishing old things and pretending that that will protect us”, he put the test in a single sentence: “If our technology and kit will not work in Ukraine, I do not want it in our armed forces.”
That, he argued, opens the door to “new technology, new thinking, new weapons”, and to designing for “the conflicts of today and the battles of tomorrow”.
“The way that the United Kingdom would now fight is fundamentally different today than it was at the point when Putin launched his full-scale invasion of Ukraine only those four and a half years ago,” he told the room, adding that learning from Ukraine means changing how Britain itself operates.
Finding, funding and firing up
Much of the speech turned on speed, and on where the useful ideas are now coming from. Many of the most critical advances in defence, in the minister’s account, are emerging from technology startups and scale-ups, agile businesses “seizing the opportunities on offer and driving change at speed”. The challenge he set the room was framed as a question. “How can we get better at finding, funding and firing up the most creative minds and enterprise to get the best technology into the hands of our armed forces and those of our allies as fast as possible?”
He was unsparing about the position two years ago, describing a defence programme that was “to be honest and to be frank, unfit to counter the dangers that we now face”. Industry, he suggested, needs no reminding. “Those who work in our supply chains know how painfully slow, wasteful and costly the procurement the MOD previously undertook was,” he said, singling out small businesses and scale-ups with good products who “struggled sometimes to find the right buyer within the MOD”.
Small firms
Against that, Pollard set out the machinery now in place: a new National Armaments Director in Rupert Pearce, recruited from a FTSE 100 company and bringing what the minister called a new corporate approach and energy to procurement; the Defence Office for Small Business Growth, established to cut red tape and remove obstacles to entry; and an SME Action Plan published so the department can be held to account for the change.
The headline commitment is a 50 per cent increase in departmental spending with medium and small firms by summer 2028, which the minister described as “moving an extra two and a half billion pounds into the pockets of SMEs by changing the way we procure”.
Regional defence and security clusters have proved successful enough that more regions are developing them, he said, creating local routes that bring together major suppliers, devolved and local government, and giving investors a forum in which to meet them.
Bringing in the City
Running through the address was an argument that public money alone will not build the capacity required in the time available, however welcome rising budgets are. “As a defence minister, of course, I would like more defence spending,” he said.
“But it’s not just from the taxpayer that there’s opportunities for investing in defence. It’s how you crowd in private capital, how you use the institutions, the networks, the structures of the City of London and the UK’s place at the heart of global financial trade, to bring more private capital into defence, creating more good jobs and more deterrence.”
Waiting was not, in his view, an option: “In a more dangerous world, we need to build more capacity now, rather than just wait for the increase in defence money that we know is coming over the next 10 years.”
Whether the two sides can understand one another is a separate problem, and one he acknowledged. “There’s a risk that we sometimes speak past each other,” he said, arguing that a shared language and shared data would improve the department’s ability to deliver. The Defence Investment Unit announced in the Defence Investment Plan is meant to close that gap, giving investors a clearer interface with the department while bringing financial expertise in to turn priorities into market-facing propositions.
Companies already through the door
To show the approach producing results rather than remaining theoretical, the minister turned to firms that have already taken the route.
Thirteen British startups won contracts of up to £4 million in May under the Defence Unicorn Fund programme. Among them was Kraken Technologies, which builds maritime uncrewed surface vessels and has since raised $175 million in a Series B round on the back of a $1 billion valuation. Green Jets, one of three firms selected to develop a low-cost drone interceptor, has also secured significant funding. Both drew money from the National Security Strategic Investment Fund and the NATO Innovation Fund, with the British Business Bank financing Kraken as well.
JET Connectivity, a small business building 5G and 6G communications tools, was the only British firm admitted to the NATO DIANA mission track programme this year from more than three and a half thousand participants, which Mr Pollard called “fantastic recognition of British innovation at its best” while adding that it is “just the tip of the iceberg”.
There was a moment of self-deprecation over how the language has shifted under the current Prime Minister, with the Minister saying, “I used to be incentivised by the MOD press office to say defence is an engine for growth in all my interviews,” he told the audience. “With Andy Burnham in Downing Street I now say re-industrialisation, but the fundamental truth is there. Investment in defence creates good jobs. It provides opportunities in particular for our young people and we should be unafraid and unapologetic of saying that truth loudly.”
His closing argument was that none of this rests with his department alone, describing defence as “a whole of society endeavour, a whole of government endeavour” which the Ministry of Defence must lead but cannot deliver by itself.
He finished on deterrence, and on what follows if it does not hold, saying “That’s why increasing our deterrence matters with new technologies. But if deterrence fails, we must be ready to fight, and we must be ready to win.”
